Add a component to the grid

A new encoder or stage enters the grid by being registered. Give it a preset if its options cannot be guessed (Compose and probe), probe its cells and regenerate. tests/unit/test_combine_grid.py fails until every cell of a registered component has a record.

python -m tools.probe_grid run --only 'encoder/*/MyEncoder' 'stage/*/*/my-preset'
python -m tools.probe_grid export
python -m tools.make_combination_docs

docs.title: Operators and their backends
docs.text:
grasppanda.ops holds the geometric operators the models are built from. Each has a pure-PyTorch reference implementation that runs on any device and defines the result. Four of them can also run on optional compiled kernels (C++/OpenMP and CUDA), which are used only where they return exactly what the reference returns.

Nothing on this page is needed to use GraspPanda: after a plain pip install without a compiler every operator runs on the reference. The kernels make inference and training faster; they never change a result.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
The conventions are part of the contract: which point wins a tie decides which seeds a checkpoint sees, so a ported checkpoint only reproduces if they are kept.

Operator Result Rules a backend must reproduce furthest_point_sample(points, num_samples, skip_near_origin, tie_break) (B, num_samples) indices The first sample is index 0. The squared distance is x² + y² + z² added left to right. tie_break="lowest_index" takes the first of several equally far points; "pointnet2_cuda" takes the one the PointNet++ CUDA kernel takes (bit-reversed thread id, then index, with min(512, 2^⌊log₂N⌋) threads). skip_near_origin never picks a point with squared norm ≤ 1e-3 after the first. ball_query(query, support, radius, nsample) (B, M, nsample) indices, (B, M) hit counts Strictly inside: d² < radius². The first nsample hits in index order; missing slots repeat the first hit; a query without hits returns index 0 in every slot and a count of 0. cylinder_query(query, support, rotation, radius, hmin, hmax, nsample) as ball_query With d = Rᵀ(p − q): hmin < d.x < hmax and d.y² + d.z² < radius², all strict; the axis is column 0 of rotation. Same ordering and padding. knn(query, support, k) (B, M, k) distances and indices Ascending Euclidean distance; equidistant neighbours in index order (a stable sort); indices start at 0.

three_interpolate, inverse_distance_weights, voxelize, grasp_nms, the view templates and the serialisation codes have a single implementation.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
Backend What runs When reference The pure-PyTorch operator. Always available. compiled The kernels of grasppanda._ops. A library has been built and its self-check passed on the device. Selecting it explicitly is an error otherwise. auto (default) compiled where it is available and passed its self-check, else reference.

The kernels take float32 tensors on a CPU or a CUDA device. Other floating types always run the reference, as does knn when gradients are requested or k > 64, and cylinder_query under autocast or with TF32 matrix products (see below).

docs.title: What "identical" means, and how it is ensured
docs.text:
A kernel has to return the same integers as the reference for every input, and the same distances bit for bit. That is checked three times: by construction, at run time on the first call on a device, and in the test suite.

The three checks
  1. By construction. Every kernel expression mirrors one expression of the reference (grasppanda/_ops/src/common.h):
  2. no fused multiply-add: a fused a·b + c rounds once where PyTorch rounds twice (-ffp-contract=off on the host, __fmul_rn / __fadd_rn on CUDA);
  3. three-term sums in PyTorch's order. Where the reference spells the order out (furthest point sampling) so do the kernels. Where it calls sum(-1) (ball query, kNN) PyTorch adds left to right on the CPU but (x + z) + y on CUDA, and the kernels follow the device;
  4. thresholds are rounded to float32 the way PyTorch rounds a Python number that is compared with a float32 tensor;
  5. the root of a kNN distance is taken by PyTorch, not by the kernel: PyTorch's float32 square root on the CPU is accurate to one unit in the last place but is not the correctly rounded one (it differed in 18 % of a million random values);
  6. NaN and infinite coordinates behave as in torch.minimum, argmax and sort.
  7. At run time. The first time an operator runs on a device, its kernel is compared with the reference on small random and lattice clouds (ties, repeated points, empty and oversized neighbourhoods, points exactly on a surface), and the kernels' squared distances are compared with PyTorch's bit for bit. A kernel that differs is not used; one log line says so.
  8. In the test-suite. tests/unit/test_ops.py runs every oracle test on both backends; tests/unit/test_ops_equivalence.py and tests/integration/test_ops_cuda.py compare the backends on some 2 700 (CPU) and 4 700 (CUDA) randomized calls; the stage-parity tests of all six ported methods (tests/integration/test_<method>_parity.py) and the backbone-oracle tests run with the default backend, auto, so with the kernels wherever they are built.
The cylinder query

The reference rotates the offsets with a batched matrix product, that is through a BLAS whose rounding is not specified: MKL and cuBLAS return different last bits for the same input. No kernel can reproduce that. The cylinder kernel therefore computes its own rotated offset together with a bound on how far any correct float32 evaluation can be from it, and gives a verdict only for support points that are further from the cylinder surface than that bound. A query that meets a point inside the band before it is complete is handed back and answered by the reference itself. On recorded GraspNet-1Billion frames that happens to 2 of 4096 queries, on synthetic table tops to 13 of 65 536; the result is the reference's in every case.

Under autocast, or with torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32, the reference's matrix product runs in half precision or TF32. The kernel is then not used, because a float32 kernel would be more accurate than the reference and so disagree with it.

docs.title: Selecting a backend
docs.text:
In a config, per operator (fps, ball_query, cylinder_query, knn); operators that are not mentioned use auto:

runtime:
  ops: {fps: reference, knn: compiled}

The values are validated when the config is loaded. The selection is applied by grasppanda.ops.backends.configure, which is also the Python interface:

from grasppanda.ops import backends

backends.configure({"fps": "reference"})      # for this process
with backends.override(knn="reference"):       # temporarily, for a comparison
    ...
print(backends.report())

grasppanda train, test and infer apply runtime.ops when the run starts, and the backend each operator settled on is written to env.json in the run directory.

The environment variable GRASPPANDA_OPS overrides the configuration for one process, either with one backend for all operators or with a list:

GRASPPANDA_OPS=reference grasppanda test ...
GRASPPANDA_OPS=fps=reference,knn=compiled python my_script.py

grasppanda env --json and the env.json of every run record what each operator uses on the CPU and on the current CUDA device, and why if that is not what auto would prefer:

"ops": {
  "fps": {"requested": "auto", "cpu": "compiled", "cuda": "compiled"},
  "knn": {"requested": "auto", "cpu": "compiled", "cuda": "reference",
          "note": {"cuda": "the compiled library has no kernels for 'cuda' tensors: ..."}},
  "library": {"path": ".../grasppanda_ops_3a33d4588d6dade9.so", "cuda": false,
              "detail": "CPU kernels only (no CUDA 11.x toolkit ...)"}
}

docs.title: Building the kernels
docs.text:
The kernels are compiled the first time an operator needs them, with PyTorch's own extension tooling (torch.utils.cpp_extension), and cached. The build takes a few seconds: the kernels use no PyTorch headers and are called through ctypes.

Needed For Without it A C++ compiler ($CXX or c++) and ninja (pip install ninja) CPU kernels One log line per process; every operator runs on the reference. Selecting reference (GRASPPANDA_OPS=reference) silences it. A CUDA toolkit of the major version PyTorch was built with CUDA kernels CPU kernels only; operators on CUDA tensors run on the reference. 
python -m grasppanda._ops.build            # build if needed, then report
python -m grasppanda._ops.build --force    # rebuild, also after a recorded failure
python -m grasppanda._ops.build --cpu-only
Cache, toolkit, failures and forked workers
  • Cache. $GRASPPANDA_OPS_CACHE, by default <cache root>/ops ($GRASPPANDA_CACHE or ~/.cache/grasppanda). One directory per PyTorch version, variant (CPU or CUDA), platform and source revision, so several environments share a cache without clashing and an upgrade rebuilds. Nothing compiled is ever part of the package.
  • Toolkit. $CUDA_HOME, nvcc on the path and /usr/local/cuda* are examined; a toolkit of exactly PyTorch's CUDA version wins, then any of the same major version. The kernels are compiled to PTX for the oldest GPU architecture PyTorch supports and specialised by the driver on first use, so one build serves every GPU of a machine and a build made on a login node serves its compute nodes. TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST overrides the architecture list as for any PyTorch extension.
  • Failures. A failed build is recorded with its log next to where the library would be, reported in one log line, and not retried until the compiler changes or --force is given. A failed CUDA build still yields the CPU kernels.
  • Never on first use. GRASPPANDA_OPS_BUILD=0 uses a library only if it is already built.
  • Forked workers run the CPU kernels on one thread (GNU OpenMP does not survive a fork); the parent uses torch.get_num_threads().

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
On synthetic table-top clouds the kernels made the four operators 4 to 62 times faster on the GPU of the measurements and 5 to 250 times on its CPU (tools/bench_ops.py). End to end, two pipelines were timed on that GPU: the forward pass of the PointNet++ encoder of GraspNet-baseline (4.2 to 4.3 times faster) and GSNet.predict, the only whole model timed (2.6 to 3.3 times). The other five methods were not timed end to end.

How it was measured

docs.title: Changing an operator or adding a kernel
docs.text:
• The reference comes first. Change behaviour there, with an oracle test written out in tests/unit/test_ops.py.
  • A kernel is accepted when it returns identical integers and bit-identical distances on tests/unit/test_ops_equivalence.py and tests/integration/test_ops_cuda.py, and when the stage-parity tests of the six methods and the backbone oracle tests pass with it as default. Add the cases your change makes interesting to the randomized comparisons, and a self-check to grasppanda/ops/backends.py.
  • Where the reference goes through arithmetic that cannot be mirrored (a BLAS, a library function that is not correctly rounded), let PyTorch compute that part, or decide only what is certain and hand the rest back, as the cylinder query does.

docs.title: Swap rules
docs.text:
Seed-based · 5 methods

This page covers the seed-based skeleton: GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp, which share the stages scene encoder → seed proposal → view → assigner → grouper → head bundle. HGGD is a family of its own, whose own slot is the image encoder; post-processing and the training recipe swap under every method.

Replacing one stage is one line. This page says which replacements the config check accepts, why it refuses the others, and which look harmless and are not; whether an accepted swap trains on real frames is on Does it run?. The tables are generated from the contract rules and every cell is exercised by tests/unit/test_swap_matrix.py.

docs.title: The one-line swap
docs.text:
grasppanda compose writes a checked config and inserts an adapter where the rules ask for one:

grasppanda compose \
    economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set backbone=ptv3
grasppanda compose \
    graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --set backbone=ptv3

The same encoder fits EconomicGrasp as it is. Under GraspNet-baseline, compose wraps it in FurthestPointSubsample and says so, because that method's proposal reads features on a sub-sample. A config written by hand without the adapter stops at the config check, before a dataset is opened, with the fix.

The refusal, and the same swap written by hand 
$ grasppanda print-config \
      graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e --check \
      --opts "model.backbone={type: PTv3, in_channels: 3, grid_size: 0.005}"
✗ 1 config problem in configs/graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e.yaml

  model
    SubsampledSeeds requires 'subsampled' scene features, but PTv3 returns 'dense' ones (one
    feature per scene point). Choose a proposal that selects seeds from dense features
    (GraspnessFPS, SampledSeeds, ScoredSeeds), or wrap the backbone in the explicit adapter
    `{type: FurthestPointSubsample, backbone: {...}}`, which keeps the features of a
    furthest-point subsample.

Under EconomicGrasp the same line passes. In a file:

_base_: [../economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e.yaml]
model:
  backbone: {type: PTv3, in_channels: 3, grid_size: 0.005}   # the options of the old type are dropped

docs.title: What the checker compares
docs.text:
Each stage declares a contract as class attributes, and the rules compare them before anything is built. They belong to the skeleton: the verdict is the same under every seed-based detector type (GraspNetBaseline, GSNet, ScaleBalancedGrasp, EconomicGrasp; FineGrasp is built as an EconomicGrasp detector), and the same for a YAML file or DETECTORS.build(...) in Python.

The rules: what each compares, and why it exists Rule Compares Why it exists Kind of refusal Where features live backbone.output with proposal.requires Features on every scene point and features on a subsample are different objects. Converting is a learned or a sampling step that changes the model, so it is a component you write down, never an interpolation behind your back. fixed-by-compose: the encoder adapter Feature axes grouper.out_axes with head.in_axes A crop with a depth axis and one without feed different heads. An axis is never added or squeezed implicitly: an axis adapter is a component you write down (DepthEmbedGroup repeats a crop over the depth bins with a learned embedding of the bin, as Scale-Balanced-Grasp repeats its seed feature; DepthPoolGroup takes the maximum over the bins). fixed-by-compose: the axis adapter. structural for an axis adapter under the head of the other family; not-implemented for a scene-support crop without a depth axis under a head with one (no adapter repeats a scene crop) Label set assigner.label_format with head.label_format and view.label_formats Dense grids (48 grasps per point and view) and compact labels (one) are different supervision; a grid cannot be recovered from one grasp. structural. Compose writes the label set the head reads into the assigner and the data recipe, so the rule is met when a request sets an assigner of the other set, or a view stage that reads dense grids only under compact labels Fields of the matched labels view.needs_matched, head.needs_matched with assigner.optional_outputs A stage that reads an optional field needs the assigner option that produces it. The error names the option. fixed-by-compose: the option; structural when the assigner never returns the field Seed weights assigner.optional_outputs["weight"] with applies_seed_weights of view stage and head Every shipped view stage and head bundle applies a weight per seed: each of its losses is the weighted mean over its supervised entries, every entry weighted by its seed. A stage that does not would train unweighted next to a weighted assigner. not a refusal: a warning in the report of grasppanda compose and when the model is built Seed scores seed_scores of proposal and view stage; head.required_seed_scores(options) One owner per score (objectness cannot be predicted and supervised twice), and a score the decoder multiplies in must be predicted by some stage. fixed-by-compose where a stage has the option: a scoring proposal predicts graspness only (ScoredSeeds with select_by: graspness_only), the head decodes without the score (OperationHead with score_decode: score_x_tolerance). structural where it has none: a proposal that selects its seeds by objectness Depth bins len(grouper.hmax) with head.num_depth One crop per depth bin of the head. not-a-combination One score definition score_target, max_friction of view stage and head Only when both use the definition of grasppanda.models.heads.friction: the view target is the best grasp score of a view. not-a-combination Loss terms loss_terms of a stage with accepts of the loss in it A classification loss on a regression term, or a loss that scores a set as a whole (DiceLoss) where a weight per element arrives, is not the same supervision under another name. structural

docs.title: Why a pair is refused
docs.text:
Every refusal carries a kind: a property of the components, or of what the toolbox implements today. grasppanda compose and the explorer use the same words:

  • incompatible by design (structural): the components cannot work together whatever their options (two label sets, two owners of one score, a classification loss on a regression term).
  • not supported yet (not-implemented): the combination makes sense, but the code that joins the two parts does not exist yet; the message names what would lift it.
  • needs a setting compose adds (fixed-by-compose): an adapter or an option lifts it, and grasppanda compose inserts or sets it and says so.
  • needs a preset's settings (not-a-combination): the components fit, but the config does not state them fully (a missing option, or two options that disagree).
  • needs your consent (policy): model code from a hub repository runs only with accept_remote_code: true.
What compose lifts by itself

Besides the encoder adapters and the projected grouper: the axis adapter between grouper and head; the assigner options a stage reads; the graspness-only option of a scoring proposal next to ObjectnessViewStage; the decode option of a head whose score no stage predicts; and the label set of a head bundle, written into the assigner and the data recipe (--set labels=dense|compact asks for it in so many words). Each is one sentence in its report and in the header of the composed file. A data recipe it does not rewrite gets the exact --set, --unset and --opts that would, in the report (Compose and probe). Its --json report lists the kinds in refusal_kinds, in the order of refusal.

docs.title: Encoders
docs.text:
29 registered scene encoders: 23 return dense features, 6 return subsampled features. Every one passes the contract under every seed-based method: as it is where its output is what the method's proposal needs, otherwise inside the adapter that grasppanda compose inserts (FeaturePropagation or FurthestPointSubsample).

Every encoder under every method

✓: the features of model.backbone: {type: <Encoder>} live where the proposal of the method needs them. in Adapter: the bare swap is refused with a message that names the adapter; model.backbone: {type: <Adapter>, backbone: {type: <Encoder>}} passes that rule.

Adapters: FeaturePropagation turns any encoder into a dense one; FurthestPointSubsample turns any encoder into a subsampled one.

Width is the number of channels the encoder returns with its constructor defaults, as it declares it (Backbone.output_channels); (out_channels) marks an encoder that has an option of that name to set it. The other stages take whatever width arrives, with these exceptions among the methods as shipped: Scale-Balanced-Grasp needs 256 channels (DepthCylinderGroup adds the seed features to its crop features). An encoder of another width is refused there by the config check, with both numbers and the ways out; grasppanda compose takes one of them by itself (the encoder's out_channels, or the projected variant of the grouper). once built: the width follows from a library model or a layout that only the constructor resolves, so the check builds the encoder once, without released weights.

What the two adapters change: they are the only bridges, and never silent
  • FeaturePropagation (subsampled → dense) invents features for points the encoder never looked at: inverse-distance interpolation over the three nearest kept points, then a shared MLP. A graspness head then scores every scene point from features that carry the resolution of the subsample (1024 points with the GraspNet-baseline layout).
  • FurthestPointSubsample (dense → subsampled) decides which points can become grasps. It samples the scene coordinates, so the seeds are spread evenly over the cloud, table included, where GraspnessFPS spreads them over the points predicted graspable. With the same sampling rules it keeps exactly the points PointNet2 ends on, in the same order (tests/unit/test_backbone_subsample.py): swapping PointNet2 for a wrapped dense encoder changes the features of the seeds and leaves the seeds where they were.

docs.title: What an encoder swap changes
docs.text:
The contract says where features live, not what a feature has seen: the unit of length, the receptive field and the recipe move with the encoder.

The defaults of each encoder, and what to re-tune first

These are the constructor defaults, which is what a bare {type: ...} gives you:

Encoder Unit of length What sets the receptive field Seeds under its method Re-tune first SparseUNet14 voxel_size, 5 mm Four stride-2 stages: the coarsest voxel is 16 × the grid, 8 cm at 5 mm 1024 by GraspnessFPS from predicted graspness — (reference of GSNet, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp) SpUNet grid_size, default 2 cm (ScanNet rooms) The same four stride-2 stages, with 2-3-4-6 residual blocks where SparseUNet14 has one: more 3³ convolutions per level, so a feature reaches further in voxels as above grid_size; out_channels (default 20, class scores); in_channels (default 6); learning rate (the training check lost most seeds in two iterations at 1e-3) PTv3 grid_size, default 2 cm (ScanNet rooms) Four stride-2 poolings, and attention over patches of 1024 serialised voxels: counted in points, not in metres as above grid_size (0.005, the unit of the sparse-U-Net methods); enc_patch_size / dec_patch_size if clouds are small; learning rate and schedule PTv3Sonata, PTv3Utonia grid_size, default 2 cm / 1 cm As PTv3, encoder only: dense features are the pooled stages copied back, no learned decoder as above everything under Traps, items 2 and 3 LitePT grid_size, default 2 cm (ScanNet rooms) 3³ sparse convolutions in the three finest stages, attention only in the two coarsest (8 × and 16 × the grid). At 5 mm a tabletop frame is a few hundred voxels there, fewer than one patch of 1024: attention is global as above grid_size; in_channels (default 6); drop_path (0.3, for long schedules); the 72-channel output OACNNs grid_size, default 2 cm (ScanNet rooms) Four stride-2 stages of 3³ sparse convolutions, plus adaptive pooling grids counted in cells (point_grid_size): the 8 to 16 cells of the first stage are 0.32 to 0.64 m at 2 cm and 0.08 to 0.16 m at 5 mm as above grid_size; point_grid_size; out_channels (default 20, class scores); in_channels (default 9); learning rate (the training check lost its seeds for three iterations at 1e-3) PointNeXt radius, default 0.1 m doubling per stage (S3DIS rooms) Ball radii per stage; stride 4 per stage as above radius (the GraspNet-baseline layout starts at 0.04 m); in_channels (default 4) PointNet2Dense radii, default 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.8 m (rooms) Ball radii and the points kept per level (1024 / 256 / 64 / 16) as above npoints, radii PointNet2 radii, 0.04 / 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.3 m Ball radii; 2048 / 1024 / 512 / 256 points the 1024 points of its second level, by furthest point sampling of the scene — (reference of GraspNet-baseline) PointNet2Transformer radii, 0.04 / 0.1 m Two levels, each with attention over 16 nearest points as above — (reference of Scale-Balanced-Grasp)

What follows from a different receptive field or seed set, whichever encoder causes it:

  • Label statistics move. The head is trained on the seeds that reach it. GSNet normalises score targets with the extrema of the batch (head.score_target: log_friction_batch_norm); EconomicGrasp supervises only seeds within 5 mm of a label point (assigner.max_match_distance), so an encoder that shifts where seeds land changes how many seeds are supervised at all (metric/supervised_seeds in the log); Scale-Balanced-Grasp weights seeds by a width histogram of the training labels.
  • The recipe was tuned for the reference encoder. Learning rate, schedule, batch size and point budget in configs/_base_/schedules/ are the authors' values for their encoder. They are a starting point for another one, not a claim.
  • Channel widths are injected, and checked when the model is built. The proposal, view stage and grouper take the encoder's out_channels. One stage needs two widths to be equal: DepthCylinderGroup with seed_residual: gated (Scale-Balanced-Grasp) adds seed features to crop features. The error names both numbers and the three ways out; grasppanda train reaches it within seconds, print-config --check does not build the model.

  • View stage. TemplateViewStage samples the training view from its own scores (train_selection: multinomial) and reads either label set. ObjectnessViewStage takes the arg-max in both modes, predicts objectness with the views and reads two optional fields of dense labels.
  • Grouper. A seeds-support crop gathers at most the other seeds of the frame, with their learned features. A scene-support crop gathers raw coordinates of the whole cloud and no learned feature. They are not one crop at two resolutions, and only the second has a depth axis.

SWADHead and OperationHead read dense label grids, EconomicHead compact labels, which the dataset must serve (compact_labels: in the dataset config, grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --compact-labels); OperationHead also needs the tolerance asset. grasppanda compose writes the label set of the head into the assigner and the data recipe.

docs.title: Every legal set of stages
docs.text:
The contracts accept 3014 of 17920 combinations of the registered stage classes (an assigner counts twice when it has options that switch optional fields on, a proposal when it has an option that leaves a seed score to the view stage). By head bundle and kind of encoder output:

Head bundle dense encoder subsampled encoder Shipped by DecoupledGridHead 880 230 — EconomicHead 280 70 EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp OperationHead 352 92 GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp SWADHead 880 230 GSNet

Every set, one per line: stage_sets.json (the stage classes by index into variants; methods holds the set of each method as shipped). A sample of them was trained on real frames: Sets of stages.

The detector type does not change which sets are legal. It names the method whose reference behaviour the config claims to follow; a set that is no reference model is a new model, whatever it is called.

Why HGGD is not in these tables

HGGD is not built on the seed-based skeleton. It proposes partial grasps from an image heat-map, has no view stage and no approach-aligned crop, and none of its stages fills a slot above; putting a seed-based stage into it, or its heat-map proposal into a seed-based detector, is not a swap the registries can express. Its image encoder is a slot of its own (Image encoders); its other parts are options of the detector (grasppanda components HGGD). Its "ResNet-34" is the block layout only, with a base width of 8 and four input channels, trained from scratch: a pretrained three-channel ResNet-34 is a different network with a different input.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
Swaps that pass every check above, or look as if they should, and are not what they seem. The numbers are stable: code comments and error messages refer to a trap by its number.

The eleven traps, by number

  1. An object-level pretrained encoder as scene encoder. Point-BERT, Point-MAE, ReCon, Uni3D were pretrained to turn one normalised object of a few thousand points into patch tokens or a single vector. Their architectures are registered here (PointViT, PointMamba, Uni3D) as sub-sampling scene encoders over patch tokens, built with random weights: features live on the token centres, not on every point. Their released weights are an initialisation from single objects, not scene features, and scaling the scene to an object's size changes the metres the cylinder radii and depth bins are written in (each preset says what it chose).

  2. “PTv3 with Sonata, Concerto or Utonia weights” as “PTv3”. The released self-supervised checkpoints are encoder-only, have other depths and widths, expect nine input channels (coordinates, colour, normal; zeros where missing) and were trained on a 2 cm or rescaled grid. They load into PTv3Sonata / PTv3Utonia, not into PTv3; loading one into the wrong type fails on the key report. Changing only a weight path changes all of the above.

  3. Keeping the grid when changing the encoder, or changing it freely. The grid is the encoder's unit of length. The same layer sees a fourfold different piece of the scene at 5 mm and at 2 cm. Pretrained weights are tied to the grid they were trained on; a model trained from scratch is tied to the grid it was trained at. No contract checks this: grid_size, voxel_size and radii are yours to set, and the defaults of room-scale encoders are wrong for a tabletop (see What an encoder swap changes).

  4. One PointNet++ for another. Seeds come from furthest point sampling and neighbours from ball queries; the start index, the tie rule and the fill order differ between implementations, so two "identical" networks hand different seeds to the head. Here they are options with names (fps_tie_break, fps_skip_near_origin); an author checkpoint reproduces only with the author's values.

  5. A head trained under one proposal, reused under another. Targets depend on which seeds reach the head (see Label statistics move). Retrain the head, and recompute any prior such as the scale-balance histogram.

  6. A seed-support grouper for a scene-support grouper “at another resolution”. See Reading the tables, Grouper; the contracts refuse the pair with the wrong head.

  7. View classification replaced by “the same thing with regression”. The label files are indexed by the 300 template views. Regressing the direction is available (direction-regression, direction-vmf), but the regressed direction is snapped to that lattice for the label lookup, so its targets still come from the 300 label views, and its training crops use the frame of the snapped view while inference uses the regressed one (up to 9 degrees apart).

  8. Scale-balanced weights on a model that does not read them. Found by the swap matrix. ScaleBalancedAssigner with SWADHead or TemplateViewStage used to build, train and report losses while the weights were dropped. Every shipped view stage and head bundle now applies MatchedLabels.weight (a weighted mean over its supervised entries); a stage of your own that does not is reported as a warning.

  9. A collision filter “on” compared across methods, and scores treated as one quantity. Post-processors are swappable in evaluation.variants, and every result is reported with and without them. But GSNet's score is an unbounded regressed value, EconomicGrasp's a weighted sum of raw logits and OperationHead's a product with a tolerance (score_kind in Registered classes). Anything that thresholds or fuses scores must be fitted per head bundle.

  10. A checkpoint carried across a swap. See Architecture, §8.3. Nothing claims a checkpoint is portable across components: runtime.load_from fails on missing, unexpected or mis-shaped keys and prints the report. Stages you did not swap keep their weights only if you load them deliberately (allow_weight_mismatch), and they were trained for the features of the old encoder.

  11. A weight file's licence inferred from its code. Sonata-family weights are CC BY-NC 4.0 under Apache-2.0 code. Using them makes the trained model non-commercial; Encoders checked against their authors' code lists each file.

docs.title: What is checked when
docs.text:
The config check runs before anything is built; model construction and the first batch check what only they can see. Never checked: whether the grid, the radii and the recipe suit your scenes, or whether the swap helps.

When each check runs, and how it fails When What How it fails grasppanda print-config <cfg> --check, and first thing in train / test Unknown keys and types; every rule of What the checker compares, with defaults resolved ConfigError listing all problems, each with the config path and the file that set it Model construction (train / test, seconds later) The same rules on the built stages; channel widths; values a constructor validates ContractError, ValueError or BuildError naming the component and the numbers First batch Shapes that depend on data: seeds per frame against the encoder's subsample, label views against the template, missing label assets ContractError naming both sides Never Whether grid_size, radii and the recipe suit your scenes; whether the swap helps —

docs.title: Ready-made swap configs
docs.text:
grasppanda compose writes a checked config for any combination, and grasppanda probe trains it for a few iterations on real frames (Compose and probe). configs/experimental/ holds a few encoder swaps written that way, with no AP attached, each stating what must be re-tuned and why (configs/experimental/README.md).

What the matrix test proves, and what it does not

tests/unit/test_swap_matrix.py runs on tiny synthetic scenes (two frames of 96 points, random dense and compact labels, a width histogram) on the CPU, with one tiny configuration per registered component. It proves that:

  • every registered scene encoder under every seed-based detector type either builds, trains one step with a gradient reaching the encoder and predicts, or is refused with the adapter by name, and the adapted model then does;
  • every grouper under every head bundle combines when the axes agree, and where they do not, the grouper inside its axis adapter trains and predicts, while a pair without an adapter is refused as structural or not-implemented;
  • every proposal under both kinds of encoder output does the same;
  • in the full product of proposals, view stages, assigners, groupers and head bundles under both kinds of encoder output, no set that passes the config check fails later: every accepted set trains one step and predicts under the barest and the strictest detector type, and every refused set is refused by the built detector too;
  • every head bundle applies a weight per seed as a weighted mean (uniform weights give the unweighted losses), the scoring proposal with select_by: graspness_only leaves objectness to the view stage that owns it, and OperationHead decodes without the objectness nobody predicts.

What it does not prove: that a combination learns, or anything about real frames. A cell of Does it run? is a probe on real frames; a synthetic probe of a composed config (grasppanda probe <config> --synthetic) is the same check as here at the sizes of the config.

docs.title: Adding a component to the matrix
docs.text:
A new stage is interchangeable when it says so in its contract and proves it in the matrix:

  1. declare the contract attributes of its slot (Registered classes, Add a component) plus status, source and, if needed, extras;
  2. add one tiny configuration to the tables of tests/unit/test_swap_matrix.py (the test fails until you do);
  3. run python -m tools.make_component_docs to regenerate the registered classes and this page.

docs.title: digest()
docs.text:
Hash of what the experiment is: resolved config minus run-location keys.

Defaults of GraspPanda's own schema and components are part of it, so a changed default changes the hash. Defaults of classes of an installed library (an optimizer or a scheduler of PyTorch named by class) are not: they differ between versions of the library, and the hash of one config must be the same on every machine. The environment a run used is recorded next to it (env.json).

docs.title: furthest_point_sample(points, num_samples, *, skip_near_origin=False, tie_break='lowest_index')
docs.text:
Iterative furthest point sampling.

The first sample is always index 0 and ties are resolved by a fixed rule, so the result is deterministic and the same on every device. Which points become seeds decides whether a ported checkpoint reproduces, so faster backends are held to exactly this behaviour (:mod:grasppanda.ops.backends).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default points Tensor

(B, N, 3) or (N, 3).

required num_samples int

Number of points to pick, at most N.

required skip_near_origin bool

Never pick points whose squared norm is ≤ 1e-3 (apart from index 0), as the widely used PointNet++ CUDA kernel does. Needed only for parity with checkpoints trained against that kernel.

False tie_break Literal['lowest_index', 'pointnet2_cuda']

Which point wins when several are equally far from the selected set. lowest_index takes the first. pointnet2_cuda reproduces the order of the PointNet++ CUDA kernel (bit-reversed thread id, then index; the kernel runs min(512, 2^floor(log2 N)) threads). Exact ties are not exotic: clouds from a depth camera lie on a lattice, and 3 of 64 sampled GraspNet-1Billion frames had one among their first 1024 samples.

'lowest_index'

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

(B, num_samples) or (num_samples,) indices into points.

docs.title: generalized_furthest_point_sample(coords, num_samples, *, feats=None, metric='concat', coord_weight=1.0, weights=None, start=None)
docs.text:
Furthest point sampling of one cloud under a feature distance and with point weights.

The generalisation the detection literature uses to make the sampler choose instead of only spread: a distance that includes features (F-FPS of 3DSSD) and a weight on the running distance of every point (S-FPS of SASA). Without features and weights it is :func:furthest_point_sample with tie_break="lowest_index". A picked point is never picked again, so the indices are distinct even on duplicated coordinates.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default coords Tensor

(N, 3) coordinates.

required num_samples int

Points to pick, at most N.

required feats Tensor | None

(N, C) features that enter the distance; None for coordinates only.

None metric Literal['concat', 'sum']

With features. concat: squared L2 distance of the concatenation [coord_weight * xyz, feats] (what the released 3DSSD code computes). sum: coord_weight * |Δxyz| + |Δfeats| with L2 norms (Eq. 1 of the 3DSSD paper, its λ being coord_weight).

'concat' coord_weight float

Weight of the coordinates against the features.

1.0 weights Tensor | None

(N,) non-negative weights; the next pick maximises weight × running distance. The running distance is the squared one unless metric="sum" (the convention of the released SASA kernel).

None start int | None

Index of the first pick. None: the heaviest point when weights are given (SASA), otherwise index 0.

None

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

(num_samples,) distinct indices into coords, in the order they were picked.

docs.title: two_vector_rotation(first, second)
docs.text:
Rotation whose first column is first and whose second lies towards second.

Gram-Schmidt on two free 3-vectors: first is normalised, second loses its component along it and is normalised, the third column is their cross product. This is the mapping of the 6-D rotation representation (Zhou et al., CVPR 2019), and, with the roles of the two vectors exchanged, how Contact-GraspNet builds a grasp frame from a predicted baseline and approach.

docs.title: grasppanda.registry
docs.text:
Component registries.

Every swappable piece of GraspPanda is a class registered in exactly one flat :class:Registry. A config node {type: Name, **kwargs} is resolved against the registry that owns the slot it sits in; the owner is decided by the parent's type annotation (Cfg[Backbone]), never by searching every registry for a name.

Design notes (see docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md §6):

  • Lookup is lazy: the first get imports every module below the registry's package, so adding a file is enough to register a component.
  • Duplicate names raise. A failed lookup lists close matches and says whether the name lives in a different registry.
  • Registered classes may not take **kwargs: every config key must be checkable against a signature before anything is constructed.

docs.title: CompactGraspLabels dataclass
docs.text:
The best grasp of every (annotated point, view) of one object instance in a frame.

The dense label set holds a grid of in-plane angles and depths per point and view (:class:~grasppanda.structures.ObjectGraspLabels). Here that grid is collapsed to its best cell, which leaves four small numbers per point and view; this is the "economic" supervision of EconomicGrasp. Points without any good grasp are absent.

Values are stored the way the label asset stores them, as small integers, and are turned into metric quantities by :meth:quality and :meth:metres. The integers travel through the data loader; only the rows a batch matches are ever converted.

Dense grasp annotations of one object instance in a frame.

The grids are stored in one of two ways. Dense: scores and widths (and, when present, collision and tolerance) are tensors. Deferred: deferred reads rows from the label store when they are asked for, and the four tensors are None. Code that consumes labels reads them through :func:gather_grids (many objects in one pass) or the gather_* methods (one object), which return the same values for both storages; :meth:dense turns deferred labels into tensors.

(P, V, A, D) gripper widths in metres.

(P, V, A, D) true where the grasp collides in this scene.

(P, V, A, D) grasp tolerance in metres: how far the grasp point may move over the object surface while the same grasp stays good. A derived label; None unless the dataset is configured to serve it.

docs.title: Observation dataclass
docs.text:
Everything available at inference time for a batch of frames.

predict(observation) gets this object and nothing else. Any input derived from ground truth must say so, either as a :class:Mask with that provenance or as an entry of provenance; it is then reported by :meth:gt_assisted and stamped on the results of the run.

Attributes:

Name Type Description keys list[SampleKey]

One :class:SampleKey per frame of the batch.

intrinsics Tensor | None

(B, 3, 3) camera matrices.

depth Tensor | None

(B, H, W) metres; zero where invalid.

rgb Tensor | None

(B, 3, H, W) in [0, 1].

points PointSet | None

Scene points the model consumes, camera frame, metres.

point_feats Tensor | None

(N, C) input features aligned with points.

full_points PointSet | None

The cloud before sub-sampling, for post-processors such as a collision filter. Never an input of the network.

masks dict[str, Mask]

Named per-point masks aligned with points (e.g. instance).

provenance dict[str, Provenance]

Where inputs that shaped this observation came from, by name. A workspace crop computed from ground-truth segmentation is recorded here as {"workspace": Provenance.GROUND_TRUTH}.

Per frame, the grasp labels of every object instance in it.

Named (N, ...) labels aligned with observation.points.

Method-specific targets, one list entry per frame. Compact grasp labels travel here under COMPACT_LABELS.

Points of a batch, concatenated, with an identity.

Attributes:

Name Type Description coords Tensor

(N, 3) coordinates in metres.

(B + 1,) boundaries; sample b owns coords[o[b]:o[b+1]]. None means a single sample.

Reference frame of the coordinates.

id of the set this one was sampled from, if any.

(N,) index into the parent when this set is a true subset.

Unique identity. Features are bound to it, so a feature tensor can never be silently reused with a different set.

docs.title: GraspPanda Architecture
docs.text:
Status Design record (v1.0), written before the implementation. It keeps the decisions and the reasons for them. Where the code, the guides or the evidence pages differ from it, they are authoritative. Date 2026-10-12 Scope Design for v1: single-view 6-DoF parallel-jaw grasp detection in cluttered scenes. Evidence Every claim about an upstream repository was read from source at the pinned commit listed in Appendix A. No model was trained, no checkpoint was loaded and no AP was measured while writing this document. AP numbers quoted here are author-reported unless marked otherwise.

Section numbers are kept as they were: docstrings in the code cite them (§5.2 to §11.2). Every section is folded; open the one you need.

Superseded since the record was written

  • §1 lists a web UI as out of scope. grasppanda explore now serves the combination explorer, a local web page that composes, compares and runs a method on one frame (Explorer).
  • §2, principle 7 ("share on second use"). The registries also hold options wrapped from papers and libraries that no shipped method uses, most scene encoders among them. Each was composed under every method it fits and, where accepted, probed on real frames; the few without a record say why (Evidence).
  • §4 and §8.2. Six methods are ported: five on the seed-based skeleton and HGGD. The dense-contact family (Contact-GraspNet) was not implemented. HGGD's image encoder is a registered slot (image_encoder); its other parts are options of the detector. grasppanda/combine/ (compose, probe, the measured records) and grasppanda/presets/ were added; tests live in tests/unit/ and tests/integration/.
  • §8 and Appendix A.2 were written with GSNet as the first user of the seed-based skeleton: the flow of §8.5, the constants of §8.6 and most examples are GSNet's. The skeleton now carries five methods on equal terms (GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp); which slots each method has is on Components.
  • §12.2 to §12.4. No command downloads weights or a sample subset: prepare builds assets from a dataset on disk, demo runs given weights on a frame or the built-in example scene, analyze reads result records, and infer writes GraspNet arrays only. compose, probe, components and explore were added. GraspInferencer takes a config and a weights file. First steps: Get started.
  • §13.3 and §13.4. No weights are published yet (Model zoo). The site is organised as Get started, Explorer, Methods, Components, Guides, Evidence and Reference.

docs.title: 1. Goals and scope
docs.text:
§1 in full

One line. GraspPanda is to 6-DoF grasp detection in clutter what MMDetection is to object detection: certified reproductions and controlled component-swap experiments, all scored by one pinned, official-equivalent evaluation.

Four requirements, and how the design answers each.

Requirement Design answer Dataset-driven A benchmark is a protocol: dataset version + split manifest + camera + allowed inputs + pinned evaluator (§11.3). Every result is stamped with its protocol id; only protocol-conformant runs enter the model zoo. GraspNet-1Billion first, GraspClutter6D second. Low-code One YAML file plus one command reproduces a method. First result within five commands after pip install (§12.4). More than reproduction Backbone, seed proposal, approach view, grouping, head bundle, loss, augmentation and post-processing are config slots with typed contracts (§8). An ablation is a base config plus an override. Professional Model zoo with provenance, docs site, CI, PyPI release on tag, changelog, citation file, brand assets (§13, §14).

v1 in scope. Single-view RGB-D or point-cloud input; 6-DoF parallel-jaw grasps; cluttered tabletop scenes; GraspNet-1Billion and GraspClutter6D.

Reserved, not implemented in v1 (the architecture leaves room, §8.7): multi-view fusion track (Generalizing-Grasp; own protocol and own leaderboard), suction (SuctionNet-1B), simulated clearing (pile/packed, GSR/DR).

Out of scope. Planar grasps, dexterous hands, object-centric datasets (ACRONYM, GraspGen), web UI, and wrapping upstream repositories in subprocesses as the core implementation.

docs.title: 2. Design principles
docs.text:
§2 in full

Each rule exists because the previous GraspPanda (v0.62) or an upstream codebase broke it.

  1. Depth before breadth. A method enters the model zoo only after it has been trained and evaluated inside this toolbox (§13.1). v0.62 had 39 method entries and no certified reproduction.
  2. Every number carries its provenance. Three classes, never mixed in one column: reported (paper/README), author-ckpt (author weights evaluated here), reproduced (trained here).
  3. Observation and supervision are separate objects. predict(observation) cannot reach ground truth. Any GT-derived input (workspace mask from GT segmentation, GT instance masks) is an explicit, named config attribute and is stamped on the result (§7.1).
  4. Slots have typed contracts. A swap is allowed only when contracts match. A mismatch is a config-check error with an explanation — never a silent interpolation, projection or axis squeeze (§8.3).
  5. One owner per constant. num_view, num_angle, num_depth, depth bins, gripper width, voxel size and seed count each live in exactly one object; everything else receives them by injection (§8.6).
  6. The head bundle is atomic. Head, target encoder, loss and decoder share one parameterization and are swapped as a unit (§8.4).
  7. Share on second use. A component becomes a public, registered slot only when two in-tree methods use it. Until then it stays private to its detector.
  8. Small core, optional weight. Core depends on torch, numpy and a few pure-Python packages. Sparse convolution, visualisation, logging backends and accelerated ops are extras. No sys.path edits, no top-level packages named pointnet2/knn/models/utils.
  9. A run is fully described by its snapshot. No behaviour is reachable only through a CLI flag (§5.6).
  10. Clean room. Upstream logic is studied; code is written here. No file is copied (§14.3).

docs.title: 3. Lessons from reference frameworks
docs.text:
§3 in full

Verified against source on 2026-10-12: PaddleSeg release/2.10, MMEngine main, Detectron2 main, Pointcept main.

Framework Borrow Avoid (with evidence) PaddleSeg YAML + _base_; every component is {type: Name, **kwargs} built recursively; a rule-based ConfigChecker that runs at load time; decorator registration; one-command train/val/predict. --opts only asserts that intermediate keys exist and then assigns the leaf unconditionally, so a misspelt leaf key silently creates a new entry (cvlibs/config.py:228-235). Top-level keys are read with dic.get, so unknown keys are ignored. The builder resolves a type by scanning all registries in order (cvlibs/builder.py:82-87), so equal names in two registries collide silently. Duplicate registration only warns and overwrites (cvlibs/manager.py:112-115). The checker mutates the config to sync num_classes (allow_update=True). Unbounded _base_ depth. Components register only if someone remembered to import them in __init__.py. Build errors are re-raised as RuntimeError(str(e)), dropping the traceback (builder.py:65-75). More than ten run settings exist only as CLI flags (--do_eval, --save_interval, --resume_model, --seed, --use_ema, --log_iters, --keep_checkpoint_max, … in tools/train.py). MMEngine Registry(locations=[...]) lazily imports its modules on first lookup; duplicate names raise unless force=True; custom_imports; _delete_; hook-based engine; dumping the resolved config. Dict merge keeps stale base keys when a child changes type unless the user remembers _delete_=True (config.py:_merge_a_into_b). No key validation: an unknown kwarg fails only inside a constructor, possibly hours into a job. A failed lookup returns None and the error offers no candidate names (registry/build_functions.py:98-106). Scope hierarchy and DefaultScope switching add a lot of machinery for a single-package toolbox. Python configs execute arbitrary code and exist in two dialects (text and lazy-import). {{_base_.x}} is substituted before child overrides apply, so overriding x does not propagate. runner.py is 2413 lines. Detectron2 tools/plain_train_net.py: a complete training loop in 221 readable lines. ShapeSpec: children are built with the parent-computed input shape instead of the user repeating channel counts. Instances: one typed container for predictions. yacs CfgNode requires every key of every component to be pre-declared in one central defaults.py. Pointcept Run snapshot: resolved config dumped into the experiment directory, code copied alongside (scripts/train.sh:87). Offset-based batching for variable-size point clouds. spconv/PTv3 integration patterns. The launcher executes the copied code via PYTHONPATH, so what runs is not what is installed. Config values are rewritten implicitly at load (data.train.loop = epoch // eval_epoch, num_worker=None → cpu_count(); engines/defaults.py:122,133).

Resulting choices: YAML with strict three-layer validation (§5.3), type-aware merge (§5.2), one flat registry family with lazy auto-import and nearest-name errors (§6), build-time injection instead of repeated channel counts (§6.3), a ~300-line trainer with hooks (§12.1), and a snapshot that records code without running from the copy (§5.6).

§4 in full 
GraspPanda/
├── configs/
│   ├── _base_/
│   │   ├── datasets/            graspnet1b_realsense.yaml, graspnet1b_kinect.yaml, graspclutter6d_d435.yaml
│   │   ├── models/              gsnet.yaml, economicgrasp.yaml, hggd.yaml, …   (full default model per method)
│   │   ├── schedules/           one file per training recipe
│   │   └── default_runtime.yaml
│   └── <method>/                README.md, metafile.yaml, <method>_<backbone>_<dataset>-<camera>_<schedule>.yaml
├── grasppanda/
│   ├── config/                  loader, schema, validation, cross-field checker, snapshot
│   ├── registry.py              Registry, build(), lazy auto-import, plugin discovery
│   ├── structures/              Observation, Supervision, PointSet, PointFeatures, SeedSet, ApproachSet,
│   │                            GroupFeatures, GraspGroup, Gripper, ReferenceFrame, SampleKey
│   ├── datasets/                manifest, derived-asset store, graspnet1b/, graspclutter6d/, samplers

│   │   ├── proposals/           graspness / objectness + FPS, OBS (HGGD's heat-map proposal stays in its detector until reused)
│   │   ├── views/               300-view classification, regression, anchors
│   │   ├── groupers/            cylinder crop: single / multi-scale / multi-depth
│   │   ├── assigners/           seed ↔ grasp-label matching shared by the GraspNet family
│   │   ├── heads/               head bundles: head + target encoder + loss + decoder
│   │   ├── losses/              primitive losses used inside stages
│   │   ├── postprocessors/      collision filter, grasp NMS, width clip, re-rankers
│   │   └── detectors/           GSNet, EconomicGrasp, HGGD, …
│   ├── ops/                     FPS, ball/cylinder query, kNN, grasp NMS: pure-PyTorch reference + optional backends

│   ├── _ops/                    compiled extension namespace (built only if a kernel proves necessary)
│   ├── evaluation/              graspnet1b/, graspclutter6d/, protocols/, result records, statistics
│   ├── engine/                  trainer, hooks, optim builders, checkpoint, distributed helpers
│   ├── apis/                    GraspInferencer and friends
│   ├── cli/                     `grasppanda` entry point, one module per sub-command
│   ├── hub/                     weight index, download, sha256 verification
│   ├── visualization/

├── tools/                       repo-only scripts: dist_train.sh, gen_model_zoo.py, make_parity_fixtures.py, convert_checkpoint.py
├── projects/                    example_project/ and experimental or third-party methods, each with a support-level badge
├── docs/                        MkDocs Material site; design/ holds this file
