docs.title: The four levels
docs.text:
A cell, one option under one method, is judged at four levels; each needs the one before it.

  • composes: the config check accepts the composed config.
  • runs: it trains on real frames without an error.
  • learns: its losses fall.
  • predicts: it ranks grasps: every frame has one, and the scores differ.
Exact definitions, and why a level can stay undecided
  • composes: the contract rules and the config check accept the composed config: grasppanda compose writes it (any verdict but refused). A refusal by policy is undecided (needs consent), and so is a request that is not a combination.
  • runs: the probe ran clean on real frames: the verdict runs or runs-empty. A runs-unstable probe counts as not running only when its repeat (repeat in the record: the same config, seed and schedule) was unstable too; without a repeat the level is undecided (unstable, not repeated); when the repeat ran clean the cell runs, and learns and predicts are read from the repeat. fails does not run.
  • learns: judge 2 only. Every loss term was active (reported, finite, not exactly 0) in at least 50 % of the iterations and fell by at least 5 % (fall = (first - mean of the last quarter) / |first| over its active iterations), and no term is flagged flat, rising or constant; a term that is 0 at the last iteration (zero_at_end) is judged on its active iterations. Every unit with trainable parameters received a gradient (no_gradient is empty) and every part changed (unchanged is empty).

  • predicts: judge 2 only. Every predicted frame has at least one grasp, and on every frame the smallest and the largest score differ (score_quantiles): a model whose scores collapsed to one value ranks nothing.

  • not checked: the record was judged by the first judge, which recorded neither the trend of the loss terms nor the scores of the predicted grasps.

  • unstable, not repeated: the probe was runs-unstable and has not been repeated: an unstable run counts as not running only when a second probe of the same config is unstable too.
  • needs consent: refused by a policy that waits for the user's consent (trust_remote_code needs accept_remote_code: true): a rule about this machine, not about the combination.
  • not a combination: the request names a component that lacks an option only a preset supplies: it is refused before any contract is compared, and is no combination.
  • not probed: the grid has the cell, but no record yet.
  • not reached by the method as shipped: the method as shipped, probed the same way, does not reach this level either (for example FineGrasp at the constant rate, whose fusion of crop scales gives every seed one feature in a short run, so every grasp gets one score): under that method the level says nothing about the option at this budget.

docs.title: Probe verdicts
docs.text:
• runs: built, trained on real frames with finite losses, and predicted grasps.
  • runs-empty: as runs, but no probed frame has a grasp.
  • runs-unstable: a loss or a weight became non-finite, or a part got no seed or no gradient.
  • fails: an exception after the config check had passed.
  • refused: the config check said no, with the fix; nothing was built.
  • wired: a synthetic scene only (no dataset): shows the stages connect, nothing else.
Exact definitions
  • runs: On real frames: the detector was built, every requested training iteration ran with finite losses and at least one real seed, every top-level part of the model that holds trainable parameters received a gradient in at least one iteration, the weights stayed finite, and prediction returned one valid grasp group for every probed frame, at least one of them with a grasp.
  • runs-empty: As runs, except that no probed frame has a grasp: prediction returned one valid grasp group for every probed frame and every group is empty. Every stage ran; a model trained for a few iterations often keeps no seed. A run that is also unstable is runs-unstable.
  • runs-unstable: On real frames: the detector was built, trained and predicted, but a loss or a weight became non-finite (a non-finite loss ends the training there), or an iteration had no real seed (no scene point passed the proposal, so only the proposal was trained), or no iteration supervised a seed, or a top-level part with trainable parameters received no gradient in any iteration, or fewer iterations ran or fewer frames were predicted than were asked for.
  • fails: An exception was raised after the config check had passed. The report names the phase (build, data, optimizer, loss, backward, step, hook, predict), the component it came from and the message.
  • refused: The config check refused the config (the same check as grasppanda print-config --check --for train). Nothing was built; the report carries the messages.
  • wired: No real frame was read. On a synthetic table-top scene with random labels the detector was built, back-propagated a loss through every stage and predicted. This shows that the stages connect; it says nothing about real data.

docs.title: Trains like shipped
docs.text:
Level 2: a swap that ran trains 250 iterations beside the shipped component, and their losses are compared term by term:

  • on a par: every comparable loss ends within the method's tolerance of its own component's.
  • worse: a comparable loss ends above that tolerance, or a part got no gradient.
  • not comparable: the option redefines every loss term.
  • diverging: a loss rises at the end, a value became non-finite, or no grasp was predicted.
  • did not train: the run did not finish (record value fails).

Level 2 needs runs, not learns: a term flat after 20 iterations can fall by iteration 250.

Exact definitions, and what level 2 leaves out
  • fails: the run did not finish: an exception, a crash, a timeout, or no real frame read. A run that died of GPU memory is not recorded (it says nothing about the config) and is run again.
  • no reference: the method as shipped has no finished run under the same settings: nothing to compare with.
  • diverging: a loss term is rising over the last half of the run (see rising), a loss or a weight became non-finite, or no grasp was predicted on any of the 4 frames while the method as shipped predicts some.
  • worse: not diverging, and a comparable loss term ends above the tolerance of the method times the shipped method's (mean of the last 25 iterations), or a part of the model that holds trainable parameters received no gradient in any iteration.
  • not comparable: not diverging, nothing worse, but the cell changes the definition of every term the method as shipped has: there is no term to compare.
  • on a par: every comparable loss term ends within the tolerance of the method, at least one term is comparable, nothing rises, every value is finite and a frame has a grasp. A term far below the shipped method's is reported (lower), not judged.

Not compared, on every page:

  • Post-processing: post-processing trains nothing: it changes predictions, not the training.
  • Schedules: level 2 holds the schedule of the method as shipped fixed (a constant rate; FineGrasp: its own warm-up), so a schedule swap is not compared.
  • A cell on a schedule of its own (a recipe preset with a scheduler, a schedule-free optimizer): it trained on a schedule of its own, not on that of the method as shipped.
  • A swap that did not run: the swap did not run at level 1; it stays named.

docs.title: Why a request is refused
docs.text:
• incompatible by design (structural): a genuine incompatibility.
  • not supported yet (not-implemented): the combination makes sense, but the code that joins the two parts does not exist yet.
  • needs a setting compose adds (fixed-by-compose): an adapter or an option lifts it, and grasppanda compose inserts or sets it.
  • needs a preset's settings (not-a-combination): the components fit, but this config does not state them fully.
  • needs your consent (policy): refused on purpose until the config says otherwise (code a model hub would run on this machine).

docs.title: What it was measured on
docs.text:
• Does it run? 20 training iterations on 8 RealSense frames of GraspNet-1Billion (one scene), seed 0, one run per cell; nothing was measured on GraspClutter6D or on Kinect frames.
  • Does it train like the shipped component? 250 iterations on 8 RealSense frames of GraspNet-1Billion (one scene), seed 0, at a constant learning rate (FineGrasp: its own warm-up), beside the method as shipped trained the same way twice.

docs.title: Combination explorer
docs.text:
Pick a method, swap a stage, and see whether it still trains. Every answer is a recorded probe, a stored answer of grasppanda compose, or says that nothing was measured. On your machine, grasppanda explore --weights-dir <dir> also runs a ported method on a scene, in this page.

The explorer needs JavaScript. The same records are on the page Does it run?.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Where do the answers come from?

From records, never from a guess. A verdict is what grasppanda compose and grasppanda probe gave for exactly the combination shown. Without a record, the page may hold the answer of compose alone, drawn with a dashed outline: it says the stages fit, not that the combination trains. It is stored for one change and for two changes of two slots; a stage together with a recipe option has no stored compose answer. Anything else is not measured, and the page prints the two commands that find out. How each level is judged: Evidence.

Does a green tile mean a good combination?

A probe shows that a combination trains on real frames of GraspNet-1Billion, not how good it is. Accuracy is claimed only for a method trained and evaluated here.

No accuracy appears on this page. Trains like shipped goes one step further: a swap that ran was trained longer, beside the component the method ships, and their losses were compared. How we measure.

Why does a method offer these options?

A slot lists what grasppanda compose <method config> --list <slot> lists for that method, and the method's page shows the same list. A method without a slot says so in Compare: HGGD reads an RGB-D image and has an image encoder instead of a scene encoder.

Can I run a method here?

On your machine. grasppanda explore serves this page from the installed package and checks a selection of any number of slots with your own compose, saves it as a config, and never trains: the probe stays a command you run. With weights, grasppanda explore --weights-dir <dir> also enables the Run tab: pick a method and a weights file, and run it on the example scene or on your depth image (Run in the browser).

Word What it means slot a stage of a detector you can replace: --set <slot>=… on the command line, model.<slot> in a config option what goes into a slot: a preset or a component name seed-based skeleton the pipeline five methods share: scene encoder → seeds → view → grouper → head; HGGD is its own family scene encoder the point-cloud encoder of the seed-based methods; its slot is backbone image encoder the image encoder of HGGD; its slot is image_encoder composes · runs · learns · predicts the levels a swap is measured at: config accepted · trains on real frames without error · its losses fall · it ranks grasps probe a short training on real frames that ends with one verdict, such as runs or refused; wired means a synthetic scene only trains like shipped a swap trained longer beside the component the method ships: on a par, worse, diverging, did not train or not comparable

docs.title: Install
docs.text: GraspPanda runs on Linux with Python 3.10 or newer and PyTorch 2.1 or newer. Installing takes a few minutes; checking it takes under a minute and needs no dataset.

docs.title: 1. Install PyTorch
docs.text: Install PyTorch for your CUDA version, following pytorch.org.

docs.title: 2. Install GraspPanda
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Daeda1used/GraspPanda.git
cd GraspPanda
pip install -e .

There is no release on PyPI yet: pip install grasppanda arrives with the first one.

docs.title: 3. Add what your method needs
docs.text:
As shipped, GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp and HGGD need nothing more. GSNet, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp use sparse convolution: add the spconv extra that matches the CUDA build of your PyTorch.

# prints your CUDA build: 11.8 means spconv-cu118
python -c "import torch; print(torch.version.cuda)"
pip install -e ".[spconv-cu118]"

A CPU-only PyTorch prints None: use spconv-cpu.

An option from another library, such as an image encoder from timm, needs its extra too. Its slot page names it, and a missing extra stops with the command for your install.

Every extra Extra Installs Needed for spconv-cu118, spconv-cu121, spconv-cu124, spconv-cu126, spconv-cpu spconv for your CUDA build GSNet, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp, and the scene encoders built on sparse convolution (sparse-voxel networks, PTv3, LitePT) timm, transformers, torchvision a model library image encoders, and the Uni3D scene encoder (timm) kornia Kornia its losses torch_geometric PyG the PyG scene encoder and grouper trimesh, roma, healpix a geometry library gripper-mesh collision, some view stages ocnn, mamba-ssm octree and selective-scan operators the OctFormer and PointMamba scene encoders optim timm, pytorch_optimizer, schedulefree optimizers and schedules beyond torch.optim fpsample, torch-cluster sampling libraries the seed samplers that bridge to them vis Open3D the window of grasppanda demo --show; pictures need no extra tensorboard, wandb a logger logging to that service dev, docs test, lint and docs tools contributing, building this site

Extras combine: pip install -e ".[spconv-cu118,timm]". From an installed wheel the same extras install with pip install "grasppanda[spconv-cu118]".

spconv on a CPU-only machine

spconv-cpu (spconv 2.3.8) returns wrong, non-repeatable results when PyTorch runs more than one thread. GraspPanda therefore runs each sparse convolution of a CPU tensor on one thread and gives the other operators their threads back; a run's log and the probe report say so once. It also compares the first sparse convolution with a dense one and stops with an explanation if they differ. No setting is needed. A CUDA build of spconv computes CPU tensors correctly with any number of threads.

Compiled operators

Furthest point sampling, ball query, cylinder query and nearest neighbours have compiled kernels that are built on first use when a C++ compiler is present. Without one, the pure-PyTorch reference runs. See Operators and backends.

docs.title: 4. Check the install
docs.text:
grasppanda env
grasppanda train projects/example_project/configs/toy_train.yaml

env prints the interpreter, the PyTorch build, the GPUs and the optional backends; paste it into bug reports. train trains a toy detector on synthetic scenes, on the CPU, in under a minute. It ends with ✓ trained: everything is wired. The toy's grasps mean nothing.

  run         work_dirs/toy_train/20261018-120000

  schedule    5 epochs · Adam(lr=0.005, weight_decay=0.0) · ExponentialLR(gamma=0.95) per epoch

epoch 1/5  iter 8/8  loss 3.9372  loss/score 3.8366  loss/width 0.1006  ...

docs.title: Tour the config (optional)
docs.text: Ten minutes with the example project, no dataset needed: how a config is checked, what a run uses, and how a mistake is caught before anything is built. The example is a tiny untrained detector, wired like a real method.

docs.title: 1. Validate a config
docs.text:
grasppanda print-config projects/example_project/configs/toy_detector.yaml \

The config inherits two shipped building blocks: the runtime defaults and a plain training recipe (_base_/schedules/adam_10e.yaml: Adam, a learning rate of 1e-3, 10 epochs).

docs.title: 3. Make a mistake on purpose
docs.text:
A misspelt key is an error that names the closest parameter:

grasppanda print-config projects/example_project/configs/toy_detector.yaml \
    --opts model.head.num_angles=6

✗ 1 config problem in projects/example_project/configs/toy_detector.yaml

  model.head.num_angles
    ToyHead has no parameter 'num_angles'. Did you mean 'num_angle'? Parameters: num_angle, num_depth, depth_step, max_width, width_weight, in_channels.
    set in: <command line>

A swap that cannot work is refused the same way, before anything is built:

grasppanda print-config projects/example_project/configs/toy_detector.yaml \
    --opts model.grouper.type=ToyDepthGrouper

✗ 1 config problem in projects/example_project/configs/toy_detector.yaml

  model
    ToyDepthGrouper emits features with axes ('seed', 'depth', 'channel'), but ToyHead expects ('seed', 'channel'). Use a grouper and a head that agree; a depth axis is never added or squeezed implicitly.
    set in: projects/example_project/configs/toy_detector.yaml

Both exit with status 2, so a script can stop on them.

docs.title: 4. Build and run from Python
docs.text:
import torch
from grasppanda.config import Config
from grasppanda.registry import DETECTORS
from grasppanda.structures import Observation, PointSet, SampleKey

config = Config.load("projects/example_project/configs/toy_detector.yaml")
model = DETECTORS.build(config["model"]).eval()
points = PointSet.from_dense(torch.rand(1, 2048, 3))
observation = Observation(keys=[SampleKey("demo", 0, "none", 0)], points=points)
grasps = model.predict(observation)[0]
print(len(grasps), grasps.to_graspnet_array().shape)   # 64 (64, 17)

The toy detector is untrained, so its grasps are arbitrary.

docs.title: Run a method
docs.text: Every ported method runs from its released weights: download the file, convert it once, and get grasps on the example scene in minutes. No dataset is needed.

docs.title: Which method first?
docs.text:
GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp and HGGD need no extra install. HGGD reads a colour image registered to the depth image as well; the others read depth alone.

Method Reads Extra Weightsfrom Licence Demo GraspNet-baseline depth none Google Drive non-commercial 10.5 s GSNet depth spconv Google Drive non-commercial 14.8 s Scale-Balanced-Grasp depth none Google Drive MIT, with non-commercial parts 10.5 s EconomicGrasp depth spconv GitHub release MIT, with non-commercial parts 14.0 s FineGrasp depth spconv Hugging Face Apache-2.0 14.8 s HGGD RGB-D none Tsinghua Cloud MIT 14.5 s
  • Extra: spconv is installed as the extra that matches your PyTorch: spconv-cu118, spconv-cu121, spconv-cu124, spconv-cu126, spconv-cpu.
  • Licence: hover for the full text; each method page states it in full.
  • Demo is the whole grasppanda demo … --example command, measured on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs; no run was timed on a CPU.
  • Every checkpoint was trained on GraspNet-1Billion, whose data and labels are under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
The example scene

--example is a synthetic table-top scene that ships with GraspPanda: six geometric primitives on a table, ray-cast into a 1280 × 720 depth image in millimetres, with a colour image, the camera matrix and an object mask.

  • It is computed from formulas, so it needs no download and carries no dataset licence.
  • It is not a camera image: surfaces are perfectly smooth, with no noise, no missing depth and no reflection. Every method was trained on real scenes, so the example is outside its training distribution.
  • It has no grasp labels, so nothing checks the quality of the predicted grasps. It shows that the installation and the weights work end to end.

docs.title: Pick a method
docs.text:
Each page walks you through it: the weights and their licence, the conversion, the demo, the same from Python and in the browser, and a first number on the benchmark.

  • GraspNet-baseline · CVPR 2020 · seed-based

    The benchmark's own baseline: a PointNet++ encoder, approach views and cylinder crops.

    Run it →

  • GSNet · ICCV 2021 · seed-based

    Finds the points worth grasping first, on a sparse U-Net encoder.

    Run it →

  • Scale-Balanced-Grasp · CoRL 2022 · seed-based

    Balances grasps of every width, so thin objects are not drowned out.

    Run it →

  • EconomicGrasp · ECCV 2024 · seed-based

    Trains on a compact set of labels with an interaction grouper.

    Run it →

  • FineGrasp · arXiv 2025 · seed-based

    Builds on EconomicGrasp with crops at several scales, for delicate objects.

    Run it →

  • HGGD · RA-L 2023 · own family

    A heat-map on the colour and depth images guides where to look for grasps.

    Run it →

docs.title: On your camera
docs.text:
A depth image and its intrinsics are enough. For the seed-based methods, --workspace crops the cloud to the objects, as they were trained; HGGD reads the whole image and crops no workspace.

grasppanda demo <method config> --weights <converted file> \
    --depth depth.png --intrinsics fx,fy,cx,cy \
    --workspace -0.25 -0.2 0.35 0.25 0.2 0.8

HGGD also reads the colour image registered to the depth image: add --rgb rgb.png and leave out --workspace. The methods were trained on GraspNet-1Billion (RealSense D435 and Azure Kinect); results on other cameras have not been measured. Units, the depth scale and the usual mistakes: Your own camera.

docs.title: From Python or in the browser
docs.text:
• From Python: GraspInferencer runs the demo's pipeline and returns the grasps.
  • In the browser: grasppanda explore --weights-dir <folder> runs a method on the example scene or an uploaded depth image.

docs.title: Swap a component
docs.text: Replace one stage of a method with one line, check it, try it on real frames, then train it. The encoder is the usual first swap.

docs.title: Pick the encoder slot of your method
docs.text:
• Scene encoder

    --set backbone= under GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp. For example ptv3.

    All scene encoders →

  • Image encoder

    --set image_encoder= under HGGD. For example dinov2-small-reg-depth-stem.

    All image encoders →

Every other slot works the same way: all slots. Whether an option works under your method is in the explorer before you run anything.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
To You need You get see what works where nothing: the explorer the measured record of each swap compose a swap the install a checked config, or a refusal with its reason probe --synthetic the install wired: the stages connect on a synthetic scene probe on real frames scene 0 of GraspNet-1Billion and the method's assets for it one verdict: runs, runs-empty, runs-unstable, fails or refused train the whole training split, its assets and a GPU a model with weights, and its AP from grasppanda test

To probe the examples below, PTv3 needs a spconv extra and the DINOv2 encoder the timm extra (Install).

docs.title: 1. Compose
docs.text:
GraspNet-baselineGSNetScale-Balanced-GraspEconomicGraspFineGraspHGGD 
grasppanda compose \
    graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --set backbone=ptv3 -o baseline_ptv3.yaml

grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set backbone=ptv3 -o gsnet_ptv3.yaml

grasppanda compose \
    scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --set backbone=ptv3 -o sbg_ptv3.yaml

grasppanda compose economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set backbone=ptv3 -o economicgrasp_ptv3.yaml

grasppanda compose finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set backbone=ptv3 -o finegrasp_ptv3.yaml

grasppanda compose hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e \
    --set image_encoder=dinov2-small-reg-depth-stem -o hggd_dinov2.yaml

compose checks every pair of stages and writes the config. Where the next stage needs an adapter, it inserts one and says so. Most swaps that cannot work are refused with the reason and the fix, before anything is built; the probe of step 2 catches the rest. --set repeats for several slots at once.

Why was my swap refused?

Each refusal names its kind: incompatible by design, not supported yet, needs a setting compose adds, needs a preset's settings, or needs your consent. The rules behind them, and the lifts compose applies: Swap rules.

docs.title: 2. Probe
docs.text:
A probe trains the swapped model for a few iterations on real frames, predicts, and ends with one verdict. Point GraspPanda to your GraspNet-1Billion download and build the method's assets for the sample split, a few frames of scene 0:

GraspNet-baselineGSNetScale-Balanced-GraspEconomicGraspFineGraspHGGD 
export GRASPPANDA_GRASPNET1B_ROOT=/path/to/graspnet1b
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels --tolerance \
    --split sample --config baseline_ptv3.yaml
grasppanda probe baseline_ptv3.yaml

export GRASPPANDA_GRASPNET1B_ROOT=/path/to/graspnet1b
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels --graspness \
    --split sample --config gsnet_ptv3.yaml
grasppanda probe gsnet_ptv3.yaml

Scale-Balanced-Grasp also reads a grasp-width histogram of the whole training split, which a few frames cannot fill. A probe reads the file of the reference repository instead (statistic/scale_distribution.npy, written <file> below), in two steps (What a probe needs). First add the two --opts that name the file by its SHA-256, and import it once:

export GRASPPANDA_GRASPNET1B_ROOT=/path/to/graspnet1b
sha256sum <file>   # prints the <sha256> of the next command
grasppanda compose sbg_ptv3.yaml -o sbg_ptv3_probe.yaml --opts \
    data.train.dataset.scale_statistic.source=legacy_import \
    data.train.dataset.scale_statistic.reference_sha256=<sha256>
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --scale-statistic --import-legacy \
    --scale-statistic-file <file> --config sbg_ptv3_probe.yaml

Then build the other assets and probe the config that carries the two --opts:

grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels --tolerance \
    --split sample --config sbg_ptv3_probe.yaml
grasppanda probe sbg_ptv3_probe.yaml

export GRASPPANDA_GRASPNET1B_ROOT=/path/to/graspnet1b
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels --graspness --compact-labels \
    --split sample --config economicgrasp_ptv3.yaml
grasppanda probe economicgrasp_ptv3.yaml

export GRASPPANDA_GRASPNET1B_ROOT=/path/to/graspnet1b
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels --graspness --compact-labels \
    --split sample --config finegrasp_ptv3.yaml
grasppanda probe finegrasp_ptv3.yaml

export GRASPPANDA_GRASPNET1B_ROOT=/path/to/graspnet1b
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels --view-grasps \
    --split sample --config hggd_dinov2.yaml
grasppanda probe hggd_dinov2.yaml

grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --check --split sample --config <your config> lists what is still missing. Without the dataset, the probe runs its synthetic check and reports wired.

A probe shows that a combination trains on real frames of GraspNet-1Billion, not how good it is. Accuracy is claimed only for a method trained and evaluated here.

docs.title: 3. Train
docs.text:
A swapped model has no weights until you train it. Training needs the whole training split with the same assets, and a GPU:

# list what is still missing
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --check --config <your config>
grasppanda train <your config>
grasppanda test <your config> --weights <run>/checkpoints/best.pth

test scores it with the collision filter on and off. Train and test has the details, and Does it train like the shipped component? shows how swaps that train trained beside the component the method ships.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Six published methods, each ported stage by stage and checked against its reference code, the same weights loaded into both. For GSNet, the reference code is a third-party implementation (graspnet/graspness_unofficial). Five share the seed-based skeleton and its slots; HGGD reads RGB-D images and is a family of its own.

docs.title: Seed-based skeleton · 5 methods
docs.text:
• GraspNet-baseline · CVPR 2020 · depth

    The baseline released with GraspNet-1Billion: PointNet++ seeds, 300 views, four depths.

    equal to the reference ✓ authors' weights scored here

  • GSNet · ICCV 2021 · depth

    Graspness-guided seeds on a sparse U-Net, one of 300 views, a grid of angles and depths.

    equal to the reference ✓ trained here

  • Scale-Balanced-Grasp · CoRL 2022 · depth

    Small grasps not drowned out: four crop radii and width-balanced losses.

    equal to the reference ✓ authors' weights scored here

  • EconomicGrasp · ECCV 2024 · depth

    One compact label per point and view; a head that classifies angle, depth and quality.

    equal to the reference ✓ authors' weights scored here

  • FineGrasp · arXiv 2025 · depth

    Surface normals as input, graspness per object, four crop radii fused by attention.

    equal to the reference ✓ authors' weights scored here

docs.title: Own family
docs.text:
• HGGD · RA-L 2023 · RGB-D

    A 2-D heat-map of grasp centres, completed in 3-D by a PointNet over local regions.

    equal to the reference ✓ authors' weights scored here

Every method page starts with a five-minute run from released weights.

GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp and HGGD need no extra install. HGGD reads a colour image registered to the depth image as well; the others read depth alone.

docs.title: EconomicGrasp
docs.text:
Seed-based skeleton ECCV 2024 depth input equal to the reference ✓ authors' weights scored here

From the point cloud of a depth image, it picks graspness-guided seeds and one of 300 views, then classifies angle, depth and quality with interacting task tokens, trained on one compact label per point and view.

Paper · Reference code · Configs, results and notes

docs.title: Run EconomicGrasp in five minutes
docs.text: Four steps from the authors' checkpoint to grasps. A test parses each command and runs the demo and the Python code on a toy detector of the method's family.

docs.title: 1. Get the weights
docs.text:
GraspPanda publishes no weights for EconomicGrasp: the file to download is the authors' checkpoint, under its licence. Download economicgrasp_realsense.tar (GitHub release) and convert it once, from the root of a GraspPanda checkout:

python -m tools.convert_checkpoint economicgrasp_realsense.tar \
    economicgrasp_realsense.pth \
    --source-format economicgrasp --camera realsense
Licence, checksum and what the converter writes
  • Licence: MIT (the repository vendors operator code derived from a non-commercial project); trained on GraspNet-1Billion (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
  • SHA-256 of the download: 33c99bf43d599bd259c53c090badd83771ca34b8bebdb4a27a9a45a80df32223
  • What the converter writes: economicgrasp_realsense.pth, every tensor of the downloaded file under the name of the module that plays its role here, no value changed, with a note of the file it came from. A tensor left over or missing stops the conversion with a report; nothing is ever loaded partially. The converter is a tool of the repository; it is not installed with the package.

docs.title: 2. Grasps on the example scene
docs.text:
grasppanda demo economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --weights economicgrasp_realsense.pth --example --collision-filter

--example is a synthetic table-top scene shipped with GraspPanda: no dataset, no download. 14.0 s for the whole command, 725 grasps kept (one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs).

What it prints and writes, and every measured run

The command prints the config and its hash, how the weights loaded (every tensor matched, none missing), the test pipeline, the cloud, how many grasps the model predicted and how many the collision filter left (the config's variant cd: ModelFreeCollisionFilter), and the ten best grasps. It writes into work_dirs/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e/demo/:

  • grasps.npy: the grasps that are left, (G, 17) float32 in the GraspNet layout, best first, camera frame, metres;
  • grasps.png and grasps.gif: the cloud with the 30 best grasps, still and swinging around the scene;
  • example/: the scene as files (depth.png, rgb.png, mask.png, intrinsics.txt).

Measured with the authors' checkpoint, converted: 14.0 s for the whole command; 20,000 points to the model, sampled from 316,254 in the workspace; 1024 grasps predicted, 725 left after ModelFreeCollisionFilter (2026-10-15, commit ea6268b, one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs).

docs.title: 3. From Python, a browser or your camera
docs.text:
PythonBrowserYour camera 
from grasppanda import GraspInferencer
from grasppanda.apis import example_scene
scene = example_scene()  # the scene of --example
inferencer = GraspInferencer(
    "economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e",
    "economicgrasp_realsense.pth")
grasps = inferencer(
    depth=scene.depth, intrinsics=scene.intrinsics,
    depth_scale=scene.depth_scale, mask=scene.mask,
    table_from_camera=scene.table_from_camera, collision_filter=True,
)
print(len(grasps), grasps.sort_by_score().to_graspnet_array()[:3])

It runs the demo's pipeline on the demo's scene and returns its 725 grasps. mask= stands in for the segmentation the config crops the workspace with; on your camera, pass a mask or workspace=(xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax) in metres. More: From Python.

# ~/grasppanda_weights: the folder that holds economicgrasp_realsense.pth
grasppanda explore --weights-dir ~/grasppanda_weights

Open http://127.0.0.1:8765/ and choose EconomicGrasp in the Run tab: economicgrasp_realsense.pth is chosen for you by its name. Keep the example scene or upload a depth image with its intrinsics, and press Run: the page shows the picture, the best ten grasps, the counts through the post-processing and the command that does the same in a terminal. The server listens on your machine only and downloads nothing: Run in the browser.

grasppanda demo economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --weights economicgrasp_realsense.pth \
    --depth work_dirs/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e/demo/example/depth.png \
    --intrinsics work_dirs/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e/demo/example/intrinsics.txt \
    --workspace -0.25 -0.2 0.35 0.25 0.2 0.8 \
    --collision-filter --out work_dirs/camera

The scene files of step 2 stand in for a camera. EconomicGrasp was trained on clouds cropped around the objects; on a camera image, --workspace (a box in the camera frame, metres) or --mask does that crop. Units, frames, the depth scale and the intrinsics: Your own camera.

docs.title: 4. A first number on the benchmark
docs.text:
With GraspNet-1Billion on disk (Datasets), score every 64th frame of the seen test scenes, 120 frames:

grasppanda test economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --weights economicgrasp_realsense.pth \
    --opts data.test.dataset.split=test_seen data.test.dataset.frame_step=64 \
    evaluation.num_workers=4

Measured with the authors' checkpoint, converted: AP 68.75 without the collision filter and 70.11 with it, within 0.72 AP of the whole split.

What it prints, and every measured run against the whole split

It prints AP, AP0.8 and AP0.4 for every variant of the config, raw (the predictions as they are) and cd (with the collision filter), and writes a result record per variant into the run directory under work_dirs/. Testing needs no derived asset; the evaluator extracts a cache from the dataset's object models the first time it runs, which the times below do not include.

Weights, provenance Collision filter AP, 120 frames of test_seen AP, whole seen split Difference Wall time, commit the authors' checkpoint, converted, author-ckpt off 68.75 69.28 (record) −0.53 44 s, ea6268b on 70.11 70.83 (record) −0.72

Provenance: author-ckpt, the authors' checkpoint, evaluated by GraspPanda. Inputs: the workspace is cropped around the ground-truth segmentation (gt_assisted: workspace), as in the reference. On these 120 frames the AP is within 0.72 AP of the whole split, so the subset tells you quickly whether your installation gives what the records say; it is not a benchmark number. Measured on 2026-10-15 on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs.

The machine: one NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB) shared with other jobs, an AMD EPYC 7262 with OMP_NUM_THREADS=3; Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.7.1 with CUDA 11.8, spconv 2.3.8.

  • adamw-onecycle, trains like shipped: not compared under GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp, HGGD: it trained on a schedule of its own, not on that of the method as shipped.
  • finetune-encoder, trains like shipped: not compared under GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp: it trained on a schedule of its own, not on that of the method as shipped; not compared under FineGrasp: the swap did not run at level 1.
  • ptv3-adamw-onecycle, trains like shipped: not compared under GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp: it trained on a schedule of its own, not on that of the method as shipped.
How to swap, and how to read these lists

Swap one option in with a single line, or list the options of a slot:

grasppanda compose economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set <slot>=<option> -o swap.yaml
grasppanda compose economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --list <slot>

The summary table:

  • Composes: the options the config check accepts under EconomicGrasp, the one it ships included. needs consent: an option it holds back until you accept the code it downloads (the row says how), neither accepted nor refused. no record: never composed; the row says why.
  • Refused: the options the config check refuses under EconomicGrasp; each row gives the first sentence of the reason. For losses, both columns count the terms (or sets of terms) a preset was tried on.
  • Runs here: the swaps whose probe trained on real frames under EconomicGrasp without an error, out of every option tried there as a swap: a refusal counts, the option the method ships does not, and a loss preset is one option. Does it run? counts the same way.

The lists of each slot:

  • Runs: the methods under which the swap trained on real frames without an error, out of every method it is a swap under; the methods that ship the option are own and not counted. Who is left out, and why, stands under the chip, or below the table when it is long. Measured: 20 training iterations on 8 RealSense frames of GraspNet-1Billion (one scene), seed 0, one run per cell; nothing was measured on GraspClutter6D or on Kinect frames.
  • Trains like shipped: trained 250 iterations beside the component the method ships, its losses fall as theirs do, out of the methods it was compared under; a method under which the swap did not run, or where it trained on a schedule of its own, is named and not counted. Level 2 needs runs, not learns: a term flat after 20 iterations can fall by 250. Measured: 250 iterations on 8 RealSense frames of GraspNet-1Billion (one scene), seed 0, at a constant learning rate (FineGrasp: its own warm-up), beside the method as shipped trained the same way twice.
  • Under EconomicGrasp: ✓ when it reached every level here; level ? (as shipped) when EconomicGrasp as shipped does not reach that level either (a note below the table says why), so the level says nothing about the option; else the level it missed and why (composes, runs, learns, predicts), or why it was refused.

The levels, the refusal kinds and the thresholds: How we measure; every record: Does it run?; every comparison at level 2: Does it train like the shipped component?.

How this port differs from the reference
  • One model instance trains and predicts.
  • A frame with fewer graspable candidates than seeds yields fewer grasps instead of repeats, and a frame with none yields an empty result.
  • Compact labels are stored in view order. Upstream sorts the views of every point by view graspness and stores the permutation; the order of equal values in that sort is not defined, so its files cannot be reproduced bit for bit, while their content can.
  • The schedule base trains 10 epochs, as the command of the upstream README does; the published Kinect checkpoint is stored as epoch 10. The default of the upstream training script is 20 (_base_/schedules/economicgrasp_20e.yaml); because the cosine spans the run, that is a different schedule.
  • The cd variant uses the collision filter of the upstream test script, which takes the sparse-convolution voxel size (0.005 m); the other five methods' configs use 0.01 m.

How it was checked, stage by stage: tests/integration/test_economicgrasp_parity.py and the README.

docs.title: FineGrasp
docs.text:
Seed-based skeleton arXiv 2025 depth input equal to the reference ✓ authors' weights scored here

From the point cloud of a depth image and its surface normals, it predicts grasps as EconomicGrasp does, with graspness normalised within every object and crops at four radii fused by attention.

Paper · Reference code · Configs, results and notes

docs.title: Run FineGrasp in five minutes
docs.text: Four steps from the authors' checkpoint to grasps. A test parses each command and runs the demo and the Python code on a toy detector of the method's family.

docs.title: 1. Get the weights
docs.text:
GraspPanda publishes no weights for FineGrasp: the file to download is the authors' checkpoint, under its licence. Download finegrasp_pipeline/model.safetensors (Hugging Face) and convert it once, from the root of a GraspPanda checkout:

python -m tools.convert_checkpoint finegrasp_pipeline/model.safetensors \
    finegrasp_realsense.pth \
    --source-format finegrasp --camera realsense
Licence, checksum and what the converter writes
  • Licence: apache-2.0 on the model card; trained on GraspNet-1Billion, whose data and labels are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
  • SHA-256 of the download: 30c1f335567dcd726c11fb60249da65e26cc92c2f82928a4e4123ac235b38f79
  • What the converter writes: finegrasp_realsense.pth, every tensor of the downloaded file under the name of the module that plays its role here, no value changed, with a note of the file it came from. A tensor left over or missing stops the conversion with a report; nothing is ever loaded partially. The converter is a tool of the repository; it is not installed with the package.

docs.title: 2. Grasps on the example scene
docs.text:
grasppanda demo finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --weights finegrasp_realsense.pth --example --collision-filter

--example is a synthetic table-top scene shipped with GraspPanda: no dataset, no download. 14.8 s for the whole command, 613 grasps kept (one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs).

What it prints and writes, and every measured run

The command prints the config and its hash, how the weights loaded (every tensor matched, none missing), the test pipeline, the cloud, how many grasps the model predicted and how many the collision filter left (the config's variant cd: ModelFreeCollisionFilter), and the ten best grasps. It writes into work_dirs/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e/demo/:

  • grasps.npy: the grasps that are left, (G, 17) float32 in the GraspNet layout, best first, camera frame, metres;
  • grasps.png and grasps.gif: the cloud with the 30 best grasps, still and swinging around the scene;
  • example/: the scene as files (depth.png, rgb.png, mask.png, intrinsics.txt).

Measured with the authors' checkpoint, converted: 14.8 s for the whole command; 20,000 points to the model, sampled from 316,254 in the workspace; 1024 grasps predicted, 613 left after ModelFreeCollisionFilter (2026-10-15, commit ea6268b, one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs). Run again at commit 0ddca31 (2026-10-15): the same counts, 15.5 s.

From Python (step 3): 613 grasps, 11.4 s for the script (2026-10-15, commit 0ddca31, one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs).

docs.title: 3. From Python, a browser or your camera
docs.text:
PythonBrowserYour camera 
from grasppanda import GraspInferencer
from grasppanda.apis import example_scene
scene = example_scene()  # the scene of --example
inferencer = GraspInferencer(
    "finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e", "finegrasp_realsense.pth"
)
grasps = inferencer(
    depth=scene.depth, intrinsics=scene.intrinsics,
    depth_scale=scene.depth_scale, mask=scene.mask,
    table_from_camera=scene.table_from_camera, collision_filter=True,
)
print(len(grasps), grasps.sort_by_score().to_graspnet_array()[:3])

It runs the demo's pipeline on the demo's scene and returns its 613 grasps. mask= stands in for the segmentation the config crops the workspace with; on your camera, pass a mask or workspace=(xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax) in metres. More: From Python.

# ~/grasppanda_weights: the folder that holds finegrasp_realsense.pth
grasppanda explore --weights-dir ~/grasppanda_weights

Open http://127.0.0.1:8765/ and choose FineGrasp in the Run tab: finegrasp_realsense.pth is chosen for you by its name. Keep the example scene or upload a depth image with its intrinsics, and press Run: the page shows the picture, the best ten grasps, the counts through the post-processing and the command that does the same in a terminal. The server listens on your machine only and downloads nothing: Run in the browser.

grasppanda demo finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --weights finegrasp_realsense.pth \
    --depth work_dirs/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e/demo/example/depth.png \
    --intrinsics work_dirs/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e/demo/example/intrinsics.txt \
    --workspace -0.25 -0.2 0.35 0.25 0.2 0.8 \
    --collision-filter --out work_dirs/camera

The scene files of step 2 stand in for a camera. FineGrasp was trained on clouds cropped around the objects; on a camera image, --workspace (a box in the camera frame, metres) or --mask does that crop. Units, frames, the depth scale and the intrinsics: Your own camera.

docs.title: 4. A first number on the benchmark
docs.text:
With GraspNet-1Billion on disk (Datasets), score every 64th frame of the seen test scenes, 120 frames:

grasppanda test finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --weights finegrasp_realsense.pth \
    --opts data.test.dataset.split=test_seen data.test.dataset.frame_step=64 \
    evaluation.num_workers=4

Measured with the authors' checkpoint, converted: AP 71.21 without the collision filter and 72.99 with it, within 0.70 AP of the whole split.

What it prints, and every measured run against the whole split

It prints AP, AP0.8 and AP0.4 for every variant of the config, raw (the predictions as they are) and cd (with the collision filter), and writes a result record per variant into the run directory under work_dirs/. Testing needs no derived asset; the evaluator extracts a cache from the dataset's object models the first time it runs, which the times below do not include.

Weights, provenance Collision filter AP, 120 frames of test_seen AP, whole seen split Difference Wall time, commit the authors' checkpoint, converted, author-ckpt off 71.21 71.56 (record) −0.35 44 s, ea6268b on 72.99 73.69 (record) −0.70

Provenance: author-ckpt, the authors' checkpoint, evaluated by GraspPanda. Inputs: the workspace is cropped around the ground-truth segmentation (gt_assisted: workspace), as in the reference. On these 120 frames the AP is within 0.70 AP of the whole split, so the subset tells you quickly whether your installation gives what the records say; it is not a benchmark number. Measured on 2026-10-15 on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs.

The machine: one NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB) shared with other jobs, an AMD EPYC 7262 with OMP_NUM_THREADS=3; Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.7.1 with CUDA 11.8, spconv 2.3.8.

Option Runs Trains like shipped Under FineGrasp adamw-onecycle 6/6 not compared ✓ finetune-encoder 4/5not FineGrasp (unstable twice in the short probe) not compared unstable twice in the short probe ptv3-adamw-onecycle 5/5 not compared ✓

Who is left out, and why:

  • adamw-onecycle, trains like shipped: not compared under GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp, HGGD: it trained on a schedule of its own, not on that of the method as shipped.
  • finetune-encoder, trains like shipped: not compared under GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp: it trained on a schedule of its own, not on that of the method as shipped; not compared under FineGrasp: the swap did not run at level 1.
  • ptv3-adamw-onecycle, trains like shipped: not compared under GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp: it trained on a schedule of its own, not on that of the method as shipped.
How to swap, and how to read these lists

Swap one option in with a single line, or list the options of a slot:

grasppanda compose finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set <slot>=<option> -o swap.yaml
grasppanda compose finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --list <slot>

The summary table:

  • Composes: the options the config check accepts under FineGrasp, the one it ships included. needs consent: an option it holds back until you accept the code it downloads (the row says how), neither accepted nor refused. no record: never composed; the row says why.
  • Refused: the options the config check refuses under FineGrasp; each row gives the first sentence of the reason. For losses, both columns count the terms (or sets of terms) a preset was tried on.
  • Runs here: the swaps whose probe trained on real frames under FineGrasp without an error, out of every option tried there as a swap: a refusal counts, the option the method ships does not, and a loss preset is one option. Does it run? counts the same way.

The lists of each slot:

  • Runs: the methods under which the swap trained on real frames without an error, out of every method it is a swap under; the methods that ship the option are own and not counted. Who is left out, and why, stands under the chip, or below the table when it is long. Measured: 20 training iterations on 8 RealSense frames of GraspNet-1Billion (one scene), seed 0, one run per cell; nothing was measured on GraspClutter6D or on Kinect frames.
  • Trains like shipped: trained 250 iterations beside the component the method ships, its losses fall as theirs do, out of the methods it was compared under; a method under which the swap did not run, or where it trained on a schedule of its own, is named and not counted. Level 2 needs runs, not learns: a term flat after 20 iterations can fall by 250. Measured: 250 iterations on 8 RealSense frames of GraspNet-1Billion (one scene), seed 0, at a constant learning rate (FineGrasp: its own warm-up), beside the method as shipped trained the same way twice.
  • Under FineGrasp: ✓ when it reached every level here; level ? (as shipped) when FineGrasp as shipped does not reach that level either (a note below the table says why), so the level says nothing about the option; else the level it missed and why (composes, runs, learns, predicts), or why it was refused.

The levels, the refusal kinds and the thresholds: How we measure; every record: Does it run?; every comparison at level 2: Does it train like the shipped component?.

How this port differs from the reference
  • No model class of its own; one model instance trains and predicts.
  • The normal images and the instance-normalised graspness files of the authors' training set are not published. Both are generated here from the paper's equations; the normals are checked through the AP of the released weights, the graspness labels cannot be checked against the authors' at all.
  • The published recipe uses eight processes with four frames each; the runnable config uses one process with 32, which keeps the learning rate and the number of steps but gives batch norm 32 frames instead of 4. With fewer frames per step, scale the rate and the two step counts of the scheduler. None of this has been run beyond a smoke test.
  • A frame with fewer graspable candidates than seeds yields fewer grasps instead of repeats, and a frame with none yields an empty result (as for EconomicGrasp).
  • The released inference processor also drops grasps as wide as the gripper, applies grasp NMS and sorts by score: deployment post-processing, not part of the benchmark metric nor of these configs (GraspNMS exists as a post-processor).

How it was checked, stage by stage: tests/integration/test_finegrasp_parity.py and the README.

docs.title: GraspNet-baseline
docs.text:
Seed-based skeleton CVPR 2020 depth input equal to the reference ✓ authors' weights scored here

From the point cloud of a depth image, it keeps 1024 PointNet++ seeds, scores 300 approach views per seed and predicts score, in-plane angle, width and tolerance at four depths along the best one.

Paper · Reference code · Configs, results and notes

docs.title: Run GraspNet-baseline in five minutes
docs.text: Four steps from the authors' checkpoint to grasps. A test parses each command and runs the demo and the Python code on a toy detector of the method's family.

docs.title: 1. Get the weights
docs.text:
GraspPanda publishes no weights for GraspNet-baseline: the file to download is the authors' checkpoint, under its licence. Download checkpoint-rs.tar (Google Drive) and convert it once, from the root of a GraspPanda checkout:

python -m tools.convert_checkpoint checkpoint-rs.tar baseline_realsense.pth \
    --source-format graspnet-baseline --camera realsense
Licence, checksum and what the converter writes
  • Licence: GraspNet-Baseline Software License Agreement (non-commercial research use only)
  • SHA-256 of the download: 60680087c61cba2b6791614fef1519071e294f6dcaf99b3f581bb95f7c51a868
  • What the converter writes: baseline_realsense.pth, every tensor of the downloaded file under the name of the module that plays its role here, no value changed, with a note of the file it came from. A tensor left over or missing stops the conversion with a report; nothing is ever loaded partially. The converter is a tool of the repository; it is not installed with the package.

docs.title: 2. Grasps on the example scene
docs.text:
grasppanda demo graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --weights baseline_realsense.pth --example --collision-filter

--example is a synthetic table-top scene shipped with GraspPanda: no dataset, no download. 10.5 s for the whole command, 285 grasps kept (one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs).

What it prints and writes, and every measured run

The command prints the config and its hash, how the weights loaded (every tensor matched, none missing), the test pipeline, the cloud, how many grasps the model predicted and how many the collision filter left (the config's variant cd: ModelFreeCollisionFilter), and the ten best grasps. It writes into work_dirs/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e/demo/:

  • grasps.npy: the grasps that are left, (G, 17) float32 in the GraspNet layout, best first, camera frame, metres;
  • grasps.png and grasps.gif: the cloud with the 30 best grasps, still and swinging around the scene;
  • example/: the scene as files (depth.png, rgb.png, mask.png, intrinsics.txt).

Measured with the authors' checkpoint, converted: 10.5 s for the whole command; 20,000 points to the model, sampled from 316,254 in the workspace; 880 grasps predicted, 285 left after ModelFreeCollisionFilter (2026-10-15, commit ea6268b, one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs).

docs.title: 3. From Python, a browser or your camera
docs.text:
PythonBrowserYour camera 
from grasppanda import GraspInferencer
from grasppanda.apis import example_scene
scene = example_scene()  # the scene of --example
inferencer = GraspInferencer(
    "graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e",
    "baseline_realsense.pth")
grasps = inferencer(
    depth=scene.depth, intrinsics=scene.intrinsics,
    depth_scale=scene.depth_scale, mask=scene.mask,
    table_from_camera=scene.table_from_camera, collision_filter=True,
)
print(len(grasps), grasps.sort_by_score().to_graspnet_array()[:3])

It runs the demo's pipeline on the demo's scene and returns its 285 grasps. mask= stands in for the segmentation the config crops the workspace with; on your camera, pass a mask or workspace=(xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax) in metres. More: From Python.

# ~/grasppanda_weights: the folder that holds baseline_realsense.pth
grasppanda explore --weights-dir ~/grasppanda_weights

Open http://127.0.0.1:8765/ and choose GraspNet-baseline in the Run tab: baseline_realsense.pth is chosen for you by its name. Keep the example scene or upload a depth image with its intrinsics, and press Run: the page shows the picture, the best ten grasps, the counts through the post-processing and the command that does the same in a terminal. The server listens on your machine only and downloads nothing: Run in the browser.

grasppanda demo graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --weights baseline_realsense.pth \
    --depth work_dirs/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e/demo/example/depth.png \
    --intrinsics work_dirs/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e/demo/example/intrinsics.txt \
    --workspace -0.25 -0.2 0.35 0.25 0.2 0.8 \
    --collision-filter --out work_dirs/camera

The scene files of step 2 stand in for a camera. GraspNet-baseline was trained on clouds cropped around the objects; on a camera image, --workspace (a box in the camera frame, metres) or --mask does that crop. Units, frames, the depth scale and the intrinsics: Your own camera.

docs.title: 4. A first number on the benchmark
docs.text:
With GraspNet-1Billion on disk (Datasets), score every 64th frame of the seen test scenes, 120 frames:

grasppanda test graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --weights baseline_realsense.pth \
    --opts data.test.dataset.split=test_seen data.test.dataset.frame_step=64 \
    evaluation.num_workers=4

Measured with the authors' checkpoint, converted: AP 32.60 without the collision filter and 48.67 with it, within 0.77 AP of the whole split.

What it prints, and every measured run against the whole split

It prints AP, AP0.8 and AP0.4 for every variant of the config, raw (the predictions as they are) and cd (with the collision filter), and writes a result record per variant into the run directory under work_dirs/. Testing needs no derived asset; the evaluator extracts a cache from the dataset's object models the first time it runs, which the times below do not include.

Weights, provenance Collision filter AP, 120 frames of test_seen AP, whole seen split Difference Wall time, commit the authors' checkpoint, converted, author-ckpt off 32.60 32.64 (record) −0.04 35 s, ea6268b on 48.67 47.90 (record) +0.77

Provenance: author-ckpt, the authors' checkpoint, evaluated by GraspPanda. Inputs: the workspace is cropped around the ground-truth segmentation (gt_assisted: workspace), as in the reference. On these 120 frames the AP is within 0.77 AP of the whole split, so the subset tells you quickly whether your installation gives what the records say; it is not a benchmark number. Measured on 2026-10-15 on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs.

The machine: one NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB) shared with other jobs, an AMD EPYC 7262 with OMP_NUM_THREADS=3; Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.7.1 with CUDA 11.8, spconv 2.3.8.

The summary table:

  • Composes: the options the config check accepts under GraspNet-baseline, the one it ships included. needs consent: an option it holds back until you accept the code it downloads (the row says how), neither accepted nor refused. no record: never composed; the row says why.
  • Refused: the options the config check refuses under GraspNet-baseline; each row gives the first sentence of the reason. For losses, both columns count the terms (or sets of terms) a preset was tried on.
  • Runs here: the swaps whose probe trained on real frames under GraspNet-baseline without an error, out of every option tried there as a swap: a refusal counts, the option the method ships does not, and a loss preset is one option. Does it run? counts the same way.

The lists of each slot:

  • Runs: the methods under which the swap trained on real frames without an error, out of every method it is a swap under; the methods that ship the option are own and not counted. Who is left out, and why, stands under the chip, or below the table when it is long. Measured: 20 training iterations on 8 RealSense frames of GraspNet-1Billion (one scene), seed 0, one run per cell; nothing was measured on GraspClutter6D or on Kinect frames.
  • Trains like shipped: trained 250 iterations beside the component the method ships, its losses fall as theirs do, out of the methods it was compared under; a method under which the swap did not run, or where it trained on a schedule of its own, is named and not counted. Level 2 needs runs, not learns: a term flat after 20 iterations can fall by 250. Measured: 250 iterations on 8 RealSense frames of GraspNet-1Billion (one scene), seed 0, at a constant learning rate (FineGrasp: its own warm-up), beside the method as shipped trained the same way twice.
  • Under GraspNet-baseline: ✓ when it reached every level here; level ? (as shipped) when GraspNet-baseline as shipped does not reach that level either (a note below the table says why), so the level says nothing about the option; else the level it missed and why (composes, runs, learns, predicts), or why it was refused.

The levels, the refusal kinds and the thresholds: How we measure; every record: Does it run?; every comparison at level 2: Does it train like the shipped component?.

How this port differs from the reference
  • One model instance trains and predicts.
  • Losses are means over the supervised entries (the reference adds 1e-6 to the count), and zero, not NaN, when nothing is supervised.
  • Validation uses the val_dev scenes, not test_seen.

How it was checked, stage by stage: tests/integration/test_baseline_parity.py and the README.

docs.title: GSNet
docs.text:
Seed-based skeleton ICCV 2021 depth input equal to the reference ✓ trained here

From the point cloud of a depth image, it scores the graspness of every point, keeps 1024 seeds where it is high, picks one of 300 approach views per seed and regresses score and width over a grid of angles and depths.

Paper · Reference code (third-party) · Configs, results and notes

docs.title: Run GSNet in five minutes
docs.text: Four steps from the released checkpoint to grasps. A test parses each command and runs the demo and the Python code on a toy detector of the method's family.

docs.title: 1. Get the weights
docs.text:
GraspPanda trained GSNet once, but those weights are not published yet: the file to download is the checkpoint of the reference implementation (graspness_unofficial, third-party). Download minkuresunet_realsense.tar (Google Drive) and convert it once, from the root of a GraspPanda checkout:

python -m tools.convert_checkpoint minkuresunet_realsense.tar gsnet_realsense.pth \
    --source-format graspness-unofficial --camera realsense

Before you use it: It loads strictly and runs, but it is far below the paper: its best-ranked grasps run into the scene, so use it with the collision filter.

Licence, checksum and what the converter writes
  • Licence: academic, non-commercial (SJTU), as the reference repository; trained on GraspNet-1Billion (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
  • SHA-256 of the download: a0b9d85b300e40c76b66d092de62138d74757d6b7c2037f0d364f33960c54aa9
  • What the converter writes: gsnet_realsense.pth, every tensor of the downloaded file under the name of the module that plays its role here, no value changed, with a note of the file it came from. A tensor left over or missing stops the conversion with a report; nothing is ever loaded partially. The converter is a tool of the repository; it is not installed with the package.
  • The weights trained here (the reproduced rows of the README): trained on GraspNet-1Billion (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); whether and where these weights are published has not been decided.

docs.title: 2. Grasps on the example scene
docs.text:
grasppanda demo gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --weights gsnet_realsense.pth --example --collision-filter

--example is a synthetic table-top scene shipped with GraspPanda: no dataset, no download. 14.8 s for the whole command, 418 grasps kept (one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs).

What it prints and writes, and every measured run

The command prints the config and its hash, how the weights loaded (every tensor matched, none missing), the test pipeline, the cloud, how many grasps the model predicted and how many the collision filter left (the config's variant cd: ModelFreeCollisionFilter), and the ten best grasps. It writes into work_dirs/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e/demo/:

  • grasps.npy: the grasps that are left, (G, 17) float32 in the GraspNet layout, best first, camera frame, metres;
  • grasps.png and grasps.gif: the cloud with the 30 best grasps, still and swinging around the scene;
  • example/: the scene as files (depth.png, rgb.png, mask.png, intrinsics.txt).

Measured with the released file, converted: 14.8 s for the whole command; 15,000 points to the model, sampled from 316,254 in the workspace; 1024 grasps predicted, 418 left after ModelFreeCollisionFilter (2026-10-15, commit 0ddca31, one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs).

Measured with the weights trained here (not published): 16.6 s for the whole command; 15,000 points to the model, sampled from 316,254 in the workspace; 1024 grasps predicted, 689 left after ModelFreeCollisionFilter (2026-10-15, commit ea6268b, one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs).

docs.title: 3. From Python, a browser or your camera
docs.text:
PythonBrowserYour camera 
from grasppanda import GraspInferencer
from grasppanda.apis import example_scene
scene = example_scene()  # the scene of --example
inferencer = GraspInferencer(
    "gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e", "gsnet_realsense.pth"
)
grasps = inferencer(
    depth=scene.depth, intrinsics=scene.intrinsics,
    depth_scale=scene.depth_scale, mask=scene.mask,
    table_from_camera=scene.table_from_camera, collision_filter=True,
)
print(len(grasps), grasps.sort_by_score().to_graspnet_array()[:3])

It runs the demo's pipeline on the demo's scene and returns its 418 grasps. mask= stands in for the segmentation the config crops the workspace with; on your camera, pass a mask or workspace=(xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax) in metres. More: From Python.

# ~/grasppanda_weights: the folder that holds gsnet_realsense.pth
grasppanda explore --weights-dir ~/grasppanda_weights

Open http://127.0.0.1:8765/ and choose GSNet in the Run tab: gsnet_realsense.pth is chosen for you by its name. Keep the example scene or upload a depth image with its intrinsics, and press Run: the page shows the picture, the best ten grasps, the counts through the post-processing and the command that does the same in a terminal. The server listens on your machine only and downloads nothing: Run in the browser.

grasppanda demo gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --weights gsnet_realsense.pth \
    --depth work_dirs/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e/demo/example/depth.png \
    --intrinsics work_dirs/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e/demo/example/intrinsics.txt \
    --workspace -0.25 -0.2 0.35 0.25 0.2 0.8 \
    --collision-filter --out work_dirs/camera

The scene files of step 2 stand in for a camera. GSNet was trained on clouds cropped around the objects; on a camera image, --workspace (a box in the camera frame, metres) or --mask does that crop. Units, frames, the depth scale and the intrinsics: Your own camera.

docs.title: 4. A first number on the benchmark
docs.text:
With GraspNet-1Billion on disk (Datasets), score every 64th frame of the seen test scenes, 120 frames:

grasppanda test gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --weights gsnet_realsense.pth \
    --opts data.test.dataset.split=test_seen data.test.dataset.frame_step=64 \
    evaluation.num_workers=4

Measured with the released file, converted: AP 19.23 without the collision filter and 39.75 with it (this file was not scored on the whole split).

What it prints, and every measured run against the whole split

It prints AP, AP0.8 and AP0.4 for every variant of the config, raw (the predictions as they are) and cd (with the collision filter), and writes a result record per variant into the run directory under work_dirs/. Testing needs no derived asset; the evaluator extracts a cache from the dataset's object models the first time it runs, which the times below do not include.

Weights, provenance Collision filter AP, 120 frames of test_seen AP, whole seen split Difference Wall time, commit the released file, converted, author-ckpt off 19.23 not scored on the whole split — 36.6 s, 0ddca31 on 39.75 not scored on the whole split — the weights trained here (not published), reproduced off 67.82 68.83 (record) −1.01 40 s, ea6268b on 70.74 71.23 (record) −0.49

Provenance: author-ckpt, the checkpoint of the reference implementation (graspness_unofficial, third-party), evaluated by GraspPanda; reproduced, trained and evaluated by GraspPanda. Inputs: the workspace is cropped around the ground-truth segmentation (gt_assisted: workspace), as in the reference. On these 120 frames the AP is within 1.01 AP of the whole split, so the subset tells you quickly whether your installation gives what the records say; it is not a benchmark number. Measured on 2026-10-15 on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs.

The machine: one NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB) shared with other jobs, an AMD EPYC 7262 with OMP_NUM_THREADS=3; Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.7.1 with CUDA 11.8, spconv 2.3.8.

(as shipped) when GSNet as shipped does not reach that level either (a note below the table says why), so the level says nothing about the option; else the level it missed and why (composes, runs, learns, predicts), or why it was refused.

The levels, the refusal kinds and the thresholds: How we measure; every record: Does it run?; every comparison at level 2: Does it train like the shipped component?.

How this port differs from the reference
  • The reference implementation is third-party; no official training code exists.
  • The reference test script enables its collision filter by default, while the published numbers are without it. Both variants are always evaluated here.
  • Point-wise graspness labels must come from grasppanda prepare. Label files made by other generators are row-aligned to a preprocessing they do not record.

How it was checked, stage by stage: tests/integration/test_gsnet_parity.py and the README.

docs.title: HGGD
docs.text:
Own family RA-L 2023 RGB-D input equal to the reference ✓ authors' weights scored here

From an RGB-D image, it predicts a heat-map of grasp centres in 2-D, lifts each peak to 3-D and completes the grasp with a PointNet over a ball of scene points.

Paper · Reference code · Configs, results and notes

docs.title: Run HGGD in five minutes
docs.text: Four steps from the authors' checkpoint to grasps. A test parses each command and runs the demo and the Python code on a toy detector of the method's family.

docs.title: 1. Get the weights
docs.text:
GraspPanda publishes no weights for HGGD: the file to download is the authors' checkpoint, under its licence. Download HGGD_realsense_checkpoint (Tsinghua Cloud) and convert it once, from the root of a GraspPanda checkout:

python -m tools.convert_checkpoint HGGD_realsense_checkpoint hggd_realsense.pth \
    --source-format hggd --camera realsense
Licence, checksum and what the converter writes
  • Licence: MIT (the upstream repository); trained on GraspNet-1Billion (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
  • SHA-256 of the download: b95da06d8723298ad28e4c720c3a6a8af73dfe6f2e8126f43de8845bf62ad6df
  • What the converter writes: hggd_realsense.pth, every tensor of the downloaded file under the name of the module that plays its role here, no value changed, with a note of the file it came from. A tensor left over or missing stops the conversion with a report; nothing is ever loaded partially. The converter is a tool of the repository; it is not installed with the package.

docs.title: 2. Grasps on the example scene
docs.text:
grasppanda demo hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e \
    --weights hggd_realsense.pth --example --collision-filter

--example is a synthetic table-top scene shipped with GraspPanda: no dataset, no download. 14.5 s for the whole command, 72 grasps kept (one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs).

What it prints and writes, and every measured run

The command prints the config and its hash, how the weights loaded (every tensor matched, none missing), the test pipeline, the cloud, how many grasps the model predicted and how many the collision filter left (the config's variant cd: ModelFreeCollisionFilter then GraspNMS), and the ten best grasps. It writes into work_dirs/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e/demo/:

  • grasps.npy: the grasps that are left, (G, 17) float32 in the GraspNet layout, best first, camera frame, metres;
  • grasps.png and grasps.gif: the cloud with the 30 best grasps, still and swinging around the scene;
  • example/: the scene as files (depth.png, rgb.png, mask.png, intrinsics.txt).

Measured with the authors' checkpoint, converted: 14.5 s for the whole command; 25,600 points to the model; 470 grasps predicted, then 287 after ModelFreeCollisionFilter → 72 after GraspNMS (2026-10-15, commit ea6268b, one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs). Run again at commit 0ddca31 (2026-10-15): the same counts, 16.9 s.

From Python (step 3): 72 grasps, 8.2 s for the script (2026-10-15, commit 0ddca31, one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs).

PythonBrowserYour camera

docs.title: 4. A first number on the benchmark
docs.text:
With GraspNet-1Billion on disk (Datasets), score every 64th frame of the seen test scenes, 120 frames:

grasppanda test hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e \
    --weights hggd_realsense.pth \
    --opts data.test.dataset.split=test_seen data.test.dataset.frame_step=64 \
    evaluation.num_workers=4

What it prints, and every measured run against the whole split

Testing needs no derived asset; the evaluator extracts a cache from the dataset's object models the first time it runs, which the times below do not include.

Provenance: author-ckpt, the authors' checkpoint, evaluated by GraspPanda. Inputs: no input is derived from ground truth (the config crops no workspace). Measured on 2026-10-15 on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 shared with other jobs.

docs.text:
Every option that fits HGGD, except target-mask, was composed under it; those accepted were probed on real frames; the others say why.

Who is left out, and why:

How to swap, and how to read these lists

Swap one option in with a single line, or list the options of a slot:

grasppanda compose hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e \
    --set <slot>=<option> -o swap.yaml
grasppanda compose hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e --list <slot>

The summary table:

  • Composes: the options the config check accepts under HGGD, the one it ships included. needs consent: an option it holds back until you accept the code it downloads (the row says how), neither accepted nor refused. no record: never composed; the row says why.
  • Refused: the options the config check refuses under HGGD; each row gives the first sentence of the reason.
  • Runs here: the swaps whose probe trained on real frames under HGGD without an error, out of every option tried there as a swap: a refusal counts, the option the method ships does not. Not counted either: encoder-lr-0.1, layer-decay, freeze-encoder, finetune-encoder and ptv3-adamw-onecycle, refused under HGGD with no probe record. Does it run? counts the same way.

The lists of each slot:

  • Runs: the methods under which the swap trained on real frames without an error, out of every method it is a swap under; the methods that ship the option are own and not counted. Who is left out, and why, stands under the chip, or below the table when it is long. Measured: 20 training iterations on 8 RealSense frames of GraspNet-1Billion (one scene), seed 0, one run per cell; nothing was measured on GraspClutter6D or on Kinect frames.
  • Trains like shipped: trained 250 iterations beside the component the method ships, its losses fall as theirs do, out of the methods it was compared under; a method under which the swap did not run, or where it trained on a schedule of its own, is named and not counted. Level 2 needs runs, not learns: a term flat after 20 iterations can fall by 250. Measured: 250 iterations on 8 RealSense frames of GraspNet-1Billion (one scene), seed 0, at a constant learning rate (FineGrasp: its own warm-up), beside the method as shipped trained the same way twice.
  • Under HGGD: ✓ when it reached every level here; level ? (as shipped) when HGGD as shipped does not reach that level either (a note below the table says why), so the level says nothing about the option; else the level it missed and why (composes, runs, learns, predicts), or why it was refused.

The levels, the refusal kinds and the thresholds: How we measure; every record: Does it run?; every comparison at level 2: Does it train like the shipped component?.

How this port differs from the reference
  • One model instance trains and predicts; the mode selects the proposal budget.
  • Camera intrinsics come from the frame, not from per-camera constants rounded to two decimals.
  • A frame without proposals, or whose regions all lack support, yields an explicit empty group (the reference writes no file, or fails). A training batch without regions still trains the image network (the reference skips the step).
  • Gradient accumulation averages the two batches where the reference sums them, so the value clip is 0.5 instead of 1 (AdamW is invariant to the scale). The reference's first step of an epoch spans three batches and it drops the gradient of the last batch; neither is reproduced.
  • In-training evaluation uses the val_dev scenes, not test scene 100.
  • The anchor label pool is per process: under torchrun each process moves its own copy of the anchors. Train the reference recipe on one GPU.

How it was checked, stage by stage: tests/integration/test_hggd_parity.py and the README.

Every option that fits Scale-Balanced-Grasp, except target-mask, was composed under it; those accepted were probed on real frames; the others say why.

A probe shows that a combination trains on real frames of GraspNet-1Billion, not how good it is. Accuracy is claimed only for a method trained and evaluated here.
