docs.title: Choosing
docs.text:
• The PointNet++ family of the ported methods: pointnet2 and pointnet2-transformer; -dense propagates features back to every point, -msg uses two balls per level.
  • Modern set abstraction: pointnext in four sizes, pointmetabase (one ball query per stage, the cheapest of them) and pointvector.
  • Full resolution, no sub-sampling: dgcnn and the pyg-* layers; memory grows with the number of points times the neighbours.
  • Cheap sampling: randlanet samples at random and pools attentively.
  • Radii are set for a table top by analogy. The published configurations are for rooms (first radius 0.1 m); sweep the radius before comparing encoders.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The settings that matter, encoder by encoder

Options are changed with --opts model.backbone.<option>=<value>; the path addresses the encoder wherever an adapter put it.

PointNet++ with multi-scale grouping (pointnet2-msg, pointnet2-msg-dense):

model:
  backbone:
    type: PointNet2MSG
    in_channels: 0
    npoints: [2048, 1024, 512, 256]
    radii: [[0.02, 0.04], [0.05, 0.1], [0.1, 0.2], [0.2, 0.3]]    # one list per level
    nsamples: [[32, 64], [16, 32], [16, 16], [16, 16]]

PointNet2MSG keeps the level sizes of GraspNet-baseline (1024 seeds, 256 channels) with two balls per level; the larger ball is what a single-scale network would use, the smaller helps where points are dense. Cost grows with the sum of nsamples over the scales.

PointNeXt sizes:

Preset blocks width sa_layers / sa_use_res Parameters with the official segmentation head pointnext (S) 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 32 2 / true 0.792 M pointnext-b 1, 2, 3, 2, 2 32 1 / false 3.828 M pointnext-l 1, 3, 5, 3, 3 32 1 / false 7.125 M pointnext-xl 1, 4, 7, 4, 4 64 1 / false 41.576 M

The presets set radius: 0.04 (the room value is 0.1). Every inverted residual block runs one ball query.

PointMetaBase and PointVector take the arguments of PointNeXt (blocks, width, strides, radius, nsample). PointMetaBase shares one ball query and one offset embedding per stage; the unit suite pins its sizes to the published ones. PointVector is the scene network of the official code. Their output width is width (32 or 64).

ASSANet: use_xyz: true (set by the preset) appends the coordinates to the input features. Without it, constant input features are normalised to zero and the encoder learns nothing; the class refuses that combination in training.

PointMLP: neighbourhoods by count, anchors by ratio, so nothing to convert from rooms. gmp_dim appends a max-pooled vector of the whole frame to every point (0 turns it off).

DeLA: grid_size[0] is the spacing of the input cloud and sets the unit of the offset encoding; keep the factor of 2 between levels unless you also change k. Level sizes depend on the frame, so DeLA is dense only.

DGCNN: k neighbours per point; dynamic: true rebuilds the graph in feature space (the paper), false keeps it spatial; emb_dims is the width of the frame-level vector (0 leaves it out). Keep coords_as_features: true with constant input features.

RandLA-Net: sub_sampling_ratio and dim_output per level. Sampling is random in training and a fixed permutation in evaluation, so inference is repeatable. A cloud needs at least num_neighbors × prod(ratios[:-1]) points.

PyTorch Geometric layers (extra torch_geometric): a stack of one library convolution at full resolution; only the layers are the library's, the stack is not a published network.

Preset conv Library layer pyg-pointnet pointnet torch_geometric.nn.PointNetConv pyg-edgeconv edge torch_geometric.nn.EdgeConv pyg-point-transformer point_transformer torch_geometric.nn.PointTransformerConv pyg-pointgnn pointgnn torch_geometric.nn.PointGNNConv (all channels equal) Released weights for PointNet++ and PointNeXt

tools/convert_backbone_weights.py cuts the encoder out of a released checkpoint, checks it strictly against the class and writes a file whose keys start with backbone.. Nothing is downloaded by the tool.

The checksums are those of the files as downloaded on 2026-10-13; the full digests are in tests/integration/test_backbone_released_weights.py, which checks them before it loads a file.

python -m tools.convert_backbone_weights --list
python -m tools.convert_backbone_weights partition8_4096_15k_pointnet.pth csc_pointnet2.pth \
    --format csc-pointnet2
grasppanda train <method config> \
    --opts runtime.load_from=csc_pointnet2.pth runtime.allow_weight_mismatch=true
  • Radii are not stored in a checkpoint. These networks were trained with room radii; they load under table-top radii without complaint, and then see the table enlarged about five times. Whether that helps is untested.
  • Input channels are part of the weights. PointNeXt reads colour and a height above the floor, VoteNet one height channel; a camera-frame table-top cloud has no floor height, so define what you feed.
  • The dataset terms of S3DIS, SUN RGB-D and ScanNet apply; treat the files as research-only until you have checked. The files were loaded strictly once; activations were not compared with the upstream code.
Pitfalls met while building this
  • The grouper of Scale-Balanced-Grasp wants 256 channels. pointnext*, pointmetabase* and pointvector* end on 32 or 64; compose puts the projected grouper in place, and the model is then a variant of Scale-Balanced-Grasp. The encoders whose width is free are set 256 wide by their presets for this reason.
  • Constant input features starve encoders that read geometry through features. DGCNN, PyGPointEncoder, RandLANet and PointMLP therefore read the coordinates themselves.
  • Absolute coordinates. RandLA-Net's neighbourhood encoding, DGCNN, PointMLP and the bridge read camera-frame coordinates as features, so their features are not translation invariant.
  • Frame-level vectors. dgcnn (emb_dims) and pointmlp (gmp_dim) append a vector of the whole frame to every point, so features depend on the workspace crop; both can be switched off.
  • Padded balls under mean or sum. A ball query pads a sparse ball by repeating its first hit; assanet (mean) and pointvector (sum) count it several times, as upstream does.
  • torch_geometric without pyg-lib cannot build a k-NN graph; the bridge builds it itself.
Not wrapped Candidate Why not KPConv (rigid and deformable) needs kernel-point dispositions, radius neighbourhoods and a grid pyramid computed in its own data pipeline with compiled code; a follow-up of its own. KPConvX / KPConvD expected to need the same; not attempted. RandLA-Net, authors' repository CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; the MIT implementation of Open3D-ML was adapted instead. Contact-GraspNet's PointNet++ layout and weights a non-commercial licence; its three-scale layout can be written as a PointNet2MSG config by hand. XConv (PointCNN), GravNetConv of PyTorch Geometric they build their graph inside the layer, which needs pyg-lib. DeepLA-Net, LinNet, PointMixer, SPoTr, X-3D, PAConv, RepSurf, PVCNN, DeepGCN not reached, or no licence file found earlier.

Sources and licences

Code base: the upstream repository, commit and licence that THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md lists for the class's file (code adapted from it, or a module tree that follows it so that its weights load); written here: no third-party code. Extra: the optional install the class needs (every extra). Output: where the features live and how many channels the preset returns; compose sets a free out_channels to the width the method's other stages need. Released weights carry licences of their own.

Released weights that load by name

Each file was downloaded and loaded strictly into its class (every tensor of the class from the file, with its shape). Write the name as pretrained: of the encoder; building the model without the file prints the command that fetches it. A file on a hub is fetched at the revision it was loaded from (the last column). No file was evaluated for grasping.

Compare under every method

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text:
• The grid is the first thing to sweep. 5 mm keeps the grid of the reference methods; weights from rooms were trained at 2 to 2.5 cm (--opts model.backbone.voxel_size=0.01).
  • Weights whose input is what the methods feed: minkunet18a-openscene was trained on three constant ones per point, so its first layer loads too (not under FineGrasp, which feeds coordinates and normals).
  • Pre-training on single partial frames: minkunet34c-pointcontrast, trained on pairs of RGB-D frames, the regime of one table-top view.
  • A permissive licence, self-supervised: spunet-gaussiancross (MIT).
  • Deeper and pretrained encoders usually want a lower rate and a warm-up than the recipes tuned for a 14-layer network; none of this was tuned here.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The settings that matter 
model:
  backbone:
    type: MinkUNet
    in_channels: 3            # what the method feeds; compose sets it
    out_channels: 512         # free 1x1 projection; null returns the decoder width
    voxel_size: 0.005         # the encoder's unit of length, in metres
    layers: [2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2]
    planes: [32, 64, 128, 256, 128, 128, 96, 96]
    stem_kernel: 5            # 5 in MinkUNet; 3 in the Res16UNet34C checkpoints

MinkUNet is one class for the whole family of MinkowskiEngine; layers, planes and block select the member (only 18A and 34C have presets):

Member layers Decoder half of planes (the encoder half is 32, 64, 128, 256) block 14A / 14B / 14C / 14D [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] 128-128-96-96 / 128-128-128-128 / 192-192-128-128 / 384-384-384-384 basic 18A / 18B / 18D [2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2] as 14A / 14B / 14D basic 34A / 34B / 34C [2, 3, 4, 6, 2, 2, 2, 2] 256-128-64-64 / 256-128-64-32 / 256-128-96-96 basic 50 / 101 34's / [2, 3, 4, 23, 2, 2, 2, 2] 256-128-96-96 bottleneck

Sparse convolutions go through grasppanda.ops.sparse (spconv underneath; one spconv extra per CUDA build).

How released weights load

Name a release as pretrained: (table below) or give a file path:

model:
  backbone:
    type: SpUNet
    in_channels: 3
    out_channels: 512
    grid_size: 0.005
    pretrained: gaussiancross-scannet-lin   # a name, or a file path
    pretrained_mismatch: skip               # error (default): refuse any tensor that does not load
  • Only the encoder is loaded. The loader finds the prefix under which the file keeps it, ignores heads and optimiser state, and re-lays kernels where the original library stores them differently. No pickled code runs.
  • pretrained_mismatch: skip keeps the initialisation of the tensors that do not fit and lists them in the log. A grasp model nearly always needs it, for two layers: the stem (releases read colour and normals, the methods feed constant ones) and the final projection when out_channels differs.
  • A grasp checkpoint still wants the released file, because pretrained loads when the encoder is built. Keep the file, or set pretrained: null to evaluate a grasp checkpoint.
  • Other files of the same releases (the other GaussianCross models, the other Volt teachers, the other Mask3D checkpoints) have the same layout and are expected to load the same way; they were not downloaded. Pass such a file as a path, with the options the load report asks for.
Pitfalls met while building this
  • The stem is the tensor that does not load, and it reads the input. A 6-channel stem loads under FineGrasp, but nothing says its six channels mean what the release was trained on. Loading says nothing about meaning.
  • Licences differ inside one family. PointContrast, Mask3D and OpenScene publish code under MIT or Apache-2.0 and say nothing about the weights, which were trained on ScanNet.
  • SpUNet is not MinkUNet34C. Same block counts and widths, but the width changes in another layer; a checkpoint of one does not fit the other, and the loader says so rather than loading half of it.
  • Two kernel sizes may not share a spconv indice key. A 5³ stem sharing the key of the 3³ blocks ran on the CPU and failed on the GPU; the stem of MinkUNet has its own key.
  • Legacy-format checkpoints that pickle foreign objects cannot be read without executing them and are refused; re-save the state dict where it was written.
Not wrapped Candidate Why not Contrastive Scene Contexts, Res16UNet34C pre-training a legacy pickle with objects of its code base; the reader refuses to execute it. FCAF3D / TR3D sparse backbones (MMDetection3D) layers the sparse facade does not have, and they return a pyramid of coarse levels, not per-point features. SPVCNN / SPVNAS runs on TorchSparse, a second sparse library with no backend here. PonderV2 SpUNet-v1m3 another module tree than SpUNet; needs a key map. Small follow-up. Mosaic3D SpUNet no licence on the model card. OA-CNNs weights none released; oacnns starts from random weights.

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text:
• Serialised voxels: ptv3 and litept run on the 5 mm grid of the sparse encoders and come with released weights (ptv3-scannet200, ptv3-ppt, litept-structured3d; the Sonata weights are non-commercial).
  • The unit of length is a setting of every encoder here: grid_sizes of point-transformer-v2, grid_size × kernel_size (the token edge) of volt, voxel_size of octformer; point-transformer-v1 sub-samples by ratio and has none.
  • Point-patch tokens (point-vit, point-mamba, uni3d) were designed for single objects; their tokens become the seeds, and num_group must equal the seeds of the method.
  • Attention cost: point-vit attends globally (quadratic in the tokens), point-mamba is linear but runs on CUDA only.
  • The encoders checked against their authors' code (PTv3, its Sonata and Utonia variants, LitePT) are on Encoders checked against their authors' code.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The settings that matter

Point Transformer V2: grid_sizes is the cell edge of the four poolings, in metres; the class defaults are for rooms, the preset divides the ScanNet values by 4.

model:
  backbone:
    type: PointTransformerV2
    grid_sizes: [0.015, 0.0375, 0.09375, 0.234375]   # metres

Volt: grid_size × kernel_size is the edge of a token (2.5 cm in the preset); smaller tokens resolve finer geometry and cost quadratically more attention. embed_dim / num_heads must be 64. The authors state that Volt overfits without their training recipe (strong augmentation, distillation, EMA), which is not part of this toolbox.

OctFormer (extra ocnn): voxel_size is the edge of an octree leaf; a frame must fit a cube of voxel_size * 2**octree_depth; patch_size octree nodes form one attention group.

PointViT, PointMamba, Uni3D (extras mamba-ssm for PointMamba, timm for Uni3D):

model:
  backbone:
    type: PointViT                 # or PointMamba, or Uni3D
    num_group: 1024                # tokens per cloud = points with features = seeds
    group_size: 32                 # nearest points per token (Uni3D: 64)
    coord_scale: 2.0               # metres -> the unit-sphere scale of the object models

PTv3 and LitePT take the sparse grid (grid_size) and, with pretrained:, a release by name (below). ptv3-encoder sets enc_mode: true: no decoder, the encoder stages concatenated on every voxel. ptv3-ppt holds one set of normalisation layers per training dataset; pretrained_condition picks one. Other files of the same releases (the larger PPT model, the later Sonata file, the large Concerto model, the larger LitePT models) have the same layout and are expected to load the same way; they were not downloaded, so pass such a file as a path.

Released weights for the point-patch encoders and Volt

These load through tools/convert_encoder_checkpoint.py, which reads the config you composed and writes the keys where the encoder sits:

python -m tools.convert_encoder_checkpoint pretrain.pth point-mae.pth \
    --config <composed config>
grasppanda train <composed config> \
    --opts runtime.load_from=point-mae.pth runtime.allow_weight_mismatch=true

The checksums are those of the files as downloaded on 2026-10-13. All but Volt were trained on single objects scaled to the unit sphere: on a metric scene they are an initialisation of the transformer, not a feature extractor. With other encoder sizes nothing is written, and the tool names the option to change.

Pitfalls met while building this
  • mamba-ssm on PyPI is a source build. Prebuilt wheels per torch, CUDA and Python are on its releases page.
  • import mamba_ssm compiles a Triton helper and fails with cannot find -lcuda when the machine has libcuda.so.1 but no libcuda.so: point TRITON_LIBCUDA_PATH at a directory with a link of that name.
  • PointMamba has no CPU path; on the CPU it says so.
  • ocnn runs its convolutions on Triton kernels by default, which did not compile here; OctFormer sets ocnn's pure-PyTorch path (conv_method: block_gemm).
  • OctFormer's features depend on the batch: attention groups are counts of z-ordered nodes of the whole batch, as in the reference.
  • The default Concerto files are not the paper's Concerto. The model card calls them pre-release Utonia models; the paper's model is concerto-base-origin.
  • Object checkpoints use other sizes. MaskPoint's ShapeNet file has the Point-BERT layout (token_dim: 256); its ScanNet file is a 3DETR encoder and does not fit PointViT.
Not wrapped Candidate Why not Swin3D built on MinkowskiEngine plus its own CUDA package, neither a dependency here. Superpoint Transformer / EZ-SP consumes a superpoint partition computed outside the network. Mamba3D, Point Cloud Mamba no licence file. PointGPT its blocks differ from PointViT's, so its checkpoints need a second block type. ReCon, ACT, PCP-MAE, Point-JEPA, Point-BERT's own file checkpoints behind links that were not downloaded; nothing is claimed. Point-M2AE a hierarchical encoder, not the shared single-scale layout. Point-MoE, D-DITR, LAM3C weights for PTv3 a mixture-of-experts block (Point-MoE); AGPL-3.0 (D-DITR) and non-commercial (LAM3C) weights, not downloaded.

The view stage chooses the approach direction of every seed: two of the three degrees of freedom of the grasp orientation. The grouper crops the scene in the frame it chooses, so it decides what the head gets to see.

docs.title: Choosing

• The labels know 300 directions. Every option snaps its choice to one of the 300 label views for training, so a finer lattice does not give finer labels.
  • Fewer classes: lattice-fibonacci-120, icosphere-162 or healpix-192; only approaches away from the camera: lattice-hemisphere-60.
  • A classification instead of 300 regressions: lattice-best-view; lattice-angular-cost makes near misses cheap.
  • No lattice at all: direction-regression, with a confidence direction-vmf; a whole grasp frame: two-vector or rotation-6d.
  • The head keeps the in-plane angle. A stage that regresses a full rotation contributes its approach axis; the rest of the frame is supervised and logged, not decoded.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Which option for which need You want Take Why the view scoring of GSNet, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp template-view a score per label view; the training view is sampled from the scores the view stage of GraspNet-baseline or Scale-Balanced-Grasp objectness-view, objectness-view-graspable also predicts objectness, which their heads read the same scoring as a base for the options below lattice-view computes what template-view computes, on a lattice of any size a smaller output layer lattice-fibonacci-120, icosphere-162, healpix-192 fewer classes; each view is supervised by its nearest label view only approaches away from the camera lattice-hemisphere-60 the 60-of-120 template of RGB Matters a classification of the best view lattice-best-view, lattice-angular-cost cross-entropy on the most graspable view; the second adds the angular class loss of RGB Matters a direction between lattice points at inference lattice-soft-argmax softmax-weighted mean of the best view directions training crops closer to what inference chooses lattice-topk samples the training view among the 10 best views no lattice in the output direction-regression, direction-vmf 3 numbers per seed and a cosine loss; or a von Mises-Fisher likelihood with a concentration a full grasp frame two-vector, two-vector-baseline, rotation-6d, rotation-9d, rotation-quaternion Gram-Schmidt of two vectors, or the rotation mappings of RoMa Input and output

approach, seeds = view(seeds), and view.loss(approach, matched) for its own loss.

receives SeedSet: M seeds of the batch, coordinates (M, 3) in metres in the camera frame and features (M, C); C is injected (in_channels) returns ApproachSet, one row per seed, and the SeedSet (a stage may add a residual to the features, a score, or mark seeds invalid) direction (M, 3) unit vectors; read by the decoder of every head: rotation = approach_to_rotation(direction, in-plane angle) rotation (M, 3, 3), column 0 the direction; the crop frame of the grouper at inference view_index (M,) index into view.template, the 300 views the labels are indexed by; the assigner looks the labels up there in training declares label_formats (dense or compact labels it can read), needs_matched, seed_scores (scores it adds), applies_seed_weights

Three facts shape every option:

  1. The labels know 300 directions. GraspNet-1Billion and GraspClutter6D labels are indexed by a 300-view Fibonacci lattice. A stage may predict on another lattice or none, but it snaps its choice to one of those views for the label lookup.
  2. Train and inference crops differ by the snap. In training the crop frame is the label frame of the snapped view; at inference it is the direction the stage returned.
  3. The head owns the in-plane angle. Every head decodes approach_to_rotation(direction, angle bin).

What each kind of stage needs:

Stage From the labels From the assigner From the head lattice stages (Lattice, Icosphere, Healpix) the graspness of all 300 label views per seed (dense or compact) the label lookup at view_index nothing DirectionViewStage the same, reduced to the most graspable view the same nothing TwoVectorViewStage, RomaRotationViewStage the same, plus the grid or angle bin of the snapped view also crop_rotation, the label frame of the snapped view the same num_angle (checked)

No new stage has released weights. A checkpoint of a ported method loaded into a model with another view stage leaves only that stage untrained.

The settings that matter

A lattice stage:

model:
  view:
    type: LatticeViewStage        # or IcosphereViewStage (subdivisions) / HealpixViewStage (nside)
    num_views: 300
    hemisphere: false             # true: only approaches away from the camera
    target: score                 # score | best_view
    selection: argmax             # inference: argmax | soft_argmax
    train_selection: multinomial  # training: multinomial | topk | argmax
    top_k: null                   # used by soft_argmax and topk
    temperature: 1.0              # softmax temperature of soft_argmax
    angular_weight: 0.0           # best_view only: weight of the angular class loss
  • Size. An icosphere has 10 · 4**subdivisions + 2 views, HEALPix 12 · nside**2. Beyond 300 views neighbouring views share one label column.
  • target: score regresses the normalised graspness of every view (GSNet's). target: best_view classifies the most graspable view; use it with train_selection: argmax and a CrossEntropy loss.
  • selection: soft_argmax changes inference only. A temperature of about 0.05 fits regressed scores in [0, 1], 1.0 fits logits; keep top_k small (8).

A regression stage:

model:
  view:
    type: TwoVectorViewStage
    keep: approach                # approach (6-D order) | baseline (Contact-GraspNet order)
    direction_weight: 1.0         # loss/view: 1 - cos to the most graspable label view
    frame_weight: 1.0             # loss/view_frame: distance to the label frame, half-turn aware
    num_angle: 12                 # must equal the head's
  • loss/view_frame takes the smaller of the distances to the label frame and to its half-turn copy: a parallel-jaw grasp turned by 180° about its approach is the same grasp.
  • representation of RomaRotationViewStage: 6d and 9d are continuous; quaternion and rotvec are there for comparison (rotvec has no preset and no probe record).
  • residual: true adds the hidden features of the stage to the seed features, as GSNet's stage does.
Sources and licences Component Idea from Code Extra TemplateViewStage, ObjectnessViewStage GSNet (ICCV 2021), GraspNet-1Billion (CVPR 2020) written for GraspPanda none LatticeViewStage the same scoring on a free lattice; the hemisphere template of RGB Matters (arXiv 2103.02184, ICRA 2021) written for GraspPanda; the angular class loss adapted from GouMinghao/rgb_matters@2e176728f6 (MIT, see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md) none IcosphereViewStage subdivided icosahedron bridge to trimesh (MIT) trimesh HealpixViewStage HEALPix (Górski et al., ApJ 2005) bridge to healpix (BSD-3-Clause) healpix DirectionViewStage the approach network of Generalizing-Grasp (arXiv 2404.01727, CVPR 2024); the vMF likelihood of vMF-Contact (arXiv 2411.03591, ICRA 2025) written for GraspPanda (both repositories have no licence file) none TwoVectorViewStage the 6-D rotation representation (arXiv 1812.07035, CVPR 2019); the order of Contact-GraspNet (arXiv 2103.14127) written for GraspPanda (the idea only) none RomaRotationViewStage 6-D, 9-D + SVD (arXiv 2006.14616), quaternion, rotation vector bridge to RoMa (BSD-3-Clause) roma Pitfalls met while building this

  • A finer lattice does not give finer labels. Angles for 200 000 random directions, computed with the lattices of grasppanda.ops:

    Lattice Views Random direction to nearest view, mean / max View to its nearest label view, mean / max Label columns read Fibonacci (the labels) 300 4.5° / 9.0° 0° 300 Fibonacci 120 7.1° / 14.1° 4.6° / 7.7° 120 icosphere 162 6.1° / 10.8° 4.5° / 7.7° 162 icosphere 642 3.0° / 5.4° 4.5° / 8.1° 300 HEALPix 192 5.6° / 11.5° 4.5° / 7.9° 190 HEALPix 768 2.8° / 5.6° 4.5° / 8.4° 300

    The third column is the price of a coarse lattice; the fourth is the crop mismatch of any lattice that is not the label lattice.

  • TemplateViewStage(num_views=N) with N ≠ 300 is not another lattice size. Its template is also the label lattice, so the assigner refuses the labels. Use LatticeViewStage(num_views=N).

  • Soft-arg-max needs a temperature that fits the outputs. With regressed scores and a temperature of 1 the weights are nearly uniform; with every view voting, opposite views can cancel (the stage then falls back to the best view).
  • A single best view is a brittle target. On a symmetric object two distant views can tie and the target flips between them; target: score and angular_weight suffer less.
  • Flip augmentation yields mirrored label frames. The frame loss skips those seeds; their direction loss still counts.
  • The vMF loss is a log-density and goes negative when the concentration is high.
  • healpy is GPL-2.0, so the bridge uses the BSD-licensed healpix package.
Not wrapped Candidate Why not Contact-GraspNet code (NVlabs/contact_graspnet) its licence limits use to non-commercial research. Its parameterisation is two-vector-baseline; its contact labels need an asset the toolbox does not have. vMF-Contact, Generalizing-Grasp and S4G code no licence files. The closed-form likelihood, the cosine regression and the 6-D representation are written here; their other terms are not. DexGraspNet 2.0 (diffusion on seed features) no licence file; a generative head is a head, not a view stage. OrbitGrasp, Edge Grasp Network detectors of their own with their own simulated labels. PyTorch3D rotation conversions a compiled package for functions RoMa has in pure PyTorch. Several grasps per seed at inference ApproachSet has one row per seed; it needs a change of the skeleton. A head that takes the regressed in-plane rotation belongs to the head slot; until it exists the frame of the rotation stages is auxiliary.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
One task per page, from a dataset on disk to a trained, tested and extended detector; each page gives the commands for every method it applies to.

  • Configuration

    One YAML file is the whole experiment: inherit a shipped config, override, validate.

  • Datasets

    GraspNet-1Billion and GraspClutter6D on disk, and the label assets each method reads.

  • Train and test

    Train one of the six methods, score it on the benchmark, resume a run.

  • Cross-dataset evaluation

    Test GraspNet-1Billion weights on GraspClutter6D, with only the test data changed.

  • Your camera and Python

    Grasps on your own depth images, from the command line, Python or a browser.

  • Read an analysis

    Where the AP of a result comes from, and whether two results really differ.

  • Compose and probe

    Another option in a slot of a method, checked on real frames in a minute.

  • Add a component

    Write, register and use your own encoder, stage, hook or evaluator without forking.

docs.title: Read an analysis
docs.text:
Goal: see where the AP of an evaluation comes from (which grasps earn it, which lose it, and why), and whether two results really differ.

You need: a run of grasppanda test (Train and test). grasppanda analyze reads its result records and nothing else: no dataset, no weights, no predictions.

docs.title: 1. Score a model
docs.text:
The example on this page scores the authors' GraspNet-baseline checkpoint on every 64th frame of the seen test scenes, 120 frames:

grasppanda test graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --weights baseline_realsense.pth \
    --opts data.test.dataset.split=test_seen data.test.dataset.frame_step=64 \
    runtime.work_dir=work_dirs/baseline runtime.run_id=test_seen_step64 evaluation.num_workers=4

Any method and any split work the same way: grasppanda test writes one result record per post-processing variant into <run>/results/.

docs.title: 3. Read the header first
docs.text: The first block is everything a number needs before it may be quoted: protocol, split and camera, how many frames were scored, which inputs were derived from ground truth, the post-processing chain, and the weights and code that produced it. extent compares the frames of the record with the split it names. This run scored every 64th frame, so it is a subset, and the report says so in capitals: its AP of 0.4867 is a measurement on 120 frames, not the AP of GraspNet-baseline on the seen split.

docs.title: 4. See where the precision comes from
docs.text:
AP is the mean of a precision table with one column per friction threshold μ. The first table gives the mean of each column; their mean is the AP. Here a grasp that needs μ ≤ 0.2 is rare (0.18), and most of what can be earned is earned by μ ≤ 0.8.

The second table attributes the AP. A frame's AP is a weighted sum over its 50 ranks: rank 1 owns about 9 % of it, rank 50 owns 0.04 %. Every rank either earns its share, or loses it for exactly one reason: the gripper collides with the scene (checked against the ground-truth models), nothing is between the fingers, the grasp is free but not force-closed at this μ, or the rank was never filled. The columns add up to one. In this run 29 % of the AP is lost to collisions although the model-free collision filter ran.

By object, by scene, and through the post-processing chain

By object applies the same split to the object each ranked grasp belongs to. The numbers are percentage points of AP: object 0 earns 3.07 points and loses 4.99 to collisions, more than any other object. success is the share an object's ranks earned of what they held. Object ids are the dataset's.

By scene lists the scenes at both ends. Scenes, not frames, are the unit to think in: the four frames of a scene show the same objects.

Grasps follows the predictions through the post-processing chain. For a chain with two steps each step has its own row. HGGD's cd variant on the same frames:

Grasps
  stage                           grasps  per frame  removed by this step  left of the predicted
  ──────────────────────────────  ──────  ─────────  ────────────────────  ─────────────────────
  predicted                       53,917  449.3
  after ModelFreeCollisionFilter  25,908  215.9      51.9 %                48.1 %
  after GraspNMS                  7,954   66.3       69.3 %                14.8 %
  frames with an empty prediction: 0

The split by cause and object and the per-step counts are stored in the record by grasppanda test (fields breakdown and grasp_counts). Records written before these fields existed are read as before; the report then gives the total the chain removed, from the grasp counts of the run's records, and says that the rest is not recorded.

docs.title: 5. Compare two results
docs.text:
grasppanda analyze --compare work_dirs/baseline:cd work_dirs/sbg:cd --scenes 5 \
    --plot work_dirs/baseline_vs_sbg.png

A:cd picks a variant of a run; --variant picks one for both. The two records must share protocol and dataset. Whatever else differs between them (split, cameras, ground-truth-assisted inputs, post-processing, weights, code) is listed under differs, so that a difference in the numbers is not credited to the wrong cause. The summary pairs scenes: a bootstrap interval of the mean difference and a sign test, both with a scene as one observation.

docs.title: Compose and probe
docs.text:
Goal: put another option into a slot of a method, check in about a minute that the combination trains on real frames, then train it.

grasppanda compose <method config> --list <slot>
grasppanda compose <method config> --set <slot>=<option> -o my.yaml
grasppanda probe my.yaml
grasppanda train my.yaml

A probe shows that a combination trains on real frames of GraspNet-1Billion, not how good it is. Accuracy is claimed only for a method trained and evaluated here.

You need: GraspPanda installed. Steps 1 and 2 need no dataset. Step 3 reads the split sample of the config's dataset with the assets of the method (What a probe needs); without them it falls back to a wiring check and says so. The explorer does steps 1 and 2 in a browser and shows what was measured for every selection.

docs.title: 1. See the options of a slot
docs.text:
grasppanda compose <method config> --list backbone

With a method config, compose lists the options of that method's slot, each with what was measured for it under that method, and the options that do not fit with the reason. Without a slot it lists every slot of the method; without a method config, every option of the slot. grasppanda compose --show backbone=ptv3 prints one option with its notes. Which slots a method has is on the Components page: the scene-encoder and stage slots exist in the five seed-based methods, the image encoder in HGGD, post-processing and the training recipe in all six.

Options, presets and components

An option is a preset or the name of a registered class. A preset is the part of a config a newcomer cannot guess: the settings of one component for table-top depth clouds of GraspNet-1Billion (grid size, radii, widths, sampling rules) and, where its stage reads a label asset, the dataset section that serves it. Its header says what must be re-tuned and why: GraspClutter6D objects are farther from the camera (0.70 m against 0.44 m), so lengths may need re-tuning there. Every scene encoder has one, because the constructor defaults of most encoders are those of room-scale benchmarks: a bare {type: PTv3} works on a 2 cm grid with six input channels.

A class named by its type (--set grouper=CylinderGroup) is built with its constructor defaults, which grasppanda components <type> lists. Presets live in grasppanda/presets/<slot>/<name>.yaml. They are config fragments, not configs, and are not inherited: compose writes their values into the child config. In a wheel the measured records come with the package; in a checkout they are read from docs/advanced_guides/measured_combinations.json.

docs.title: 2. Compose
docs.text:
Pick a method; each example puts one option into one slot:

GraspNet-baselineGSNetScale-Balanced-GraspEconomicGraspFineGraspHGGD 
grasppanda compose graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --set backbone=ptv3 -o baseline_ptv3.yaml

PTv3 returns a feature for every point, and GraspNet-baseline takes the encoder's subsample as its seeds: compose wraps PTv3 in the adapter FurthestPointSubsample.

grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set grouper=roi-grid -o gsnet_roi-grid.yaml

The PV-RCNN RoI-grid pooling in place of GSNet's cylinder grouper; nothing else changes.

grasppanda compose scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --set backbone=ptv3 -o sbg_ptv3.yaml

Compose wraps PTv3 in FurthestPointSubsample and, because PTv3 returns 64 channels where the grouper needs 256, puts the projected variant of the grouper in place.

grasppanda compose economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set grouper=multi-scale -o economicgrasp_multi-scale.yaml

FineGrasp's grouper (crops at four radii, fused by attention) under EconomicGrasp.

grasppanda compose finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --set head=swad -o finegrasp_swad.yaml

GSNet's head reads dense labels and FineGrasp trains on compact ones: compose rewrites the training data and the assigner to serve the dense labels.

grasppanda compose hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e \
    --set image_encoder=resnet34 -o hggd_resnet34.yaml

HGGD has its own stage slot, the image encoder; here a timm ResNet-34 with ImageNet weights.

Each example was probed and recorded as runs under its method; a unit test holds these examples to the records. A refused combination writes nothing, and every refusal says in brackets why: incompatible by design (structural), not supported yet (not-implemented), needs a setting compose adds (fixed-by-compose), needs a preset's settings (not-a-combination) or needs your consent (policy). The rules are on Swap rules.

What compose prints (the Scale-Balanced-Grasp example) 
grasppanda compose scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e --set backbone=ptv3

slot      component                       from
────────  ──────────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
backbone  PTv3 in FurthestPointSubsample  preset `ptv3`, in the adapter FurthestPointSubsample
proposal  SubsampledSeeds                 base config
view      ObjectnessViewStage             base config
assigner  ScaleBalancedAssigner           base config
grouper   DepthCylinderProjectionGroup    base config, projected
head      OperationHead                   base config

what compose did
  • backbone: preset `ptv3` (PTv3). Point Transformer V3 (encoder + decoder, Pointcept PT-v3m1) on a
    5 mm grid.
  • wrapped PTv3 in the adapter FurthestPointSubsample (preset `furthest-point-subsample`):
    SubsampledSeeds requires 'subsampled' scene features, but PTv3 returns 'dense' ones (one feature
    per scene point). An adapter changes the model; its notes below say how.
  • FurthestPointSubsample.npoint: 1024, the number of seeds of the proposal
    (`model.proposal.num_seeds`): the points the adapter keeps are the seeds.
  • FurthestPointSubsample: fps_skip_near_origin: true, fps_tie_break: pointnet2_cuda, the sampling
    rules of the encoder it replaces (PointNet2Transformer), so that the adapter keeps the very
    points that encoder ends on.
  • grouper: DepthCylinderProjectionGroup in place of DepthCylinderGroup. DepthCylinderGroup as
    configured adds the seed features to its 256-channel crop features, but FurthestPointSubsample
    returns 64-channel features. DepthCylinderProjectionGroup is the same crop with a linear layer
    in front of its seed residual; it changes the model (the base method has none). `--no-adapter`
    leaves the pair refused.

contracts
  ✓ backbone · proposal
  ✓ backbone · grouper
  ✓ proposal · view
  ✓ view · assigner
  ✓ assigner · head
  ✓ grouper · head
  ✓ view · head
  ✓ proposal · view · head

config check
  ✓ valid  (hash 7f9112c56063)

✓ written sbg_ptv3.yaml
  next: grasppanda probe sbg_ptv3.yaml

The file is a child config of the method config. Its header repeats the command, what compose did and the re-tuning notes of every preset; its body is what you would have written by hand:

_base_:
  - /…/configs/scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e.yaml

model:
  backbone:
    type: FurthestPointSubsample  # `dense` -> `subsampled`, written down
    npoint: 1024                  # = model.proposal.num_seeds
    fps_skip_near_origin: true    # the rule of the encoder it replaces: same seeds
    fps_tie_break: pointnet2_cuda   # the rule of the encoder it replaces: same seeds
    backbone:
      type: PTv3                  # `dense`: one feature per input point
      in_channels: 3              # constant ones; geometry enters through the grid
      grid_size: 0.005
  grouper:
    type: DepthCylinderProjectionGroup   # the same crop with a linear layer in front of its seed residual
    radius: 0.08
    ...

Outside the shipped config tree the base is named by its absolute path: the file can be moved on this machine, and on another one the command in its header composes it again.

What compose does for you, each time saying so

No rule about what fits what lives in compose: every verdict is the contract rules of the config checker, quoted. Where exactly one registered piece bridges a refused pair, compose puts it in and says so; --no-adapter leaves the pair refused.

  • An encoder adapter: FeaturePropagation around a sub-sampling encoder under a proposal that scores every point, FurthestPointSubsample around a dense encoder under a proposal that takes the encoder's subsample as its seeds. The adapter gets the seed count of the proposal and the sampling rules of the encoder it replaces.
  • A fitted width: where the new encoder has an out_channels option it is set to the seed width the grouper fixes, otherwise to the width of the encoder it replaces. Where the encoder has no such option, the projected variant of the grouper (DepthCylinderProjectionGroup) takes its place. Where the method feeds real point features (FineGrasp's normals), in_channels is set to their number.
  • An axis adapter between a grouper and a head bundle whose feature axes differ: DepthEmbedGroup (preset depth-embed) or DepthPoolGroup (preset depth-pool).
  • The options a stage declares for the other stages: assigner options that return a field a stage reads, graspness only for a scoring proposal next to ObjectnessViewStage, the decode option of a head that would multiply in a score no stage predicts.
  • The label set of the head bundle: a head of dense label grids on a recipe of compact labels, or the reverse, gets the dataset section and the assigner of a shipped recipe that serves them (--set labels=dense|compact asks for it explicitly). Compact labels are an asset to build (grasppanda prepare <dataset> --compact-labels --config <the composed config>).
  • The dataset section a stage reads, when its preset carries one (tolerance, scale_statistic, graspness). The asset still has to be built; the preset says how.
  • Replace, never merge: a --set of the base's own component type gets _delete_: true. --unset key.path writes a component default back. -o refuses an existing file without --force and never writes onto the base config.

A composed file can be the base of a new command: compose reads the request in its header and composes again from its base with both requests merged (a config chain is two levels deep). Further overrides go through --opts; a path below a slot you set addresses that component wherever an adapter put it:

grasppanda compose scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --set backbone=ptv3 --opts model.backbone.grid_size=0.01 -o sbg_ptv3_1cm.yaml
Two refusals, and what they say

Stages that do not fit each other. A head bundle supervised with compact labels, fed by an assigner of dense ones that you set yourself:

$ grasppanda compose economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
      --set assigner=NearestLabelAssigner
...
  ✗ assigner · head [structural]: NearestLabelAssigner returns 'dense' matched labels, but
    EconomicHead is supervised with 'compact' ones. A head bundle and the assigner that feeds it
    must agree on the label set; the dataset must serve that label set too.
...
✗ refused: nothing was written. The messages above name the conflict and a fix.
  → EconomicHead reads compact labels and NearestLabelAssigner returns dense ones; the request set
    the assigner (`--set assigner=...`). Without it compose gives EconomicHead an assigner and
    training data of compact labels; or keep NearestLabelAssigner with a head bundle that reads
    dense labels (DecoupledGridHead, OperationHead, SWADHead).

Leave the assigner to compose and swap the head instead: compose then rewrites the recipe, as in the FineGrasp example above.

What compose would insert, refused without it. With --no-adapter, or in a config written by hand:

$ grasppanda compose graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
      --set grouper=ball --no-adapter
...
  ✗ grouper · head [fixed-by-compose]: LocalGroup emits features with axes ('seed', 'channel'), but
    OperationHead expects ('seed', 'depth', 'channel'). An axis is never added or squeezed
    implicitly: wrap the grouper in the axis adapter DepthEmbedGroup (preset `depth-embed`), `{type:
    DepthEmbedGroup, num_depth: <the head's num_depth>, grouper: {...}}`, which `grasppanda compose`
    inserts, or use a grouper and a head bundle that agree.

A slot the method does not have is refused with the slots it has:

$ grasppanda compose hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e --set backbone=ptv3
✗ HGGD has no slot 'backbone'. Its slots: image_encoder. HGGD is a detector family of its own: the
  stages of the seed-based methods (backbone, proposal, view, grouper, head) do not exist in it.

docs.title: 3. Probe it
docs.text:
grasppanda probe my.yaml

A probe is a miniature of grasppanda train: the real trainer with the config's optimizer, schedule and hooks, 20 iterations on the eight frames of the split sample of the config's dataset (GraspNet-1Billion: scene 0, frames 0, 32, …, 224), then prediction on two of them. Nothing is written. The line probe of the report lists the overrides that turn the config into that miniature.

What a probe prints (GraspNet-baseline with PTv3, the file of step 2, one run) 
$ grasppanda probe baseline_ptv3.yaml
  config      baseline_ptv3.yaml  (hash 147c5d6fd28d)
  model       GraspNetBaseline · 46,418,380 parameters
  data        8 frames of the config's dataset · 2 per iteration
  probe       as `grasppanda train` with data.train.dataset.split=sample data.train.num_workers=0 evaluation.interval=0 evaluation.save_best=null train.epochs=5 data.val.dataset.split=sample data.val.dataset.frame_step=4 data.val.num_workers=0
  device      cuda
  trained     20 of 20 iterations · 0.22 s per iteration (median, without data; data 0.20 s), measured on this machine now
  memory      peak 4.1 GiB on the GPU, this process
  losses      first → last · fall from the first active value to the mean of the last quarter
    loss/objectness             0.7379 → 0.3549       fell 43 %
    loss/view                   0.2098 → 0.05278      fell 74 %
    loss/score                  0.07834 → 0.02856     fell 59 %
    loss/angle                  0.525 → 0.4638        fell 17 %
    loss/width                  0.491 → 0.1616        fell 65 %
    loss/tolerance              1.145 → 0.3681        fell 65 %
    loss                        3.187 → 1.43          fell 52 %
  seeds       real: min 1.00, mean 1.00 of the seed slots per iteration
              supervised: 0.51 → 0.50, min 0.47
  predicted   2 frame(s) · 492, 494 grasps
  scores      min / median / max per frame: -17.1 / 1.9 / 49.9; -17 / 2.19 / 32
  gradient    reached every one of 9 units of 4 part(s)
  changed     every part
  lr          0.001 at the first step → 0.001 at the last, ×1 at the last step

✓ runs: trained 20 iterations on 8 frames of the dataset and predicted on 2 frame(s), with finite losses and real seeds in every iteration.
  (28 s)
What each line of the report says Line What it tells you losses Every loss term at the first and the last iteration, then its fall: from its first active value (reported and not exactly 0) to the mean of the last quarter of its active iterations, and its flags: flat (moved less than 5 %), rising (the last half of the active iterations more than 10 % above the first half), zero at end (0 or missing at the last iteration), constant (the very same value every time). Falling on eight frames means the stages and the labels fit together, nothing more; --json has every iteration's value. seeds, real The fraction of seed slots that held a real seed. Below 1 the proposal let fewer points through than it has seeds; at 0 an iteration trained the proposal only. seeds, supervised The fraction of seeds that took part in the grasp losses: about half for GraspNet-baseline (seeds on an object), 1 for GSNet by construction, about a tenth for EconomicGrasp with an untrained proposal (a seed counts only within 5 mm of a label point). predicted Grasps per frame. A model trained for twenty iterations often predicts few, and the count changes from run to run. scores The smallest, the median and the largest score of the grasps of each predicted frame, in the detector's own score unit. gradient The units of the model that never received a gradient before an optimizer step: sub-modules at depth 2 and parameters a top-level part holds itself. A top-level part none of whose units was reached is a dead stage and makes the run runs-unstable. changed The top-level parts whose trainable weights did not change between the first and the last optimizer step. A frozen encoder is expected here; a stage that should learn is not. lr The learning rate of the first optimizer at the first and at the last step, and their ratio. With --schedule constant the line is schedule and names the one rate every step used. The schedule of a probe, and why a probe does not repeat

To fit 20 iterations the probe sets train.epochs to as few epochs as the eight frames need, and the recipe's learning-rate schedule runs over those epochs: GraspNet-baseline's first step (epoch 8) is never reached, so its rate stays (the line lr above); GSNet's decay of 0.95 per epoch ends at 0.63 of its rate, EconomicGrasp's cosine at 2.4 %, and FineGrasp's warm-up of 800 iterations keeps the whole probe below 2.5 % of its rate. --schedule constant removes the scheduler and trains every step at the recipe's peak rate, scaled by the ratio of batch sizes when the probe's batches hold fewer frames than the recipe's (FineGrasp's 0.008 for batches of 32 becomes 0.002), and holds a per-epoch batch-norm momentum decay (GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, HGGD) at its first value. The config hash does not change. The default, --schedule recipe, runs the recipe as shipped; the probes behind Does it run? use constant, so that the trends of different methods compare.

A probe is one run. Run it again and the hash, the parameter count and the first losses are the same; the last losses, the seed fractions and the grasp counts are not. Training on a GPU is not bit-reproducible here, and after the first optimizer step two runs are two trajectories. Read the numbers as "of this run".

What a probe needs

The dataset and the label assets of its split sample. They are small; for GraspNet-1Billion, RealSense:

grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels --split sample
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --graspness --camera realsense --split sample
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --compact-labels --split sample \
    --config economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e     # EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --graspness --camera realsense --split sample \
    --config finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e             # FineGrasp
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --tolerance --split sample \
    --config graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --view-grasps --camera realsense --split sample \
    --config hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e                         # HGGD

The width histogram of Scale-Balanced-Grasp is the exception. It is a statistic of a whole training split, and eight frames leave bins of it empty, which its generator refuses. So a config that reads it (scale_statistic in its training dataset: every config composed from Scale-Balanced-Grasp, or with --set assigner=scale-balanced) is probed with the reference's own file. Import it once, through a config that names the file by its SHA-256:

sha256sum <reference repository>/statistic/scale_distribution.npy    # the <sha256> below
grasppanda compose scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --opts data.train.dataset.scale_statistic.source=legacy_import \
           data.train.dataset.scale_statistic.reference_sha256=<sha256> -o sbg_reference_histogram.yaml
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --scale-statistic --import-legacy \
    --scale-statistic-file <reference repository>/statistic/scale_distribution.npy \
    --config sbg_reference_histogram.yaml

From then on, compose with those two --opts, or hand them to grasppanda probe <config> --opts .... Training on the full split does not need the import: grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --scale-statistic --config <config> builds the native histogram of that split.

Without the dataset, or without an asset, the probe says what is missing and how to build it, falls back to two iterations on a synthetic scene with random labels and reports wired, never runs. --synthetic asks for that check directly. --iters, --frames, --predict-frames, --split, --device and --workers change what is run; --json prints the whole report; grasppanda probe --help repeats the verdicts and exit statuses.

docs.title: 4. Read the verdict
docs.text:
A probe ends with exactly one of six verdicts. What the levels composes, runs, learns and predicts add to them is on How we measure.

Verdict Meaning Exit status runs On real frames: the detector was built, every requested training iteration ran with finite losses and at least one real seed, every top-level part of the model that holds trainable parameters received a gradient in at least one iteration, the weights stayed finite, and prediction returned one valid grasp group for every probed frame, at least one of them with a grasp. 0 runs-empty As runs, except that no probed frame has a grasp: prediction returned one valid grasp group for every probed frame and every group is empty. Every stage ran; a model trained for a few iterations often keeps no seed. A run that is also unstable is runs-unstable. 0 runs-unstable On real frames: the detector was built, trained and predicted, but a loss or a weight became non-finite (a non-finite loss ends the training there), or an iteration had no real seed (no scene point passed the proposal, so only the proposal was trained), or no iteration supervised a seed, or a top-level part with trainable parameters received no gradient in any iteration, or fewer iterations ran or fewer frames were predicted than were asked for. 1 fails An exception was raised after the config check had passed. The report names the phase (build, data, optimizer, loss, backward, step, hook, predict), the component it came from and the message. 1 refused The config check refused the config (the same check as grasppanda print-config --check --for train). Nothing was built; the report carries the messages. 2 wired No real frame was read. On a synthetic table-top scene with random labels the detector was built, back-propagated a loss through every stage and predicted. This shows that the stages connect; it says nothing about real data. 0 with --synthetic, else 3

runs and runs-empty mean the combination works in this sense: every stage ran. The lines losses, gradient and changed tell a stage that learns from one that is only wired in, in every verdict.

Reading runs-unstable, runs-empty and fails

runs-unstable is what an untuned recipe looks like. A deep encoder under a learning rate chosen for a shallow one can lose every seed for a few iterations and recover; the verdict says which iterations. Because a probe is one run, a combination near that edge can be runs in one probe and runs-unstable in the next. Treat the two as one answer, "it works", and watch metric/real_seeds when you train.

runs-empty is common for a method that keeps only grasps above a score threshold: after twenty iterations no seed may pass it yet. Train longer before you read anything into it.

fails is a combination that passed the config check and then broke, and the probe says where. The check compares what components and datasets declare; it cannot know whether options suit your data. An encoder named by its type is built with its own defaults:

$ grasppanda compose gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e --set backbone=OACNNs -o gsnet_oacnns_bare.yaml
...
  • backbone: OACNNs with its constructor defaults; no preset was named. ...
$ grasppanda probe gsnet_oacnns_bare.yaml
...
✗ fails: at loss (iteration 1), in the backbone OACNNs: ContractError: OACNNs: cloud 0 of the batch has no voxel left after 4 of 4 down-sampling steps. ...

The default grid of OA-CNNs is 2 cm, for rooms; its preset (--set backbone=oacnns) sets 5 mm. A combination that fails for a reason the contracts could have known is a bug of the contract rules: please report it. A probe that ends with CUDA out of memory is fails too, with a note: on a shared machine that says something about the device at that moment, not about the combination.

docs.title: 5. Train it
docs.text:
grasppanda train my.yaml

The composed config is an ordinary config: Train and test applies. It is not a tuned recipe: optimizer, schedule, batch size and point budget are the base method's. The header of the composed file lists what to re-tune first. Report a number from such a run as trained here, next to the method as shipped under the same recipe.

docs.title: Where the measured answers are
docs.text:
• Explorer: every option under every method, with its verdict and the commands.
  • Does it run?: these steps for every option under each method it fits; refusals and options without a record are named with the reason.
  • Does it train like the shipped component?: the options that run, trained longer beside the component the method ships.
  • configs/experimental/: composed configs kept in the repository, each with the command in its header.
Adding a preset 
# One sentence that says what this is.
#
# Free text: where it comes from, what it is not.
#
# What must be re-tuned, and why:
# * option: value, and the reason it will have to change
model:
  backbone:
    type: MyEncoder               # a comment that travels with the line
    grid_size: 0.005

Save it as grasppanda/presets/<slot>/<name>.yaml. A registered scene encoder without a preset, a stage without a preset or a stated reason, and a component without measured cells each fail a unit test that says what to run (tests/unit/test_combine_presets.py, tests/unit/test_combine_grid.py). How to write the component itself: Add a component.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Goal: read a config, start your own from a shipped one, change it, and check it before anything runs.

A config is one YAML file. It describes the whole experiment: model, data, optimisation, evaluation and runtime. No behaviour is reachable only through a command-line flag.

You need: GraspPanda installed (Install). Every command on this page runs without a dataset.

docs.title: 1. Read a config
docs.text:
Every component is written as {type: Name, ...arguments}. The toy detector of the example project, shortened:

_base_:
  - _base_/default_runtime.yaml
  - _base_/schedules/adam_10e.yaml       # Adam, lr 1e-3, x0.95 per epoch, 10 epochs

model:
  type: ToyDetector
  backbone: {type: ToyBackbone, out_channels: 64}
  head:     {type: ToyHead, num_angle: 12, num_depth: 4}

type names a registered class of the slot's registry: model in DETECTORS, model.backbone in BACKBONES, optimizer in OPTIMIZERS (every torch.optim optimizer is there). grasppanda components lists every registered class with its contract; the Registered classes page shows the same list.

The top-level keys

The top level is a closed set. An unknown key is an error.

Key Content _base_ Parent files to inherit from. custom_imports Out-of-tree modules to import before validation. model The detector. data train, val, test: each {dataset, batch_size, num_workers, shuffle, drop_last}. optimizer, scheduler Optimisation. train epochs, amp, accumulate, grad_clip, grad_clip_mode, ema, sync_bn, scheduler_unit. evaluation interval, evaluator, variants, save_best, split, weights, num_workers. hooks Extra training hooks. runtime work_dir, run_id, device, seed, deterministic, resume, allow_config_mismatch, load_from, allow_weight_mismatch, checkpoint, log, ops.

What each key does during a run: Train and test.

docs.title: 2. Start from a shipped config
docs.text:
Name a shipped config in _base_ and change what you need:

_base_: [economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e.yaml]

train:
  epochs: 20        # overrides the schedule of the method

An entry of _base_ is a path relative to the file. When no such file exists, it is the name of a shipped config, with or without .yaml: _base_/default_runtime.yaml for a building block, <method>/<config> for a whole method. This works from any directory and from an installed wheel. A base that is neither is an error, reported at the file that names it (set in: <that file>).

docs.title: Merge rules
docs.text:
1. At most two levels. A config may inherit from a file that itself inherits from _base_/ building blocks. A third level is an error.
  2. Sibling bases must not disagree. If two files of one _base_ list set the same value, loading fails and names both files. There is no "last one wins".

  3. Mappings merge deeply, unless type changes. A child that sets another type replaces the inherited node, and the dropped keys are printed:

    # base:   optimizer: {type: Adam, lr: 1e-3, betas: [0.9, 0.99]}
optimizer: {type: SGD, momentum: 0.9}
# result: optimizer: {type: SGD, momentum: 0.9}     (lr and betas are dropped)

  4. _delete_: true replaces a mapping that has no type.

  5. Lists replace wholesale.

docs.title: 3. Change a value from the command line
docs.text:
grasppanda print-config <config> --opts train.epochs=20 optimizer.lr=3e-4 hooks.0.interval=5

Values are read as YAML, so true, null, 1e-3 and [1, 2] mean what they mean in a file. Overrides go through the same validation as the file, and overriding type follows merge rule 3.

docs.title: 4. Check it
docs.text:
grasppanda print-config projects/example_project/configs/toy_train.yaml --check

Validation runs before any dataset is opened or any module is built, and reports every problem at once. Add --for train to also require what train needs, or --no-check to print a broken config while you debug it.

Expected output 
✓ projects/example_project/configs/toy_train.yaml is valid
  inherits    toy_detector.yaml, default_runtime.yaml, adam_10e.yaml
  components  evaluation.variants.centre.0: ToyCentreFilter · evaluation.evaluator: ToyEvaluator · optimizer: Adam · scheduler: ExponentialLR · model: ToyDetector · model.backbone: ToyBackbone · model.grouper: ToyGrouper · model.head: ToyHead · data.train.dataset: ToyScenes · data.val.dataset: ToyScenes · data.test.dataset: ToyScenes
  hash        be81c4b1301a

The hash identifies the experiment. It ignores runtime.work_dir, runtime.run_id, runtime.resume and runtime.allow_config_mismatch, so moving, naming or resuming a run does not change it.

Troubleshooting: what a refused config looks like

Three layers check a config: the schema (top-level and fixed-structure keys), the signature of every component ({type: X} against X.__init__) and the contracts between components. A misspelt key and a misspelt argument, both given with --opts:

✗ 2 config problems in projects/example_project/configs/toy_train.yaml

  runtim
    unknown top-level key 'runtim'. Did you mean 'runtime'? Valid keys: custom_imports, model, data, optimizer, scheduler, train, evaluation, hooks, runtime.
    set in: <command line>

  model.head.num_angles
    ToyHead has no parameter 'num_angles'. Did you mean 'num_angle'? Parameters: num_angle, num_depth, depth_step, max_width, width_weight, in_channels.
    set in: <command line>

A contract message names both sides, for example ToyDepthGrouper emits features with axes ('seed', 'depth', 'channel'), but ToyHead expects ('seed', 'channel').

Interpolation: ${path.to.value}

${path.to.value} refers to another value. It is resolved after all merging and all overrides, so changing the source changes every reference:

runtime:
  work_dir: work_dirs/${config_name}/seed${runtime.seed}

${config_name} is the file name of the config without its extension.

Out-of-tree components: custom_imports 
custom_imports:
  - my_package.my_heads          # an importable module
  - ../my_components.py          # or a file, relative to this config

A .py path is loaded as a standalone module, so a single-file plugin next to its config works without installation. See Add a component.

What a run records

config.resolved.yaml (everything above, expanded, defaults written out), the original files and overrides, the git commit and diff, a code archive and the environment. The run directory is described in Train and test.

Notes on YAML
  • lr: 1e-3 is a number here. (Plain PyYAML reads it as a string.)
  • Duplicate keys in one mapping are an error rather than "last one wins".
