docs.text:
• Datasets: put GraspNet-1Billion on disk and build what your method reads.
  • Train and test: run a config.
  • Compose and probe: let grasppanda compose write a config with another component in one slot.

docs.title: Cross-dataset evaluation
docs.text:
Goal: test a model trained on GraspNet-1Billion on GraspClutter6D, with nothing changed but the frames that are scored and the evaluator.

You need: GraspClutter6D on disk (Datasets) and the weights of a GraspNet-1Billion config: trained with Train and test, or the released checkpoint converted as its method page shows. Testing needs no derived asset.

docs.title: 1. Run the transfer config of your method
2. Try a subset or another camera
docs.text:
--opts data.test.dataset.split=test_mini     # 24 scenes, 312 frames
--opts data.test.dataset.camera=zivid        # or realsense-d415, azure-kinect
--opts evaluation.num_workers=8              # evaluator processes

A number measured on test_mini is a subset number, not a benchmark result.

docs.title: What changes with the dataset, and what must not
docs.text:
• Changes: the frames (GraspClutter6D, realsense-d435, test), the intrinsics and depth scale (read per image), the workspace crop (SegmentationRectWorkspace, the crop of the official tool; HGGD crops nothing on either dataset) and the evaluator (width clip 0.14 m, foreground filter, no table).
  • Fixed: the model with every length and grid it was trained in, its gripper of 0.10 m, the points per cloud and input features, both post-processing variants and the point-sampling seed.
Every row of it, and why In the transfer config Why Frames changes: GraspClutter6D, realsense-d435, test The benchmark. The D435 is the camera of the paper's table and the sensor model of GraspNet-1Billion's realsense. Intrinsics, depth scale changes, read per image Nothing in a model or a transform holds a camera constant; DepthToCloud and HGGD read the calibration of the frame. Workspace crop changes to SegmentationRectWorkspace (margin 0.1) The crop of the official tool, and of the authors' released baseline code. GraspNet-1Billion's crop (SegmentationBoxWorkspace) is a box in a table frame that this dataset does not have; see the measured effect below. HGGD has no crop on either dataset. Evaluator changes to GraspClutter6DEvaluator Width clip 0.14 m, foreground filter, no table: the protocol of the benchmark. Model, including every length fixed The units the weights were trained in: the ball-query radii of the PointNet++ encoders (GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp), the 5 mm voxels of the sparse U-Net (GSNet, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp), the crop radius of every seed-based grouper, the 300 views and 4 depth bins of the five seed-based methods, HGGD's anchors and grid. Gripper of the model (0.10 m) fixed It bounds the labels the model learnt from and clamps its decoded widths. See "The gripper" below. Points per cloud, input features fixed Part of the recipe (20 000 points for GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp, 15 000 for GSNet, 25 600 for HGGD); fewer or more points change the density the encoder was trained on. HGGD network image (640 × 360) fixed The 1920 × 1080 image is reduced by 3 instead of 2; the focal length of the network image comes out nearly the same (465 to 472 px against 464 px). Post-processing (raw, cd) fixed The collision filter of each reference, with its own voxel size, approach distance and threshold. Point-sampling seed fixed (0) The same points every run.

What shifts without being a setting, and is therefore not corrected:

  • Distance. Objects are 0.70 m from the D435 in the median (0.36 to 1.04 m), against 0.44 m (0.31 to 0.52 m) in GraspNet-1Billion. The image is larger, so a pixel covers about the same length on an object (0.50 mm against 0.47 mm); how much noisier the depth is at that distance was not measured. No depth range is clipped on either dataset.
  • Extent and density. The reference crop here spans 0.91 × 0.57 × 0.81 m, about twice that of GraspNet-1Billion in each direction (0.48 × 0.35 × 0.26 m), and a scene holds 14.5 object instances instead of 9.0. With the same point budget an object gets roughly half the points.
  • Objects. All 68 test objects are unseen, also by a model trained on GraspClutter6D.
The gripper

The benchmark gripper opens to 0.14 m and the evaluator clips widths there. A model trained on GraspNet-1Billion was supervised with grasps up to 0.10 m and clamps what it decodes to 0.10 m. On the 68 test objects, 38 % of the valid label grasps are wider than 0.10 m (4 % are wider than 0.14 m); for 18 objects more than half are, for 3 objects more than 90 %. This part of the transfer gap is structural. --opts model.gripper.max_width=0.14 only moves the clamp of the decoder; it is a controlled variant, measured below for GSNet, not the default.

Why a config and not a list of overrides

A transfer config inherits the method's GraspNet-1Billion config and replaces two nodes, data.test and evaluation.evaluator. GraspNet-baseline's, without comments:

_base_:
  - graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e.yaml

data:
  test:
    dataset:
      type: GraspClutter6D
      camera: realsense-d435
      split: test
      load_labels: false
      preprocess:
        - {type: DepthToCloud}
        - {type: SegmentationRectWorkspace, margin: 0.1}
      transforms: ${data.val.dataset.transforms}
      keep_full_points: true
      seed: 0

evaluation:
  evaluator: {type: GraspClutter6DEvaluator}
  interval: 0
  • What the weights depend on cannot drift. The model, the point count, the input features and both post-processing variants are not restated; they are the inherited values, and transforms is an interpolation of the recipe's own evaluation transforms. A unit test compares every other section of each transfer config with its parent.
  • The same change as --opts would be about ten overrides including two lists, because a changed type replaces a node and all its arguments must be given again. That is easy to get wrong and leaves no name to quote in a result table.
  • The config has a name, a hash in every result record, and is validated by grasppanda print-config --check in the test suite.

A transfer config is a test config. Its evaluator cannot score the inherited GraspNet-1Billion validation loader, so it sets evaluation.interval: 0; to train, use the config it inherits from.

docs.title: Subset results
docs.text:
Measured on test_mini before the whole split was run, with controlled variants that exist for the subset only: the workspace crop, the camera, Kinect weights and the gripper width.

Subset numbers and controlled variants

Everything in this fold was measured on test_mini: 24 of the 235 test scenes, 312 frames per camera. These are not benchmark results and do not enter the model zoo. Per-scene AP ranges from below 1 to above 60 for one model, so the mean over 24 scenes has a scene-clustered standard error of about 3 AP (given per row).

AP / AP0.8 / AP0.4 in percent, RealSense D435, protocol graspclutter6d-sv-v1, 312 of 312 frames scored. raw: predictions as emitted; cd: with the reference's model-free collision filter. Provenance of the weights: author is the authors' released GraspNet-1Billion RealSense checkpoint, converted; local is a checkpoint the maintainers trained with the upstream code on their own variant of the graspness labels (epoch 18), used because no usable author checkpoint of GSNet is at hand.

Method Weights Input crop raw cd SE of AP (raw / cd) Reported, whole test split GraspNet-baseline author ground-truth rectangle 8.71 / 10.48 / 7.01 17.39 / 20.99 / 13.03 1.5 / 2.7 17.95 / 21.54 / 13.53 GSNet local ground-truth rectangle 27.62 / 33.67 / 21.50 28.74 / 35.11 / 22.12 3.7 / 3.9 none published Scale-Balanced-Grasp author ground-truth rectangle 20.92 / 25.50 / 15.89 23.03 / 27.86 / 17.61 2.8 / 3.2 22.69 / 27.57 / 16.95 EconomicGrasp author ground-truth rectangle 22.38 / 27.45 / 16.62 23.10 / 28.29 / 17.00 3.3 / 3.4 21.67 / 26.62 / 15.90 HGGD author none (gt_assisted: none) 15.40 / 19.67 / 8.84 16.67 / 21.30 / 9.39 2.0 / 2.2 none published

Reported is Table IX of the GraspClutter6D paper (arXiv 2504.06866 v3): models trained on GraspNet-1Billion, tested on the 235 test scenes with the D435, "workspace-cropped inputs", collision filter not stated. HGGD is not like-for-like with the other rows: it reads the whole image and no ground truth shapes its input.

Against the reported numbers.

  • GraspNet-baseline: the reported number is reproduced by cd and not by raw. cd is 0.56 AP below the reported value (0.2 standard errors), and AP0.8 and AP0.4 agree as closely; raw is 9.2 AP below (6 standard errors). The reference test script filters collisions by default, and the one baseline whose code the GraspClutter6D authors released (Contact-GraspNet) is run with the same filter values (voxel 0.01 m, approach 0.05 m, threshold 0.01 m). The evidence says that number was produced with the collision filter.
  • Scale-Balanced-Grasp and EconomicGrasp: consistent, but the subset cannot say which variant was reported. raw and cd differ by 0.7 to 2.1 AP, both lie within 0.6 standard errors of the reported value, and the subset resolves about 3 AP.
  • What cannot be checked from here: which checkpoints the authors evaluated (the GraspNet-1Billion column of their table equals the published numbers of Scale-Balanced-Grasp and EconomicGrasp to two decimals, 44.85 and 51.63, which suggests the public RealSense weights); their point sampling; and their input code for three of the four methods, which is not public.
  • GSNet and HGGD have no published GraspClutter6D number. The GSNet row uses a local checkpoint (on 120 frames of GraspNet-1Billion test_seen it scores 68 / 71 AP raw / cd, a subset number as well), so it says how this checkpoint transfers, not how the published model does.

Controlled variants on the same 312 frames. Each row changes one thing. The last column is the change of raw AP against the first row of the method, with the standard error of the per-scene differences: rows of one method are scored on the same frames, so their difference is resolved far better than the 3 AP of a single number.

Method Variant raw AP cd AP Change of raw GraspNet-baseline as above 8.71 17.39 GraspNet-1Billion crop 8.91 18.76 +0.2 (cd: +1.4 ± 0.4) GSNet as above 27.62 28.74 GraspNet-1Billion crop 28.23 29.29 +0.6 ± 0.4 model.gripper.max_width=0.14 28.38 29.47 +0.8 ± 0.2 Scale-Balanced-Grasp as above 20.92 23.03 GraspNet-1Billion crop 24.04 26.88 +3.1 ± 0.9 EconomicGrasp as above 22.38 23.10 GraspNet-1Billion crop 23.20 23.84 +0.8 ± 0.6 camera realsense-d415 25.30 25.70 +2.9 ± 1.7 camera zivid 29.76 30.81 +7.4 ± 1.8 Kinect weights (...g1b-kinect-to-gc6d-d435...) on the D435 21.52 22.10 −0.9 ± 0.9 Kinect weights on azure-kinect 15.72 16.31 −5.8 ± 2.0 against the row above

"GraspNet-1Billion crop" is the crop the weights were trained with, applied in the world frame of the rig:

--opts "data.test.dataset.preprocess.1={type: SegmentationBoxWorkspace, margin: 0.02, invalid_depth_foreground: include}"
  • The crop matters for some methods and not for others. The official crop keeps a wide margin of table and background: on view 0 of the subset scenes 30 % of its points are on objects, against 46 % for the box. Scale-Balanced-Grasp gains 3.1 AP from the tighter box and GraspNet-baseline 1.4 AP with the collision filter; for EconomicGrasp and GSNet the change is within its error. A table that mixes crops would rank methods by their input.
  • The sensor moves the result as much as the choice of method. The same EconomicGrasp weights score 22.4 AP on the D435 and 29.8 on the Zivid.
  • The sensor a model was trained on does not carry over by name. The Kinect weights score 21.5 AP on the D435 and 15.7 on the Azure Kinect of this dataset, whose 3840 × 2160 frames give a crop of 2.4 million points of which a quarter are on objects. Why that pairing is the weakest was not investigated.
  • The width clamp costs GSNet 0.8 AP. Letting the decoder open to 0.14 m raises raw from 27.62 to 28.38. The larger part of the gripper mismatch is in what the model learnt, which no test-time setting changes.
  • The collision filter is worth 8.7 ± 1.4 AP for GraspNet-baseline and 0.7 to 2.1 AP for the other four methods of the table.
  • The subset cannot rank Scale-Balanced-Grasp against EconomicGrasp (−1.5 ± 1.3 AP raw; the paper has Scale-Balanced-Grasp 1.0 AP ahead). The GSNet checkpoint is ahead of EconomicGrasp by 5.2 ± 1.4 AP, with the caveat on its provenance above.

docs.title: The whole test split
docs.text:
Run so far for five methods, 3 055 of 3 055 frames scored each: GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp and HGGD with the authors' converted checkpoints (author-ckpt), and GSNet with the model trained from scratch by this toolbox (reproduced; its weights are not published yet). AP / AP0.8 / AP0.4 in percent, RealSense D435; the rows, with the reported numbers beside them, stand in the model zoo and the result records in configs/<method>/records/.

Method Weights raw cd Reported GraspNet-baseline author-ckpt 8.69 / 10.35 / 6.96 17.14 / 20.60 / 12.86 17.95 / 21.54 / 13.53 GSNet reproduced 25.58 / 31.38 / 19.42 26.87 / 33.00 / 20.04 none published Scale-Balanced-Grasp author-ckpt 21.77 / 26.49 / 16.46 22.71 / 27.61 / 17.01 22.69 / 27.57 / 16.95 EconomicGrasp author-ckpt 21.69 / 26.64 / 15.79 22.25 / 27.30 / 16.06 21.67 / 26.62 / 15.90 HGGD author-ckpt 14.25 / 17.41 / 9.23 14.56 / 17.79 / 9.33 none published

The four seed-based rows read the cloud inside the ground-truth rectangle of the official tool (gt_assisted: [workspace]). HGGD is not like-for-like with them: it reads the whole image (gt_assisted: none), and its cd is its own filter followed by NMS. The GSNet row is one training run with one seed; its weights are another model than the local checkpoint of the subset numbers above.

The reported value lies 0.81 AP above cd and 9.26 above raw for GraspNet-baseline, 0.02 AP below cd and 0.92 above raw for Scale-Balanced-Grasp, and 0.02 AP below raw and 0.58 below cd for EconomicGrasp. So the reported table is closest to the filtered run for two methods and to the unfiltered run for the third. The paper does not state the collision filter, and whether it was applied to some methods and not to others was not investigated.

Entering a result into the model zoo

A result of such a run is an author-ckpt number of the transfer config, stamped with the protocol, the split, the camera, the variant and gt_assisted. It enters the zoo with its result records:

python -m tools.record_result <work directory of the run> --method <directory below configs/>

which checks that every frame was scored by clean code with hashed weights, copies the records to configs/<method>/records/ and prints the rows for the method's metafile.yaml.

docs.title: Checking a run against the official tool
docs.text:
grasppanda test writes predictions/<variant>/scene_NNNN/<camera>/<view>.npy; the official tool names files by image id. GraspPanda links a dump into the official layout, and reads one written for it.

Both directions

To score a dump with graspclutter6dAPI:

from grasppanda.datasets.graspclutter6d import GraspClutter6D
from grasppanda.evaluation.graspclutter6d import export_official_layout
from grasppanda.utils.paths import dataset_root

keys = GraspClutter6D.load_manifest(dataset_root("graspclutter6d")).keys("test", "realsense-d435")
export_official_layout("<run>/predictions/raw", "official_dump", keys)
# then: GraspClutter6DEval(root, "realsense-d435", split="test").eval_all("official_dump")

The other way round, evaluation.evaluator: {type: GraspClutter6DEvaluator, layout: official} scores a dump that was written for the official tool. One difference is deliberate: the official tool scores a frame without a file as zero, GraspPanda reports it as missing and gives no headline number for an incomplete run.

docs.title: Training on GraspClutter6D
docs.text:
Two configs carry a GraspNet-1Billion recipe over and change the gripper to 0.14 m: gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e and economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e. They are this toolbox's choice, not a reproduction: no recipe of these methods for this dataset has been published, and no model has been trained with them.

Commands and what has run

Each config has run for 20 iterations on one scene (the loss fell from 20.1 to 1.9 and from 28.6 to 2.5). The assets and their cost are listed under Datasets › GraspClutter6D.

grasppanda prepare graspclutter6d --labels
grasppanda prepare graspclutter6d --graspness --camera realsense-d435
grasppanda prepare graspclutter6d --compact-labels --config economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e
grasppanda train gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e
grasppanda train economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e

docs.text:

  • Model zoo: the transfer rows beside the reported numbers.

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text:
Goal: put GraspNet-1Billion on disk and build the label assets your method trains from. GraspClutter6D is read the same way and is optional.

GraspPanda starts from GraspNet-1Billion and also reads GraspClutter6D, whose grasp labels have the same format. Both are read in place: nothing is written into a dataset tree. Derived assets live in their own store under $GRASPPANDA_CACHE, each found by a hash of its generator, parameters and preprocessing, so a config never reads misaligned labels. Testing needs none of them.

You need: the GraspNet-1Billion download (190 scenes, two cameras) and room for the asset store.

docs.title: 1. Tell GraspPanda where things are
docs.text:
export GRASPPANDA_GRASPNET1B_ROOT=/data/graspnet1b      # the unpacked download
export GRASPPANDA_CACHE=/data/grasppanda_cache          # where derived assets go
Where a dataset is looked for, and the expected tree What Resolved from, in this order GraspNet-1Billion root in the dataset config, $GRASPPANDA_GRASPNET1B_ROOT, $GRASPPANDA_DATA/graspnet1b, ./data/graspnet1b GraspClutter6D root in the dataset config, $GRASPPANDA_GRASPCLUTTER6D_ROOT, $GRASPPANDA_DATA/graspclutter6d, ./data/graspclutter6d Derived assets $GRASPPANDA_CACHE

GraspNet-1Billion as the official download unpacks it, 256 frames per scene and camera:

scenes/scene_XXXX/object_id_list.txt
scenes/scene_XXXX/{realsense,kinect}/{rgb,depth,label}/NNNN.png
scenes/scene_XXXX/{realsense,kinect}/meta/NNNN.mat          intrinsics, depth factor, poses
scenes/scene_XXXX/{realsense,kinect}/annotations/NNNN.xml   poses, four decimals
scenes/scene_XXXX/{realsense,kinect}/{camera_poses,cam0_wrt_table}.npy
grasp_label/NNN_labels.npz
collision_label/scene_XXXX/collision_labels.npz
models/NNN/nontextured.ply,  dex_models/NNN.pkl

Splits (shipped in grasppanda/datasets/splits/graspnet1b.yaml): train (scenes 0 to 99), test_seen (100 to 129), test_similar (130 to 159), test_novel (160 to 189), test (their union), train_dev / val_dev (90 and 10 training scenes) and sample (eight frames of scene 0, for smoke tests and probes).

docs.title: 2. Check the tree
docs.text:
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --check

It reports what the tree lacks, then which derived assets exist, and prints the command for whatever is missing. Add --config <method config> to report the assets that config reads.

docs.title: 3. Build the grasp-label store
docs.text:
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels

The store holds the dense grasp labels of every object as memory-mapped files. Every other asset is generated from it. During training it is read by the methods on dense labels (GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp); the others read their own asset.

docs.title: 4. Build what your method reads
docs.text:
Method Assets after the label store Read during training GraspNet-baseline grasp tolerance label store, tolerance GSNet point-wise graspness (camera-specific) label store, graspness Scale-Balanced-Grasp grasp tolerance, scale statistic label store, tolerance, statistic EconomicGrasp point-wise graspness, compact labels graspness, compact labels FineGrasp graspness normalised per object, compact labels graspness, compact labels HGGD per-view grasps (camera-specific) per-view grasps

The commands for the RealSense configs (EconomicGrasp and HGGD also ship a Kinect config: use --camera kinect with it):

GraspNet-baselineGSNetScale-Balanced-GraspEconomicGraspFineGraspHGGD 
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --tolerance \
    --config graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e

grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --graspness --camera realsense

grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --tolerance \
    --config scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --scale-statistic \
    --config scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e

grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --graspness --camera realsense
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --compact-labels \
    --config economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e

grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --graspness --camera realsense \
    --config finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --compact-labels \
    --config finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e

The compact labels are EconomicGrasp's asset: when it exists, nothing is generated.

grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --labels
grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --view-grasps --camera realsense \
    --config _base_/datasets/graspnet1b_realsense_hggd.yaml

Every action reads a dataset config: the one named with --config, or else the shipped base of the dataset and camera (_base_/datasets/graspnet1b_<camera>.yaml, the graspness recipe of GSNet, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp). What is built is exactly what that config later asks for. --split and --scenes 5,9,13 restrict the scenes; generation is resumable and finished shards are skipped.

Expected result: grasppanda prepare graspnet1b --check --config <method config> marks the tree and every asset of that config with ✓. The test suite holds the commands above to the dataset sections of the six method configs.

Troubleshooting
  • "grasp labels of object N are not in the store": run --labels first; every other action needs the store.
  • "the dataset config has no compact_labels section" (or tolerance, view_grasps): pass --config with the method config that declares it.
  • A probe needs the same assets for the split sample only: add --split sample (What a probe needs).
  • The scale statistic of Scale-Balanced-Grasp reads 3200 training frames; its README says how to import the reference file instead (configs/scale_balanced_grasp).

docs.title: GraspClutter6D
docs.text:
GraspClutter6D (RA-L 2025, arXiv 2504.06866, data licence CC BY-SA 4.0) holds 1 000 scenes in BOP layout, 648 of them in its grasp splits. Every label generator of this toolbox runs on it unchanged. Download and unpack it as its README says, set GRASPPANDA_GRASPCLUTTER6D_ROOT, then run grasppanda prepare graspclutter6d --check. Testing a GraspNet-1Billion model on it is the subject of Cross-dataset evaluation.

The tree the reader needs 
split_info/grasp_{train,test}_scene_ids.json    the grasp splits (authoritative)
split_info/obj_ids_per_scene.json
scenes/<scene:06d>/{rgb,depth,label}/<image:06d>.png
scenes/<scene:06d>/{mask,mask_visib}/<image:06d>_<instance:06d>.png
scenes/<scene:06d>/scene_camera.json    per image: cam_K, depth_scale, cam_{R,t}_w2c
scenes/<scene:06d>/scene_gt.json        per image and instance: cam_{R,t}_m2c, obj_id
grasp_label/obj_<object:06d>_labels.npz
collision_label/<scene:06d>.npz         one array per instance, in scene_gt order
models_m/obj_<object:06d>.ply           object models in metres
dex_models/obj_<object:06d>.pkl         force-closure data of the evaluator
Cameras

A scene has 13 annotated views, and every view was taken by four cameras. All 52 images of a scene share the directories; the camera is encoded in the image id, image = 4 * view + c. A SampleKey holds the camera name and the view (0 to 12).

Camera (camera:) c Image Raw depth unit Focal length (px) Base config realsense-d415 1 1920 × 1080 1 mm 1404 or 1429 graspclutter6d_d415.yaml realsense-d435 2 1920 × 1080 1 mm 1394 or 1415 graspclutter6d_d435.yaml azure-kinect 3 3840 × 2160 0.1 mm 1996 or 2112 graspclutter6d_kinect.yaml zivid 4 1920 × 1200 0.1 mm 2790 graspclutter6d_zivid.yaml

Intrinsics and depth scale are read per image from scene_camera.json. Three of the cameras have two calibrations in the grasp splits (in the scenes inspected, view 0 has one and views 1 to 12 the other), so one constant camera matrix per camera would be wrong here. The depth scale was the same on all 8 424 images of each camera. The paper reports its benchmark on the RealSense D435.

Splits Split Scenes Frames per camera Object models Source train 413 5 369 123 (ids 69 to 198) split_info/grasp_train_scene_ids.json test 235 3 055 68 (ids 1 to 68) split_info/grasp_test_scene_ids.json all 648 8 424 191 union of the two sample 1 (scene 5) 13 6 first training scene, for smoke tests test_mini 24 312 66 of the 68 every tenth test scene by rank; shipped val_dev 41 533 110 of the 123 every tenth training scene by rank; shipped train_dev 372 4 836 123 train without val_dev
  • The test objects are all unseen. No object model occurs in both splits: the benchmark has no "seen" part, unlike GraspNet-1Billion.
  • The three subsets are fixed scene lists in grasppanda/datasets/splits/graspclutter6d.yaml. They exist only when the split files of the tree contain them. test_mini is for quick checks; a number measured on it is a subset number, not a benchmark result. Per-scene AP varies widely on this dataset (from below 1 to above 60 for one model), so the mean over 24 scenes carries a standard error of about 3 AP.
  • All objects of val_dev are training objects, so it measures fit to new arrangements, not to new objects.
  • The other 352 scenes of the dataset are in neither grasp split and are not read.
  • The paper states 132 training objects. The split files give 123: object ids 112 to 117, 191, 199 and 200 occur in no scene of either grasp split.
What a frame holds
  • Scenes are denser than in GraspNet-1Billion: 14.5 object instances per scene on average (5 to 20), and in 84 % of the scenes at least one object model occurs more than once. The label image stores object ids and cannot tell two copies apart, so the reader builds the instance map from the per-instance visibility masks (mask_visib), and grasp labels, collision labels and compact labels are keyed by instance (position in scene_gt.json), not by object id.
  • The instance list and its order are the same for all 52 images of a scene (checked on all 648 scenes). The reader and the evaluator refuse a frame for which that fails.
  • Lengths in the JSON files are millimetres; poses leave the reader in metres.
  • cam_R_w2c / cam_t_w2c hold the camera pose in the world frame (camera to world), contrary to what the names say. The world frame is fixed to the rig, not to the table: bounds of a TableBoxWorkspace are world coordinates here.
  • scene_camera.json also has entries -4 to 0; they have no image and are ignored.
Derived assets and their cost

Built on three training scenes (5, 9 and 13; 11 object models, 49 instances) on the development machine while it was heavily loaded, so the times are upper bounds:

Asset Command (add --scenes 5,9,13 for the three scenes) Three scenes Whole train split, extrapolated Grasp-label store grasppanda prepare graspclutter6d --labels 2.8 GB about 55 GB (236 MB per object model, 62 MB per scene) Graspness, one camera ... --graspness --camera realsense-d435 2.2 MB, 3 min with 3 workers about 0.3 GB, 5 h with 4 workers Compact labels ... --compact-labels --config economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e 24 MB, 11 s about 3 GB, 25 min Tolerance ... --tolerance --config _base_/datasets/graspclutter6d_d435_tolerance.yaml 332 MB, 1 min with 4 workers about 4 GB, 10 min Per-view grasps, one camera ... --view-grasps --camera realsense-d435 --config _base_/datasets/graspclutter6d_d435_hggd.yaml 96 kB, 1 min with 3 workers about 15 MB, 1.5 h with 4 workers

The whole-split figures are extrapolations from the three scenes, not measurements. The label store is the large one; only training reads it. The evaluator keeps a cache of its own, extracted from dex_models/ and models_m/ on first use: about 7 MB per object model, 0.5 GB for the test objects.

Two facts measured on those scenes that matter for training:

  • Only 9.6 % of the annotated grasp points keep a collision-free grasp of friction ≤ 0.4 (10 401 of 108 094); on GraspNet-1Billion 39 % do. The scenes are far more cluttered, so compact labels supervise far fewer seeds per frame.
  • The per-view labels of HGGD come to 17 to 67 per frame (GraspNet-1Billion scene 0: 59), from 471 to 1 964 candidate grasps per scene.
Dataset configs for GraspClutter6D Config Data recipe carried over from Cloud Assets it reads for training _base_/datasets/graspclutter6d_d435_tolerance.yaml GraspNet-baseline, Scale-Balanced-Grasp 20 000 points, official workspace crop label store, tolerance _base_/datasets/graspclutter6d_{d415,d435,kinect,zivid}.yaml the graspness recipe of GSNet, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp 15 000 points, official workspace crop label store, graspness economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_gc6d-d435_10e.yaml (on the D435 base) EconomicGrasp 20 000 points, official workspace crop compact labels, graspness _base_/datasets/graspclutter6d_d435_hggd.yaml HGGD colour and depth images, 25 600 points, no crop per-view grasps

These carry the GraspNet-1Billion recipe of each method over and change only what the dataset fixes. None reproduces a published GraspClutter6D training recipe: none exists for the ported methods. HGGD's network image is 640 × 360, and the detector takes any sensor image that is an integer multiple of it: the D415, D435 (×3) and Azure Kinect (×6) images fit, the Zivid images (1920 × 1200) do not.

What differs between the two benchmarks

Measured values are medians over 20 test frames of GraspNet-1Billion (two frames of every ninth test scene, RealSense unless a camera is named) and over 104 test frames of GraspClutter6D (all 13 views of every third test_mini scene).

GraspNet-1Billion GraspClutter6D Scenes, frames 190 scenes × 256 frames per camera 648 scenes in the grasp splits × 13 views per camera Cameras realsense (D435), kinect (Azure Kinect), one directory each D415, D435, Azure Kinect, Zivid, interleaved by image id Image 1280 × 720 1920 × 1080, 3840 × 2160 (Kinect), 1920 × 1200 (Zivid) Intrinsics one calibration per camera per image; two calibrations for three of the cameras Raw depth unit 1 mm 1 mm (RealSense), 0.1 mm (Azure Kinect, Zivid); per image Camera to objects 0.44 m (0.31 to 0.52) 0.70 m (0.36 to 1.04) on the D435; the paper states 0.31 to 1.37 m over all cameras Size of a pixel on the objects 0.47 mm (RealSense), 0.74 mm (Kinect) 0.50 mm (D435), 0.47 (D415), 0.36 (Kinect), 0.26 (Zivid) Object ids 0 to 87; the segmentation stores id + 1 1 to 200; the segmentation stores the id Instances an object occurs once per scene repeated objects; instances from mask_visib Label files grasp_label/NNN_labels.npz, collision_label/scene_XXXX/collision_labels.npz grasp_label/obj_NNNNNN_labels.npz, collision_label/NNNNNN.npz Label grid 300 views × 12 angles × 4 depths the same Label widths gripper of 0.10 m up to 0.15 m; gripper of 0.14 m Object poses meta/*.mat or annotations/*.xml scene_gt.json (millimetres) Table frame cam0_wrt_table.npy, z up, origin on the table the rig's world frame; the table is not at z = 0 Reference workspace crop 3-D box around the ground-truth segmentation, 2 cm margin (SegmentationBoxWorkspace) image rectangle around the ground-truth segmentation, 10 % margin (SegmentationRectWorkspace) Cloud in that crop 554 000 points, 0.48 × 0.35 × 0.26 m, 39 % on objects 908 000 points, 0.91 × 0.57 × 0.81 m, 32 % on objects (D435) Splits train / seen / similar / novel train / test, disjoint objects Evaluator GraspNet1BEvaluator, protocol graspnet1b-sv-v1 GraspClutter6DEvaluator, protocol graspclutter6d-sv-v1 Ranks and frictions top 50; μ = 0.2, 0.4, …, 1.2 the same Width clip 0.10 m 0.14 m Foreground filter none grasps 5 cm or more from every object model are dropped before NMS Collision scene object models and a synthetic table object models only

Both reference crops are derived from the ground-truth segmentation, at test time too. Results on them are stamped gt_assisted: [workspace]. HGGD crops nothing.

The evaluators, checked against the official tools

The evaluator constants are those of the official tools (graspnetAPI 1.2.x and graspclutter6dAPI at ddb2ee7). For GraspNet-1Billion every stage equals graspnetAPI value for value on 1,592 recorded frames: six whole test scenes of a detector's dump, grasps drawn from the labels on both cameras and edge cases (tests/integration/test_eval_parity.py; two frames with tied scores have no single official result and are left out). For GraspClutter6D the equality is checked stage by stage on label-derived grasps for all four cameras and on the dumps that grasppanda test wrote for several detectors (tests/integration/test_eval_clutter_parity.py).

docs.title: Your camera and Python
docs.text:
Goal: get grasps from a trained detector on frames of your own camera: on the command line, from Python, or in a browser page.

You need: weights for one of the six methods. GraspPanda downloads no grasp checkpoint: you take the released file yourself, under its licence, and convert it once. Each method page walks through it, with the file, its licence and the command, then a first picture of the example scene: GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp, FineGrasp, HGGD. Weights you trained yourself work the same way (Train and test).

docs.title: Your own camera
docs.text:
1. A depth image: single-channel, 16-bit PNG or TIFF, or a .npy. An integer image is read as millimetres, a float image as metres; --depth-scale N says otherwise (N depth units per metre).
  2. The intrinsics of the depth camera in pixels, for the resolution the image has: --intrinsics fx,fy,cx,cy, or a file with those four numbers or the 3 × 3 matrix.
  3. A crop of the workspace (see below), and for HGGD the colour image registered to the depth image pixel for pixel (--rgb).

Then run grasppanda demo with the config of your weights:

GraspNet-baselineGSNetScale-Balanced-GraspEconomicGraspFineGraspHGGD 
grasppanda demo graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --weights baseline_realsense.pth --collision-filter \
    --depth camera/depth.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360 \
    --workspace -0.25 -0.2 0.35 0.25 0.2 0.8

grasppanda demo gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --weights gsnet_realsense.pth --collision-filter \
    --depth camera/depth.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360 \
    --workspace -0.25 -0.2 0.35 0.25 0.2 0.8

Needs the sparse-convolution extra (Install).

grasppanda demo scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --weights sbg_realsense.pth --collision-filter \
    --depth camera/depth.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360 \
    --workspace -0.25 -0.2 0.35 0.25 0.2 0.8

grasppanda demo economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --weights economicgrasp_realsense.pth --collision-filter \
    --depth camera/depth.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360 \
    --workspace -0.25 -0.2 0.35 0.25 0.2 0.8

Needs the sparse-convolution extra (Install).

grasppanda demo finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --weights finegrasp_realsense.pth --collision-filter \
    --depth camera/depth.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360 \
    --workspace -0.25 -0.2 0.35 0.25 0.2 0.8

Needs the sparse-convolution extra. FineGrasp also computes the surface normal of every point from the depth image.

grasppanda demo hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e \
    --weights hggd_realsense.pth --collision-filter \
    --depth camera/depth.png --rgb camera/rgb.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360

HGGD reads the whole image and crops nothing. Its image must be a multiple of its 640 × 360 network input, with the same aspect ratio.

It prints the pipeline, the cloud, how many grasps were predicted and how many the collision filter kept, and the best ten. It writes grasps.npy ((G, 17), GraspNet layout, best first, camera frame, metres), a picture and an animation into work_dirs/<config name>/demo/. Add --out DIR to choose the folder, --show for an interactive window (pip install -e ".[vis]").

What it prints (GraspNet-baseline, on the example scene saved as files)

The files under camera/ are the example scene that --example writes to disk; they stand in for a camera so that the command can be shown with its output.

  input     camera/depth.png: 1280 x 720 uint16, read as millimetres
  cloud     20,000 points to the model, sampled from 445,990 in the workspace
  grasps    942 predicted in 3.51 s (first call, includes warm-up); 240 left after ModelFreeCollisionFilter

docs.title: The workspace matters
docs.text:
GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp were trained and tested on clouds cropped to the objects: their GraspNet-1Billion pipelines crop to a box around the ground-truth segmentation, at test time too (which is why their results are stamped gt_assisted: [workspace]). HGGD crops nothing. Your camera has no ground truth. The inferencer does what the input allows and says what it did:

You pass What happens --workspace XMIN YMIN ZMIN XMAX YMAX ZMAX only points inside this box of the camera frame are kept (metres; x right, y down, z forward) --mask FILE (object pixels non-zero, from any segmentation) and --table-from-camera FILE the config's own crop runs, with your mask in the place of the dataset's segmentation --mask FILE alone the same kind of crop with the box aligned to the camera axes instead of the table; a note says so nothing every pixel with depth is used, and a note says what that means The note printed when nothing restricts the input 
  note      The test pipeline of this config crops the cloud with SegmentationBoxWorkspace, which reads a ground-truth segmentation; the weights were trained and tested on clouds cropped that way. No mask was given, so every pixel with depth is used. Expect grasps on the surroundings too and fewer points on the objects; pass mask=... (object pixels) or workspace=... (a box in the camera frame) to restrict the input.
  cloud     20,000 points to the model, sampled from 699,022 in the workspace
Troubleshooting: the usual mistakes, verbatim

Each ends with exit code 1 and one line that says what to change.

$ grasppanda demo ... --depth camera/depth.png
✗ InputError: --depth needs --intrinsics fx,fy,cx,cy: the focal lengths and the principal point of the depth camera in pixels. Without them a depth image cannot become a point cloud. Your camera's SDK reports them (RealSense: rs-enumerate-devices -c).

$ grasppanda demo ... --depth camera/depth.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360 --depth-scale 1
✗ InputError: the depth image (median value 545, depth_scale=1) has a median range of 545 m. The values are probably millimetres: pass depth_scale=1000 (--depth-scale 1000).

$ grasppanda demo ... --depth camera/depth.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360 --workspace -0.2 -0.2 1.5 0.2 0.2 2.0
✗ InputError: the workspace is empty: no pixel with depth lies inside it (CameraBoxWorkspace). The cloud spans x -0.45 to 0.45, y -0.19 to 0.16, z 0.42 to 0.84 metres in the camera frame (x right, y down, z forward).

$ grasppanda demo hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e --weights hggd_realsense.pth --depth camera/depth.png --intrinsics 925,925,640,360
✗ InputError: HGGD reads the colour image; pass the colour image registered to the depth image: rgb=... (--rgb FILE)

Intrinsics of another resolution, a colour image of another size than the depth image, a colour-mapped picture of depth instead of a depth image, and a cloud in millimetres are refused in the same way.

Point clouds and dataset frames

--points cloud.npy|.ply|.pcd takes a cloud in the camera frame, in metres, that you have already cropped to the workspace. The image-space steps of the pipeline do not apply to it; sampling and input features do. A method that reads images refuses it and lists what it needs instead.

--frame graspnet1b:scene_0100/realsense/0000 reads a frame of the dataset the config names, through the config's own dataset reader. With the GSNet config (its recipe samples 15 000 points):

  input     dataset frame graspnet1b:scene_0100/realsense/0000, read by the config's dataset reader
  cloud     15,000 points to the model, sampled from 519,612 in the workspace; ground-truth-assisted inputs: workspace
  grasps    1024 predicted in 2.58 s (first call, includes warm-up); 816 left after ModelFreeCollisionFilter

The grasps are those grasppanda test dumps for that frame (tests/integration/test_inference_api.py): for GraspNet-baseline, GSNet, Scale-Balanced-Grasp and EconomicGrasp the arrays are bit-identical to the engine's dump on all eight frames compared, raw and collision-filtered, and the same holds for GSNet on GraspClutter6D frames. FineGrasp is not in that test. HGGD draws random numbers while it predicts (it jitters its regions): a test run seeds once and draws frame after frame, a call here seeds per call. HGGD therefore reproduces the first frame of a run (within 1e-5) and gives another, equally valid, draw for later frames.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
from grasppanda import GraspInferencer

inferencer = GraspInferencer("<method config>", "<weights>.pth")
depth = np.array(Image.open("camera/depth.png"))  # (720, 1280) uint16, millimetres
grasps = inferencer(
    depth=depth, intrinsics=(925.0, 925.0, 640.0, 360.0), depth_scale=1000.0,
    workspace=(-0.25, -0.2, 0.35, 0.25, 0.2, 0.8), collision_filter=True,
)
best = grasps.sort_by_score()[0]

The config and weights are those of the commands above (HGGD also takes rgb=). The call takes exactly one kind of input: depth= with intrinsics= (and rgb=, mask=, depth_scale=, table_from_camera=, workspace=), or points=, or frame=. It returns a GraspGroup in the camera frame, in metres.

The fields of a grasp, and an example output Field Meaning translation (G, 3) the grasp point between the fingers, metres rotation (G, 3, 3) column 0 the approach direction, column 1 the closing direction, column 2 the finger-height direction width (G,) jaw opening, metres depth (G,) how far the fingers reach past the grasp point along the approach, metres score (G,) higher is better; score_kind says what it is. It is not a calibrated probability frame camera: the optical frame of the depth sensor, x right, y down, z forward

to_graspnet_array() gives the 17 columns other GraspNet tools read: [score, width, height, depth, R (9, row-major), t (3), object_id]. To move the grasps into your robot's base frame, apply your hand-eye calibration as a 4 × 4 tensor: grasps.transform(base_from_camera, frame="base").

With the GraspNet-baseline config and baseline_realsense.pth, on the files above:

print(len(grasps), "grasps in frame", repr(grasps.frame), "score:", grasps.score_kind)
print("grasp point   ", best.translation[0].tolist())
print("approach axis ", best.rotation[0, :, 0].tolist())
print("width, depth  ", float(best.width), float(best.depth))

240 grasps in frame 'camera' score: predicted_quality_x_tolerance
grasp point    [-0.23671351373195648, -0.01879783719778061, 0.6439999938011169]
approach axis  [0.022774772718548775, 0.4925254285335541, 0.8700000047683716]
width, depth   0.10000000149011612 0.009999999776482582
Things worth knowing
  • Order. Grasps come in the order the detector emits them. Use sort_by_score().
  • Repeatable. Point sampling and the detector's random draws are seeded per call, from the config (data.<split>.dataset.seed, runtime.seed), so the same input gives the same grasps. seed= changes both.
  • Post-processing. collision_filter=True applies the config's variant that holds a collision filter (cd in the shipped configs); variant="name" applies any chain of evaluation.variants. The filter tests the gripper against the observed points only; it knows nothing about what the camera did not see.
  • Two halves. inferencer.observe(...) returns the Observation the model reads (the sampled cloud, the cloud before sampling, the images), inferencer.predict(observation) the grasps. Use them to look at what the pipeline did to your input.
  • Warnings. Differences from the conditions of the test pipeline (no mask where the pipeline crops with one, a cloud that cannot be checked for a crop) are raised once per inferencer as InferenceWarning.

docs.title: Run in the browser
docs.text:
grasppanda explore --weights-dir ~/grasppanda_weights

grasppanda explore serves the combination explorer on your machine. Started with a folder of weights (every .pth, .pt, .tar and .ckpt under it), its Run tab runs a method in the page, with no code: pick the method, the weights file, the input (the example scene or your depth image with its intrinsics; HGGD also needs the colour image) and the collision filter, then press Run.

The page shows each step while it happens, then the picture grasppanda demo draws, the best ten grasps, the counts through the post-processing chain, two downloads (grasps.npy and the picture) and the terminal commands that do the same. A run that cannot go ahead says why in the words of grasppanda demo. --weights NAME=PATH names files one by one, and --device cpu runs on the CPU. On the documentation site the tab is disabled, since a run needs your weights on your computer.

With your own selection of slots

When you have changed slots in Build a combination, the panel also offers with your changes: the composed config runs, so the weights must fit the composed model. A change of post-processing or of the training recipe keeps the model; a new stage needs weights trained with it. A composed selection is built with pretrained: false, since the weights file supplies every parameter.

What the server allows, and nothing more
  • It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, answers requests addressed to a loopback name, and takes a run only from its own page (Host and Origin are checked; a run is JSON, which a page of another site cannot send without the server's consent).
  • It reads weights only from the files its command line named: under --weights-dir (resolved, so .. and links that leave the folder are refused) and each --weights NAME=PATH. The page picks one of those; a path it sends is never opened as it is.
  • An upload is limited to 20 MB and 4096 pixels a side, checked against the format its name claims, and decoded into a temporary directory that is removed when the run ends. A run writes nowhere else and downloads nothing. The only other file the server ever writes is a composed config you ask it to save, into the working directory.
  • One run at a time: a second request is answered with "another run is in progress".
  • A run predicts on one frame. Nothing is trained.
How long a run takes

On the development machine (one RTX A6000, shared), the first run after the server started took 7.9 s for GSNet on the example scene, most of it building the model, loading 176 MB of weights and the first CUDA calls; switching to HGGD took 2.3 s, and GraspNet-baseline on the example scene uploaded as depth.png with the workspace box above 1.0 s, with the same 942 predicted and 240 kept as the command. Running the same method again keeps its model in memory.

docs.title: What is not claimed
docs.text: The weights were trained on GraspNet-1Billion: two cameras, 1280 × 720, objects on a table 0.4 to 0.7 m away. Nothing here has been measured on another camera, another resolution or a real robot. Treat grasps on your own data as predictions of a model outside its test conditions until you have checked them on your setup.

docs.title: Train and test
docs.text:
Goal: train one of the six methods on GraspNet-1Billion, score it on the benchmark, and resume or reuse a run.

grasppanda train, grasppanda test and grasppanda infer take a config and nothing else. Every setting lives in the config; the few flags are shorthand for overrides and are recorded with the run like any other override.

You need: the dataset and the assets of your method (Datasets), a GPU, and for GSNet, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp the sparse-convolution extra (Install). Step 1 needs none of these.

docs.title: 1. Check the engine on a CPU (optional)
docs.text:
The example project trains a toy detector on synthetic scenes. It goes through every step a real method goes through:

CFG=projects/example_project/configs/toy_train.yaml
grasppanda train $CFG --opts runtime.run_id=demo
grasppanda test  $CFG --weights work_dirs/toy_train/demo/checkpoints/best.pth
Expected output of train 
ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ  GraspPanda 0.1.0  ·  6-DoF grasp detection in clutter

  config      projects/example_project/configs/toy_train.yaml  (hash be81c4b1301a)
  run         work_dirs/toy_train/demo
  device      cpu · 1 process · seed 0 · deterministic off
  model       ToyDetector · 7,601 parameters (7,601 trainable)
  data        32 frames · 8 batches of 4 per epoch
  schedule    5 epochs · Adam(lr=0.005, weight_decay=0.0) · ExponentialLR(gamma=0.95) per epoch
  evaluation  data.val every 1 epoch(s) · variants raw, centre · best by raw/AP
  hooks       EvaluationHook, CheckpointHook, TextLoggerHook
epoch 1/5  iter 4/8  loss 3.9746  loss/score 3.8631  loss/width 0.1115  cell_accuracy 0.0410  lr 5.000e-03  data 0.001s  iter 0.012s  eta 0:00:00
...
evaluation after epoch 1 (8 frames, 0.1 s)

variant  frames  AP     AP_tight
───────  ──────  ─────  ────────
raw      8/8     1.31   0.68

best checkpoint: raw/AP = 1.3054 at epoch 1

The commands exit with 0 on success, 2 when the config is invalid (nothing was started) and 1 when the run failed, with a one-paragraph reason on stderr.

docs.title: 2. Train a method
docs.text:
Each method trains from its shipped config, with the recipe of its authors:

GraspNet-baselineGSNetScale-Balanced-GraspEconomicGraspFineGraspHGGD 
grasppanda train graspnet_baseline/graspnet-baseline_pointnet2_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --opts runtime.run_id=first

grasppanda train gsnet/gsnet_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --opts runtime.run_id=first

grasppanda train scale_balanced_grasp/sbg_pointnet2-transformer_g1b-realsense_18e \
    --opts runtime.run_id=first

grasppanda train economicgrasp/economicgrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --opts runtime.run_id=first

grasppanda train finegrasp/finegrasp_sunet14_g1b-realsense_10e \
    --opts runtime.run_id=first

grasppanda train hggd/hggd_r34w8_g1b-realsense_15e \
    --opts runtime.run_id=first

The run lives in work_dirs/<config name>/first/. Every epoch is scored on the validation scenes (val_dev, held out from the training scenes) and checkpointed as checkpoints/epoch_NNNN.pth; the last part of the config name is the number of epochs. The recipe of each method is on its method page.

docs.title: 3. Test it
docs.text:
grasppanda test <method config> \
    --weights work_dirs/<config name>/first/checkpoints/epoch_NNNN.pth

It scores the test split (test: seen, similar and novel) once per post-processing variant of the config, raw and cd (with the collision filter) in the shipped configs. It writes one result record per variant into results/ of its own run directory. Read a record with grasppanda analyze (Read an analysis).

docs.title: 4. Resume or reuse a run
docs.text:
grasppanda train <method config> --opts runtime.run_id=first --resume  # its newest checkpoint
grasppanda train <method config> --resume path/to/epoch_0004.pth       # a given checkpoint

A run continues in its own directory when the config hash is unchanged. runtime.load_from (--weights for test and infer) loads weights only, also to start a training from them; any mismatch of keys is an error unless runtime.allow_weight_mismatch: true.

docs.title: The run directory
docs.text:
Every invocation works in <runtime.work_dir>/<run id>/. The run id is runtime.run_id, or the start time (20261012-101500, with -test or -infer appended for those commands) when it is not set.

work_dirs/toy_train/demo/
├── config.resolved.yaml      the config with every default written out
├── config.sources/           the files it was merged from, and overrides.txt
├── run.json  git.json  env.json  code.tar.gz  diff.patch
├── log.txt
├── checkpoints/              epoch_0001.pth … (and best.pth with evaluation.save_best)
├── predictions/<variant>/    scene_0100/<camera>/0000.npy, GraspNet (G, 17) arrays
├── results/                  <variant>.json (test) · epoch_0005/<variant>.json (training)
└── resumes/<time>/           the snapshot of each later invocation that resumed this run

One directory is one run. A fresh train, and every test and infer, refuses to write into a directory that already holds a run.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
What the config controls Key Meaning data.train / val / test {dataset, batch_size, num_workers, shuffle, drop_last}. batch_size is per process. Training shuffles unless shuffle: false; prediction never shuffles. optimizer, scheduler Any torch.optim optimizer and scheduler, {type: ..., ...}. train.epochs Length of the run. train.amp Mixed precision for the training forward pass. Prediction always runs in full precision. The config check refuses it unless the detector class declares amp_ready = True; none of the shipped detectors does yet. train.accumulate Batches whose gradients are summed before one optimizer step. train.grad_clip, train.grad_clip_mode Limit and norm (global L2 norm) or value (element-wise clamp). train.ema Decay of the moving average of the weights; null turns it off. train.sync_bn Synchronised batch norm across processes (CUDA only). train.scheduler_unit epoch (default) or iteration: when the scheduler steps. evaluation.interval Evaluate on data.val every N epochs and after the last one; 0 turns it off. evaluation.evaluator The scorer. evaluation.variants Named post-processing chains, each scored separately. evaluation.save_best <variant>/<metric> that selects best.pth; higher is better. evaluation.split The data section test and infer read (default test). evaluation.weights model or ema: which weights are scored. evaluation.num_workers Worker processes of the evaluator. runtime.work_dir, runtime.run_id Where the run lives. Neither enters the config hash. runtime.device auto, cpu, cuda, cuda:N. runtime.seed, runtime.deterministic See Reproducibility below. runtime.resume, runtime.allow_config_mismatch See Checkpoints and resuming below. runtime.load_from, runtime.allow_weight_mismatch See Loading weights below. runtime.checkpoint {interval, keep_last}. runtime.log {interval, backends} with backends text, tensorboard, wandb. hooks Extra hooks; see Hooks below. The training loop

The loop is one method, Trainer.train, 36 lines long. Per batch:

  1. losses = model.loss(observation, supervision), under autocast when train.amp is on.

  2. Entries whose key starts with loss/ are summed. Everything else is a metric: it is logged, never summed. If the sum is NaN or infinite the run stops and names the term, the iteration and the frames of the batch:

    ✗ NonFiniteLossError: non-finite loss at epoch 1, iteration 3: loss/aux = nan.
  Frames in the batch: tiny/scene_0000/cam/0002, tiny/scene_0000/cam/0005

  3. total / train.accumulate is back-propagated.

  4. Every train.accumulate batches, and on the last batch of an epoch, the gradients are clipped and applied, the weight average is updated, and the scheduler steps when train.scheduler_unit is iteration. A tail group smaller than accumulate therefore takes a smaller step; with a scheduler per iteration, "iteration" means optimizer step.

After the last batch the scheduler steps when its unit is epoch.

Schedulers that need the length of the run. OneCycleLR (total_steps), CosineAnnealingLR (T_max) and PolynomialLR (total_iters) are given the number of scheduler steps of the run, so the config does not repeat what train.epochs and the dataset size already say:

scheduler: {type: OneCycleLR, max_lr: 1e-3}     # no total_steps
train: {epochs: 10, scheduler_unit: iteration}

A value written in the config is kept. ReduceLROnPlateau and schedulers that take Python functions or other schedulers are rejected with an explanation.

Parameter groups and several optimizers. By default one optimizer covers every trainable parameter. A detector that needs more defines configure_optimizers, which receives the optimizer node of the config:

def configure_optimizers(self, optimizer: dict):
    return [
        {"params": self.backbone.parameters(), "lr": optimizer["lr"] * 0.1},
        {"params": self.head.parameters()},
    ]
    # or several optimizers: {"backbone": self.backbone.parameters(), "head": ...}

Return parameter groups for one optimizer, or a mapping name -> parameters | optimizer for several. Every optimizer steps on the same total loss and gets its own scheduler.

Hooks

Whatever is not the arithmetic of a step is a hook. Three are added by default from the config: a logger per runtime.log.backends entry, in-training evaluation (when data.val, evaluation.evaluator and evaluation.interval > 0 are set) and checkpointing. Others are listed under hooks:

hooks:
  - {type: BNMomentumHook, initial: 0.5, decay: 0.5, step: 2, minimum: 0.001}
  - {type: StageTimerHook, sync: true}
Hook Does TextLoggerHook One line every runtime.log.interval iterations and on the last batch of an epoch, to the console and log.txt: running means of every loss term and metric, learning rate, gradient norm (when clipping by norm), data and iteration time, peak GPU memory, ETA. TensorBoardLoggerHook, WandbLoggerHook The same scalars to TensorBoard (<run>/tensorboard) or Weights & Biases. Optional: pip install -e ".[tensorboard]" or ".[wandb]". A missing package fails before training starts. EvaluationHook Scores data.val; see Evaluation below. CheckpointHook epoch_NNNN.pth every interval epochs and after the last one, the newest keep_last kept, best.pth by evaluation.save_best. BNMomentumHook Sets the momentum of every batch-norm layer to max(initial * decay ** (epoch // step), minimum) before each epoch. StageTimerHook Seconds per iteration spent in the forward pass of each stage (child module) of the detector, as forward.<stage> in the log. With sync: true it waits for the GPU around every stage, which makes the numbers honest and the training slower.

A hook listed under hooks replaces the default of the same class. Hooks run in priority order (evaluation 70, checkpointing 80, loggers 90, everything else 50), so a checkpoint always knows the metrics of its epoch. To write one, subclass grasppanda.engine.hooks.Hook, annotate the constructor parameters, register it with @HOOKS.register() and load the module through custom_imports:

@HOOKS.register()
class FreezeBackbone(Hook):
    def __init__(self, epochs: int = 1) -> None:
        self.epochs = epochs

    def before_epoch(self, state) -> None:          # state.epoch: index of the epoch to run
        state.model.backbone.requires_grad_(state.epoch >= self.epochs)

state is a TrainState: model, optimizers, schedulers, epoch and iteration counters, the outputs of the last iteration, the latest evaluation metrics, the run directory.

Checkpoints and resuming

A checkpoint holds the model, optimizer(s), scheduler(s), gradient scaler, weight average, the random-number states of every process, epoch, iteration, best metric, config hash and package version. It is written to a temporary file and renamed, so an interrupted job never leaves a truncated file, and it contains only tensors and plain values: files are read with weights_only=True and loading never executes pickled code.

The run continues in the directory that owns the checkpoint when it is the same run: the checkpoint was written under the current config hash, and runtime.work_dir (and runtime.run_id, when set) point at that directory. The new invocation's snapshot is kept beside the original one, in resumes/<time>/.

Otherwise the resumed run starts a new directory below runtime.work_dir and writes nothing into the checkpoint's directory: a checkpoint resumed with another --work-dir or runtime.run_id, a checkpoint file outside a run directory, and a config continued with runtime.allow_config_mismatch=true. Its run.json records resumed_from, and the log says why:

resuming work_dirs/toy/one/checkpoints/epoch_0002.pth in a new run directory, because
runtime.work_dir and runtime.run_id ask for elsewhere; the run that owns the checkpoint,
work_dirs/toy/one, is left as it is

The new directory starts with the best metric stored in the checkpoint, so its best.pth appears when one of its own epochs beats that value; the earlier best stays in the original run. A checkpoint written under a different config hash is refused before anything is written:

✗ ResumeError: …/epoch_0001.pth was written under config hash f77ba11a0ed6, but the current
  config hashes to 590caa0a40d9: this is a different experiment. Resume with the original
  config (config.resolved.yaml in the run directory), or set
  runtime.allow_config_mismatch=true to continue it as a new run.

runtime.work_dir, runtime.run_id, runtime.resume and runtime.allow_config_mismatch are not part of the hash. Anything else is, including train.epochs: training longer than planned needs runtime.allow_config_mismatch=true, and the longer run lives in a directory of its own.

Loading weights

runtime.load_from (--weights for test and infer) loads weights and nothing else. The key report is always printed, and any difference is an error unless runtime.allow_weight_mismatch: true; there is no silent non-strict load.

✗ WeightMismatchError: weights from w.pth: 1 matched, 0 missing, 5 unexpected, 3 with a different shape
  unexpected (in the file, not in the model):
    encoder.1.weight
    encoder.1.running_mean
    ...
  different shape:
    encoder.0.weight: file (8, 3), model (16, 3)
    head.weight: file (1, 8), model (1, 16)
    ...
Nothing was loaded. Fix the model config or the file, or set
runtime.allow_weight_mismatch=true to load the keys that match.

Accepted layouts: a GraspPanda checkpoint, a bare state dict, or a mapping with a state_dict / model_state_dict entry; a uniform module. prefix is stripped. Each of these is stated in the report. Files that pickle other objects must be converted first; the released checkpoints of the six methods are converted by tools/convert_checkpoint.py (each method page has the command).

Evaluation, result records and partial results

In-training evaluation and grasppanda test run the same routine:

  1. model.predict runs over the split. The raw predictions are written once, to predictions/raw/. An empty prediction is a valid result and is written too.
  2. For every entry of evaluation.variants with a non-empty chain, the chain is applied to each frame's raw grasps, with the observation of that frame, and the result is written to predictions/<variant>/. A variant with an empty chain is the raw predictions. The name raw is reserved for it.
  3. The evaluator scores each variant against every key of the split, so a frame without a prediction is reported as missing rather than skipped.
  4. One result record per variant is written, and metrics are reported as <variant>/<metric>.
evaluation:
  evaluator: {type: ToyEvaluator}
  variants:
    raw: []
    centre: [{type: ToyCentreFilter, radius: 0.15}]
  save_best: raw/AP

results/<variant>.json holds what was measured and under which conditions: protocol, dataset, split, cameras, requested / scored / coverage / missing, postprocessing (the chain with every parameter), gt_assisted, evaluator (class, config and the info it reported), config_hash, code (commit, dirty flag, version), weights (path, sha256, model or ema, epoch, the config hash they were trained under), seed, metrics and per_scene. Per-scene numbers are the mean of the evaluator's per-frame precision tables, overall and per column, as fractions in [0, 1]. gt_assisted lists the inference inputs that were derived from ground truth, collected from observation.gt_assisted() over all frames.

When not every requested frame was scored, the record is still written, but with "partial": true, "metrics": null and the aggregates under "partial_metrics", so nothing that reads metrics can mistake them for a headline number. The console prints coverage and per-scene numbers only:

variant  frames  AP
───────  ──────  ──────────────────
raw      6/6     1.00
best1    5/6     withheld (partial)
best1: PARTIAL, 5 of 6 frames scored (83.3 %), 1 missing. Per-scene mean precision only:
  cam/scene_0020  frames 5  0.5000

A partial variant contributes no <variant>/<metric> and never becomes the best checkpoint.

grasppanda test <config> --weights <checkpoint> [--split val] [--work-dir DIR] [--opts ...]: --weights is runtime.load_from, --split is evaluation.split (a data section: train, val or test). Which frames a section holds is the dataset's business: --opts data.test.dataset.<parameter>=.... To score the averaged weights of a run trained with train.ema, set evaluation.weights=ema.

grasppanda infer: predictions without a score 
grasppanda infer <config> --weights <checkpoint> --input <split|dir> --output <dir>

Predicts and writes, scores nothing and needs no evaluator. --output DIR makes DIR the run directory (runtime.work_dir and runtime.run_id), so the grasps land in DIR/predictions/<variant>/ next to the snapshot that says how they were made. --input is a data section, or a directory that is handed to the reader of data.<evaluation.split> as its root (data.<split>.dataset.root=DIR).

Grasps are written as GraspNet (G, 17) arrays; a native .npz format does not exist yet. Reading a plain folder of RGB-D frames needs a dataset reader with a root parameter, and none is shipped yet. infer checks the directory before anything runs (the reader must have root and read the first frame) and otherwise stops with what to do instead:

✗ InputError: --input mydata: the reader of data.test, GraspNet1B, reads a directory as
  the root of a GraspNet-1Billion tree and cannot read this one: [Errno 2] No such file or
  directory: 'mydata/scenes/scene_0100/realsense/meta/0000.mat'. No reader for a plain
  folder of frames (depth images and intrinsics) is shipped yet. For frames of your own
  camera, run `grasppanda demo <config> --weights <file> --depth FILE --intrinsics
  fx,fy,cx,cy` on one frame, or loop over your files in Python with GraspInferencer ...

For frames of your own camera: Your own camera and From Python.

Distributed training 
torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 -m grasppanda.cli.main train <config>
torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 -m grasppanda.cli.main test  <config> --weights <checkpoint>

Nothing in the config says "distributed": the processes read their rank from the environment torchrun sets. Then

  • every process builds the model from the same seed and draws its own random numbers afterwards (runtime.seed + rank);
  • the training set is one common shuffle dealt out to the processes; batch_size is per process;
  • train.sync_bn: true converts batch norm to its synchronised form (on CUDA; with several CPU processes it is an error, because PyTorch has no such layer for the CPU);
  • for evaluation each process predicts a disjoint share of the frames (no padding), the keys are merged and de-duplicated by SampleKey, and the main process scores;
  • only the main process writes files and prints; a checkpoint stores the random state of every process.

What has been exercised: two CPU processes with the gloo backend, in the unit suite (training, in-training evaluation, test, identical weights on both processes) and, by hand, an exact resume. Also by hand: the wrapper, synchronised batch norm and mixed precision on one GPU in a one-process NCCL group. Not tested: several GPUs. The development machine has one. While the main process scores an evaluation the others wait in a collective; its timeout is raised to 24 hours for that reason, which has not been observed under NCCL. DistributedDataParallel runs with its defaults: a detector with parameters that receive no gradient in some iterations needs find_unused_parameters, which is not exposed yet.

Reproducibility
  • runtime.seed seeds Python, NumPy and PyTorch. The order of an epoch depends on the seed and the epoch only, and the seeds of data-loader workers on seed, rank and epoch, so neither depends on how many epochs ran in this process.
  • Prediction runs under its own seed (runtime.seed + rank) and puts the random state back afterwards. Evaluating during training therefore does not change what is trained, and the same weights give the same predictions in training and in grasppanda test (same seed, batch size and number of processes), even when the data pipeline or the detector draws random numbers at inference time.
  • runtime.deterministic: true selects deterministic kernels where PyTorch has them and warns where it has none. It costs speed.
  • With deterministic: true, training N epochs and training N/2, stopping and resuming give bit-identical weights. This is a unit test on CPU (with dropout, augmentation noise, batch norm, Adam, a one-cycle schedule, the weight average, clipping and accumulation all on, with and without worker processes) and was checked once by hand on a GPU with mixed precision. It is a property of this engine with those toy components; a detector that uses an operator without a deterministic implementation (the sparse convolutions of GSNet, EconomicGrasp and FineGrasp, for example) will not have it.
From Python 
from grasppanda.config import Config
from grasppanda.engine import commands

config = Config.load("projects/example_project/configs/toy_train.yaml", ["train.epochs=2"],
                     command="train")
state = commands.train(config)            # state.run.dir, state.model, state.best

commands.test(config) returns an Evaluation (.records, .metrics, .partial) and commands.infer(config) a Dump (.root, .keys, .gt_assisted). To validate a config without running it: grasppanda print-config <config> --for train --check.
